A USB barcode scanner is an input peripheral: it types each product code into the till software as if it were a keyboard.

docs.title: 1.2 Types of Compute: CPU, GPU, TPU, NPU, MCU and the xPU Family
docs.text:
Not every processor is a CPU. Engineers build different kinds of compute chips for different jobs: all-rounders (CPUs), massively parallel number crunchers (GPUs), AI specialists (TPUs and NPUs), tiny low-power controllers (MCUs), rewireable chips (FPGAs) and single-purpose custom chips (ASICs). Most modern devices combine several of them, and this topic is your map of the whole family before later chapters zoom in.

The compute family tree. Moving down the tiers, chips become more specialised: less flexible, but faster and more energy-efficient at their own job.

Think of it like…

Think of a hospital: the general doctor (CPU) can handle anything, a team of nurses (GPU) does thousands of routine checks at once, the radiologist (TPU or NPU) only reads scans but does it brilliantly, and the door sensor (MCU) does one tiny job all day on almost no energy.

Real-world example

Priya's photo app shows the whole family at work. The phone's CPU runs the app, the GPU draws the screen, the NPU recognises faces, and an MCU in the camera module controls autofocus. When she uploads the album, a data-centre CPU receives it, a DPU handles the network traffic, and GPUs or TPUs tag the pictures with AI.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Start from the job: is it general logic, huge parallel maths, AI, signal processing, networking or one fixed task?
  2. General, branch-heavy work goes to a CPU; the same sum on millions of numbers goes to a GPU or AI accelerator.
  3. Tiny, battery-powered or real-time control goes to a microcontroller (MCU).
  4. Fixed jobs made in huge volume justify an ASIC; jobs that change or ship in small volume suit an FPGA.
  5. A host CPU almost always stays in charge, handing work to accelerators over PCIe, NVLink or an on-chip bus.
  6. Compare chips using the right metric: IPC and GHz for CPUs, FLOPS and memory bandwidth for GPUs, TOPS per watt for NPUs, microamps per MHz for MCUs.

Who uses it

Everyone in computing meets this map: hardware buyers, cloud and AI engineers choosing instances, embedded developers choosing chips, and students facing the classic interview question "CPU vs GPU vs TPU?".

Key takeaway

Remember the flexibility-efficiency trade-off: CPU → GPU → FPGA → NPU/TPU → ASIC, each step more efficient at its job but less flexible.

Going deeper

  • The "xPU" names are mostly marketing shorthand, not formal standards: the same letters can mean different things (IPU is Graphcore's Intelligence Processing Unit and also Intel's Infrastructure Processing Unit), so always check who makes the chip.
  • Typical power budgets span nine orders of magnitude: a sleeping MCU draws microwatts, a phone SoC a few watts, a desktop CPU 65-250 W, and a 2026 data-centre AI GPU around 1,000 W or more.
  • Most chips today are heterogeneous: a laptop or phone SoC puts CPU cores, a GPU, an NPU, an ISP, a DSP, video engines and a security processor on one die, and the operating system sends each task to the best engine.
  • A typical AI server contains several types at once: two host CPUs, four to eight GPUs or accelerators, one or more DPUs/SmartNICs for networking, and a small baseboard management controller (BMC) chip for remote management.
  • Each type is programmed differently: CPUs with ordinary languages, GPUs with CUDA, ROCm or SYCL, NPUs and TPUs through AI frameworks and compilers (ONNX Runtime, XLA), MCUs in C or MicroPython, and FPGAs and ASICs with hardware description languages such as Verilog.
  • Economics decides between FPGA and ASIC: an ASIC can cost tens to hundreds of millions of dollars to design at leading-edge nodes but is cheap per unit, so it only pays off at high volume or for huge efficiency gains.
  • "Compute" in cloud price lists also means virtual machine families — general-purpose, compute-optimised, memory-optimised, GPU/accelerator instances — which map back to these chip types (see the cloud chapter).

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Mixing up the two TPUs: Tensor Processing Unit is Google's AI chip, while Trusted Platform Module is a security chip that stores keys — completely different things.
  • Thinking a GPU or NPU replaces the CPU: accelerators cannot boot or run the operating system on their own; a host CPU sends them work.
  • Comparing TOPS or FLOPS across vendors at face value: check the number format (FP16, FP8, INT8, FP4) and whether sparsity is included, or the comparison is meaningless.
  • Assuming a microcontroller is just a slow CPU: it is a whole computer on a chip, with its own flash, RAM and peripherals, designed for low power and real-time response.

Get-PnpDevice -Class ComputeAccelerator -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue   # NPUs show here on many AI PCs

lscpu | head -n 15
lspci | grep -iE 'vga|3d|display|processing|accelerator'
nvidia-smi -L        # only if an NVIDIA GPU and driver are installed

docs.title: Key chips, architectures, standards, tools & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example CPU — the general-purpose processorIntel, AMD, Arm-based designs (Apple, Qualcomm, AWS Graviton), RISC-V vendors · Processor · Current · Beginner A few to a few hundred powerful cores that run any program, excelling at branchy, sequential logic and running the operating system. A web server's CPU parses requests, checks passwords, queries a database and decides what each user sees. GPU — the parallel throughput processorNVIDIA, AMD, Intel, Apple, Arm (Mali), Qualcomm (Adreno) · Accelerator · Current · Beginner Thousands of simple cores running the same instruction on many data items, first for graphics, now also for AI and science. A game's GPU shades millions of pixels per frame; in a data centre the same kind of chip trains a language model. TPU — Tensor Processing UnitGoogle (in-house since 2015; Cloud TPU) · Accelerator · Current · Beginner Google's AI ASIC built around systolic arrays for matrix multiplication, sold only as a Google Cloud service and used in its own products. A start-up rents a Cloud TPU pod slice to train a translation model instead of buying GPUs. NPU — Neural Processing UnitQualcomm (Hexagon), Intel, AMD (XDNA), Apple (Neural Engine), MediaTek · Accelerator · Current · Beginner A small, power-efficient AI engine inside phone and laptop chips, rated in TOPS, for on-device features like blur, captions and assistants. Copilot+ PCs need an NPU of at least 40 TOPS so features like live captions run locally without draining the battery. MCU — microcontroller unitSTMicroelectronics (STM32), Microchip (AVR, PIC), Espressif (ESP32), Raspberry Pi (RP2350), NXP, Renesas · Processor · Current · Beginner A complete tiny computer on one chip — CPU core, flash, RAM and peripherals — running one dedicated program with very low power. An Arduino Uno's ATmega328P has 32 KB of flash and 2 KB of RAM at 16 MHz, enough to run a greenhouse watering controller. MPU — microprocessor / application processorBroadcom (Raspberry Pi), NXP i.MX, TI Sitara, Rockchip, MediaTek · Processor · Current · Intermediate A processor with a memory-management unit and external DRAM, powerful enough to run a full OS such as Linux or Android. A Raspberry Pi 5's quad-core Cortex-A76 chip runs Linux and a web browser; a small MCU could not. SoC — system on a chip (as a compute package)Apple, Qualcomm, MediaTek, Samsung, Google, Intel, AMD · Concept · Current · Beginner One chip combining several compute types — CPU, GPU, NPU, ISP, DSP, modem — plus memory controllers, so a device needs few other parts. A smartphone's whole computer is one SoC the size of a fingernail, drawing only a few watts. APU — accelerated processing unitAMD (term), also used in consoles · Processor · Current · Intermediate AMD's name for a chip with CPU cores and a capable GPU sharing the same memory, avoiding a separate graphics card. PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X use custom AMD APUs; Ryzen AI Max chips put a large GPU beside 16 CPU cores. DSP — digital signal processorTexas Instruments, Analog Devices, Cadence Tensilica, CEVA, Qualcomm Hexagon · Processor · Current · Intermediate A processor optimised for fast multiply-accumulate maths on streams of samples, used for audio, radio, sensors and motor control. Noise-cancelling earbuds use a DSP to calculate and play anti-noise thousands of times per second. FPGA — field-programmable gate arrayAMD (Xilinx), Altera, Lattice, Microchip · Accelerator · Current · Intermediate A chip of blank logic blocks and wiring that you configure into almost any digital circuit, and can reconfigure later. A stock-trading firm loads a custom FPGA design to decode market data in under a microsecond. ASIC — application-specific integrated circuitDesigned by anyone, made by foundries such as TSMC, Samsung, Intel Foundry · Accelerator · Current · Intermediate A chip designed for one fixed job: the fastest, most efficient option, but costly to design and impossible to change after manufacture. Bitcoin mining machines use SHA-256 ASICs that are thousands of times more efficient than GPUs at that single task. DPU / IPU — data or infrastructure processing unitNVIDIA (BlueField), AMD (Pensando), Intel (IPU), AWS (Nitro, similar idea) · Component · Current · Intermediate A network-card processor with its own cores that runs networking, storage and security tasks so host CPUs are free for customer work. A cloud provider's DPU encrypts traffic and runs the virtual switch, so customers get every CPU core they pay for. Other AI accelerators (LPU, IPU, wafer-scale)Groq, Graphcore (SoftBank), Cerebras, AWS Trainium/Inferentia, Microsoft Maia, Meta MTIA · Accelerator · Current · Intermediate Custom AI chips with their own names and designs, competing with GPUs on speed, cost or energy for training or inference. A chatbot company serves answers on Cerebras or Groq hardware because tokens stream out faster than on its GPUs. Coprocessor and host modelGeneral computer-architecture idea · Concept · Current · Beginner A coprocessor or accelerator does specialised work that a host CPU sends it, then hands results back; the CPU stays in charge. The CPU loads an AI model, copies data to the GPU over PCIe, launches the job, then collects the answer. BMC — baseboard management controllerASPEED (AST2600 and newer), OpenBMC project · Component · Current · Intermediate A small separate processor on a server motherboard that lets administrators power-cycle, monitor and repair the server remotely, even when it is off. An engineer in London reboots a frozen server in Frankfurt through its BMC web page without visiting the data centre. QPU — quantum processing unitIBM, Google, Quantinuum, IonQ, Rigetti · Processor · Emerging · Intermediate A processor built from qubits that solves certain problems in a completely different way; it is controlled by ordinary CPUs and is still experimental. A chemistry researcher sends a small molecule-simulation circuit from a laptop to a cloud QPU and gets back measurement statistics.

docs.title: 1.3 Specialised Compute Engines: ISPs, Media Engines, Modems, Security Processors and More
docs.text:
Besides the famous CPU and GPU, chips hide many smaller engines that each do one job very efficiently: turning camera data into photos, compressing video, running the mobile radio, guarding passwords and keys, or controlling machines in real time. Knowing they exist explains why a phone can record 4K video all day while a general-purpose processor alone would overheat.

Engines inside a smartphone SoC. One chip, many specialists: the CPU coordinates while each engine handles the job it was built for.

Think of it like…

A big restaurant kitchen has a head chef, but also a pastry station, a grill station and a dishwasher machine; each station is narrow but much faster at its own task than the head chef would be.

Real-world example

When Tomás joins a video call on his phone, the ISP cleans up the camera image, the NPU blurs his background, the video engine compresses the stream to AV1 or H.264, the modem sends it over 5G, and the security processor confirmed his face unlock beforehand. The CPU mostly coordinates, so the battery lasts the whole meeting.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Find a task that is common, repetitive and expensive on a CPU, such as video encoding or image processing.
  2. Designers build a fixed-function or narrowly programmable engine for it inside the SoC.
  3. The operating system or driver exposes it through an API, for example a video-encode API or a camera framework.
  4. Apps call the API; the engine does the work at a fraction of the CPU's energy.
  5. If the engine cannot handle a format or feature, software falls back to the CPU or GPU, more slowly.

Who uses it

Embedded, mobile and media engineers, industrial automation engineers and security engineers work with these engines daily; everyone else benefits from them unknowingly.

Key takeaway

When a device does something demanding for hours on a small battery — video, camera, radio, face unlock — a dedicated engine is almost certainly doing it, not the CPU.

Going deeper

  • Fixed-function engines are often 10-100 times more energy-efficient than running the same task in software on a CPU, because they skip instruction fetch and decode and keep data in local buffers.
  • Video engines support specific codecs and profiles: most 2026 chips decode H.264, HEVC, VP9 and AV1, and many also encode AV1; an older chip without AV1 encoding falls back to slow, power-hungry software encoding.
  • Security processors run their own firmware in isolation from the main OS: Apple's Secure Enclave, Google's Titan M2, Microsoft Pluton and discrete TPM chips store keys so even a compromised operating system cannot read them.
  • Modems (baseband processors) run a separate real-time operating system and certified radio firmware; Qualcomm dominates, while Apple introduced its own C1 modem in 2025.
  • Real-time processors such as Arm Cortex-R cores sit inside car ECUs, SSD controllers and hard drives, where a guaranteed response time matters more than raw speed.
  • Industrial PLCs are rugged computers that run control logic in a fixed scan cycle, programmed in IEC 61131-3 languages like ladder logic, and can run for decades.
  • Soft-core processors are CPU designs loaded into an FPGA's fabric (for example AMD MicroBlaze V and Altera Nios V, both RISC-V based), letting one FPGA hold both custom logic and a small CPU.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming every format is hardware accelerated: if your chip's video engine lacks a codec, encoding silently falls back to the CPU and battery life collapses.
  • Treating 'neuromorphic' or 'quantum' processors as drop-in faster CPUs: they solve narrow classes of problems with very different programming models.
  • Forgetting that hidden engines run firmware too: modems, BMCs and security processors need updates, and vulnerabilities in them are real security risks.

docs.title: Try it: Check which hardware video engines your computer offers
docs.text:
# Linux with Intel/AMD graphics (package: vainfo)
vainfo | grep -iE 'profile|entrypoint' | head -n 20

# NVIDIA GPU: list encoders and decoders FFmpeg can use
ffmpeg -hide_banner -encoders | grep -iE 'nvenc|qsv|amf|vaapi'

# macOS: hardware encoders are exposed through VideoToolbox
ffmpeg -hide_banner -encoders | grep -i videotoolbox

A phone's ISP merges several exposures into one HDR photo the instant the shutter is tapped. Video engine (hardware encoder / decoder)NVIDIA (NVENC/NVDEC), Intel (Quick Sync), AMD (VCN), Apple (Media Engine) · Component · Current · Intermediate A fixed-function block that compresses and decompresses video formats such as H.264, HEVC and AV1 using very little power. A streamer's GPU encodes a 1080p game stream with NVENC so the game itself keeps its frame rate. VCU — video coding unit (data-centre transcoder)Google (Argos VCU), NETINT and others · Accelerator · Current · Advanced A data-centre ASIC dedicated to transcoding video into many resolutions and formats far more efficiently than CPUs. A video platform converts each uploaded clip into eight resolutions on VCUs instead of hundreds of CPU cores. Modem / baseband processorQualcomm, MediaTek, Samsung, Apple (C1) · Component · Current · Intermediate The processor that runs the cellular radio protocols (4G, 5G), turning radio signals into data and back. When a phone moves between towers on a train, the modem handles the handover without dropping the call. Real-time processor (RPU)Arm (Cortex-R52, Cortex-R82), Infineon AURIX, TI · Processor · Current · Intermediate A processor designed for guaranteed, predictable response times rather than peak speed, often with lockstep cores for safety. A car's airbag controller must react within milliseconds every time, so it uses a lockstep real-time processor. PLC — programmable logic controllerSiemens (SIMATIC), Rockwell Automation (Allen-Bradley), Schneider Electric, Mitsubishi Electric · System · Current · Intermediate A rugged industrial computer that reads sensors and drives motors and valves in a fixed, repeating scan cycle. A bottling line's PLC starts the conveyor, counts bottles and stops the filler if a sensor reports a jam. Soft-core processorAMD (MicroBlaze V), Altera (Nios V), open RISC-V cores · Processor · Current · Advanced A CPU described in a hardware language and loaded into FPGA fabric, so you can add a processor exactly where you need one. A small team puts a RISC-V soft core in their FPGA to run the control menu beside custom video logic. LPU — language processing unitGroq · Accelerator · Current · Intermediate An inference chip that keeps model weights in on-chip SRAM and runs on a fixed, compiler-planned schedule for very fast token output. A voice assistant uses LPU-based cloud inference so spoken replies start with almost no delay. Wafer-scale engineCerebras · Accelerator · Current · Advanced A single AI processor made from almost a whole silicon wafer, with huge on-chip memory and hundreds of thousands of cores. A pharmaceutical lab trains a protein model on one wafer-scale system instead of wiring up dozens of GPU servers. Neuromorphic processorIntel (Loihi 2), IBM (NorthPole), SpiNNaker (University of Manchester) · Processor · Emerging · Advanced A brain-inspired chip that computes with spikes and local memory, aiming for ultra-low-power pattern recognition. A research drone uses a neuromorphic chip to react to motion while drawing only milliwatts. Always-on sensor hub / low-power islandApple (Always-On Processor), Qualcomm (Sensing Hub), Google, MediaTek · Component · Current · Intermediate A tiny low-power processor that stays awake while the main chip sleeps, listening for wake words, steps and gestures. A phone hears 'Hey, assistant' through its sensor hub and only then wakes the power-hungry CPU cores. Cryptocurrency mining ASICBitmain (Antminer), MicroBT (WhatsMiner), Canaan · Accelerator · Current · Beginner A chip that does nothing but repeated SHA-256 hashing for Bitcoin mining — the textbook example of extreme specialisation. A mining farm replaced GPUs with ASIC miners because GPUs could no longer cover the electricity cost on Bitcoin. Fixed-function vs programmable engineGeneral computer-architecture idea · Concept · Current · Beginner Fixed-function engines do one task in hardwired logic; programmable ones run software. Fixed is more efficient, programmable more adaptable. A phone's video encoder is fixed-function; its NPU is programmable, so it can run AI models invented after the phone shipped.

docs.title: 1.4 Binary, Hexadecimal and Units of Data
docs.text:
Computers store everything using only two symbols, 0 and 1, because an electronic switch is easy to make either off or on. One 0-or-1 is called a bit, and eight bits make a byte — enough for one letter of text. Long strings of bits are hard for humans to read, so programmers write them in hexadecimal (base 16), where one hex digit stands for exactly four bits.

One value, three notations

Binary Hexadecimal 0 (decimal) 0000 0 9 1001 9 10 1010 A 15 1111 F 16 0001 0000 10 200 1100 1000 C8 255 1111 1111 FF 65,535 1111 1111 1111 1111 FFFF

Each hex digit maps to exactly four bits, so converting is a lookup, not arithmetic.

Think of it like…

Binary is like a row of light switches where each switch is worth double the one to its right (1, 2, 4, 8 ...): the number is simply the total of the switches that are on.

Real-world example

Leo is styling a web page and sees the colour #FF8800. He splits it into three bytes: FF (255 red), 88 (136 green) and 00 (0 blue) — a bright orange. Later he buys a '1 TB' external drive and Windows shows only about 931 GB. Nothing is missing: the box counts 1,000,000,000,000 bytes, while Windows divides by 1024 × 1024 × 1024 (and labels the result 'GB' even though it really means GiB).

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Each position in a binary number is worth a power of 2: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 and so on.
  2. To turn binary into decimal, add up the place values of the 1s: 1011 = 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11.
  3. To turn decimal into binary, keep dividing by 2 and read the remainders from bottom to top.
  4. Group bits in fours from the right; each group becomes one hex digit (0-9, then A-F for 10-15).
  5. Measure sizes in bytes: decimal (SI) units step by 1000 (kB, MB, GB) and binary (IEC) units by 1024 (KiB, MiB, GiB).

Who uses it

Programmers, network engineers (IP and MAC addresses), security analysts (hex dumps) and web designers (colour codes) use binary and hex every day.

Key takeaway

Memorise the powers of two up to 2^16 = 65,536, plus 2^10 = 1024 and 2^32 ≈ 4.3 billion — they come up constantly.

Going deeper

  • n bits give 2^n distinct values: 8 bits give 256, 16 bits 65,536, 32 bits about 4.29 billion and 64 bits about 1.8 × 10^19 — limits that decide the size of counters, addresses and IDs.
  • Hex is written differently by context: 0x in C, Python and most languages, # in CSS colours, an h suffix in some assemblers, and %XX percent-encoding inside URLs.
  • Drive makers use decimal units (1 TB = 10^12 bytes) while Windows divides by powers of 1024 but keeps decimal labels; macOS has shown decimal units since 2009, so the same drive looks different on each.
  • Byte order shows up when reading binary files or packet captures: the 32-bit value 0x12345678 is stored as 78 56 34 12 on little-endian x86 but sent as 12 34 56 78 on the network.
  • Bit masks pack many yes/no flags into one integer: Unix permissions, CPU feature flags reported by CPUID and network header fields are all read with AND masks and shifts.
  • To convert quickly, memorise the 16 nibble patterns (0000-1111 ↔ 0-F); any binary number then converts to hex by grouping bits in fours from the right, and back again.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Mixing up b and B: 100 Mbit/s is 12.5 MB/s, not 100 MB/s — a small b means bits and a capital B means bytes.
  • Assuming a '1 TB' drive is faulty when Windows shows 931 GB: it is a units difference (10^12 bytes ÷ 2^30), not missing space.
  • Grouping bits from the left when converting to hex: always group in fours from the least significant (right) end, padding the leftmost group with zeros.

docs.title: Try it: Convert between number bases in Python
Key chips, architectures, standards, tools & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example BitTerm popularised by Claude Shannon (1948), credited to John Tukey · Concept · Current · Beginner Short for binary digit: the smallest unit of data, either 0 or 1. One bit is enough to record a yes/no fact, such as whether a light is switched on. ByteTerm coined by Werner Buchholz at IBM (1956); 8-bit byte standardised by IBM System/360 · Concept · Current · Beginner A group of 8 bits that can hold 256 different values (0-255); the basic unit for memory and file sizes. The capital letter 'A' is stored in one byte as 01000001. NibbleGeneral computing term · Concept · Current · Beginner Half a byte — 4 bits — which matches exactly one hexadecimal digit. The byte 0x3C is made of two nibbles: 3 (0011) and C (1100). Binary (base 2)Positional number system · Format · Current · Beginner Number system using only 0 and 1, where each place is worth twice the place to its right. 13 in decimal is 1101 in binary: 8 + 4 + 0 + 1. Hexadecimal (base 16)Positional number system · Format · Current · Beginner Number system using 0-9 and A-F; a compact shorthand for binary because each digit equals four bits. Memory addresses like 0x7FFE, MAC addresses like 3C:22:FB:1A:09:4D and web colours like #00FF00 are all written in hex. Octal (base 8)Positional number system · Format · Legacy · Beginner Number system using digits 0-7, each worth three bits; today mostly seen in Unix file permissions. chmod 755 gives the owner read-write-execute (7 = 111) and everyone else read-execute (5 = 101). Word size (32-bit vs 64-bit)Defined by each processor architecture · Concept · Current · Beginner The natural number of bits a processor handles in one go — 64 on almost all modern PCs, servers and phones. A 64-bit CPU adds two 64-bit numbers in one instruction and can address far more than the 4 GB limit of 32-bit systems. SI decimal prefixes (kB, MB, GB, TB)BIPM — International System of Units (SI) · Standard · Current · Beginner Powers of 1000: 1 kB = 1000 bytes, 1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes. Used for drive capacities and network speeds. A '2 TB' SSD holds 2,000,000,000,000 bytes, which Windows reports as roughly 1.82 'TB' (really TiB). IEC binary prefixes (KiB, MiB, GiB, TiB)IEC (introduced 1998; now in IEC 80000-13) · Standard · Current · Beginner Powers of 1024: 1 KiB = 1024 bytes, 1 MiB = 1,048,576 bytes; they remove confusion with decimal units. Linux's free -h reports memory in Gi units, so a 16 GB laptop shows something like 'Mem: 15Gi'. Bits vs bytes per secondGeneral convention (b = bit, B = byte) · Metric · Current · Beginner Network speeds are quoted in bits per second, file sizes in bytes; divide bits by 8 to get bytes. A 500 Mbit/s broadband line can download at most about 62.5 MB per second. Most / least significant bit (MSB / LSB)General computing term · Concept · Current · Beginner The MSB is the leftmost, highest-value bit; the LSB is the rightmost bit, worth 1. In 10000001 the MSB is worth 128 and the LSB is worth 1, so the value is 129. EndiannessTerm coined by Danny Cohen (1980) · Concept · Current · Intermediate The order in which a multi-byte number's bytes are stored: big-endian puts the most significant byte first, little-endian the least significant. x86 and most Arm systems are little-endian, while Internet protocols send numbers big-endian ('network byte order'). Bitwise operationsSupported by every CPU and most programming languages · Concept · Current · Intermediate AND, OR, XOR, NOT and shifts applied to every bit of a number at once; fast tricks for flags and masks. x & 1 tells you whether x is odd, and x << 3 multiplies x by 8. Hex dump (xxd, hexdump, Format-Hex)xxd (ships with Vim); util-linux/BSD hexdump; PowerShell Format-Hex · Tool · Current · Beginner Tools that print a file's raw bytes in hexadecimal beside their ASCII characters, for inspecting binary formats and text encodings. xxd photo.png | head -1 starts with 8950 4e47 — the PNG signature bytes 0x89 'P' 'N' 'G' at the very beginning of the file. Binary-coded decimal (BCD)IBM mainframes; legacy x86 instructions; real-time clock chips · Format · Legacy · Intermediate Stores each decimal digit in its own 4-bit nibble, making decimal display and exact decimal arithmetic easy at the cost of space. A real-time clock chip stores 59 seconds as 0101 1001 (0x59), so firmware can display the digits without any division.

docs.title: 1.5 Whole Numbers: Integers, Two's Complement and Overflow
docs.text:
Computers store whole numbers (integers) in a fixed number of bits, such as 8, 32 or 64. Unsigned integers count upwards from zero; to include negative numbers almost every computer uses a trick called two's complement, where the top bit means 'minus a big amount'. Because the box has a fixed size, a number that grows too big wraps around — this is called overflow.

The same 8 bits read two ways

As unsigned As two's complement 00000000 0 0 00000101 5 5 01111111 127 127 (int8 max) 10000000 128 −128 (int8 min) 11111011 251 −5 11111111 255 (uint8 max) −1

The bit patterns are identical; the meaning changes only once the top bit is 1.

Think of it like…

A fixed-size integer is like a car's six-digit mileage counter: after 999,999 it rolls back to 000,000.

Real-world example

Sam writes a small game that stores a player's coins in an 8-bit unsigned variable (0-255). A player with 250 coins picks up 10 more and suddenly has 4 — the value wrapped around (260 − 256). Switching to a 32-bit integer raises the limit to about 4.29 billion. In the real world, the first Ariane 5 rocket was lost in 1996 partly because a 64-bit floating-point value was converted into a 16-bit signed integer that was too small to hold it.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Choose a width: n bits give 2^n different patterns (8 bits give 256).
  2. Unsigned numbers run from 0 to 2^n − 1 (8-bit: 0 to 255).
  3. In two's complement the top bit is worth −2^(n−1), so 8-bit signed numbers run from −128 to +127.
  4. To make a number negative, flip every bit and add 1: 5 = 00000101 becomes 11111011 = −5.
  5. The same adder circuit works for signed and unsigned numbers; a carry out of the top bit is simply dropped.
  6. If the true answer does not fit, overflow happens: depending on the language the value wraps, saturates or raises an error.

Who uses it

C/C++ and embedded programmers, game developers, database designers and security researchers (who hunt integer-overflow bugs) must all understand integer sizes.

Key takeaway

Know the ranges by heart: int8 −128 to 127, uint8 0 to 255, int32 about ±2.1 billion, uint32 0 to about 4.29 billion.

Going deeper

  • One ADD instruction serves signed and unsigned numbers; only the flags differ — the carry flag signals unsigned overflow and the overflow flag signals signed overflow, and the program chooses which to test.
  • In C and C++ signed overflow is undefined behaviour, so optimisers may assume it never happens, while unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo 2^n; building with -fsanitize=undefined catches signed overflow during testing.
  • Languages handle overflow differently: Java and Go wrap silently, Rust panics in debug builds and wraps in release builds unless you use checked_ or saturating_ methods, C# offers a checked keyword, and Python integers never overflow.
  • Sign extension copies the top bit when widening (−5 as int8, 0xFB, becomes 0xFFFFFFFB as int32), while zero extension pads unsigned values with zeros; x86 MOVSX and MOVZX do exactly this.
  • The two's complement range is asymmetric: int8 holds −128 but not +128, so negating or taking abs() of the minimum value overflows — a classic edge case for unit tests.
  • Integer division truncates toward zero in C, Java and Rust (−7 / 2 = −3), but Python's // rounds down (−7 // 2 = −4), and the sign of the remainder differs to match.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Checking for overflow after it happens in C (if (a + b < a)) on signed integers: the compiler may delete the check; test before adding or use __builtin_add_overflow.
  • Mixing signed and unsigned values in C comparisons: -1 < 1u is false, because -1 is converted to a huge unsigned number.
  • Assuming int is always 32 bits: C only guarantees at least 16, so use int32_t or int64_t when the exact width matters.
  • Storing money as floating point instead of whole pence or cents (or a decimal type), which introduces rounding errors into totals.

docs.title: Try it: Watch 8-bit integers wrap around and see two's complement
docs.text:
import ctypes
print(ctypes.c_uint8(250 + 10).value)   # 4    (260 - 256: unsigned wrap)
print(ctypes.c_int8(127 + 1).value)     # -128 (signed overflow)
print(format(-5 & 0xFF, '08b'))         # 11111011 = -5 in 8-bit two's complement
print(2**31 - 1, 2**32 - 1)             # int32 max, uint32 max

docs.title: Key chips, architectures, standards, tools & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example Unsigned integerSupported by all CPUs and most languages · Format · Current · Beginner A whole number with no sign, using every bit for size; n bits store 0 up to 2^n − 1. A 16-bit unsigned network port number ranges from 0 to 65,535. Signed integerSupported by all CPUs and most languages · Format · Current · Beginner A whole number that can be negative or positive, today almost always stored in two's complement. A freezer sensor's reading of −18 °C is stored in a signed 16-bit integer. Two's complementUniversal practice; required by the C23 and C++20 standards · Format · Current · Beginner Representation where the top bit has negative weight; negate by flipping all bits and adding 1. One zero and simple adder hardware. In 8 bits, 11111111 means −1 and 10000000 means −128. Sign-magnitudeEarly computers; still used for the sign of floating-point numbers · Format · Legacy · Beginner Uses one bit for the sign and the rest for the size; awkwardly has both +0 and −0. In 8-bit sign-magnitude, 10000101 means −5; floating-point numbers still keep a separate sign bit this way. Ones' complementSome 1960s computers; IETF RFC 1071 (Internet checksum) · Format · Legacy · Intermediate Negate a number by flipping all its bits; it also has two zeros, so it fell out of favour. The IPv4 header checksum is still calculated using ones' complement addition. Integer overflowGeneral computing concept · Concept · Current · Beginner When a calculation's true result does not fit in the available bits, causing wraparound, saturation or an error. Adding 1 to an 8-bit unsigned counter holding 255 gives 0. Carry and overflow flagsStatus flags in CPU architectures such as x86 and Arm · Component · Current · Intermediate Status bits set by the CPU after arithmetic: carry signals unsigned overflow, the overflow flag signals signed overflow. An x86 'jo' instruction jumps to an error handler when the overflow flag is set after an ADD. Fixed-width integer types (int8_t to int64_t)ISO C99 <stdint.h>; also C++, Rust (i8...i64), Go · Standard · Current · Intermediate Types that guarantee an exact number of bits, so code behaves the same on every platform. A file-format parser uses uint32_t for a length field that is always exactly 4 bytes. Arbitrary-precision integers (bignums)Python int, Java BigInteger, GNU GMP library · Technology · Current · Intermediate Integers that grow as large as memory allows, avoiding overflow at the cost of speed. Python calculates 2**200 exactly — a 61-digit number — with no overflow. Saturating arithmeticSIMD instructions on x86 and Arm; DSPs · Technology · Current · Intermediate Instead of wrapping, results stick at the largest or smallest value; common in image and audio processing. Brightening a pixel of value 250 by 20 gives 255 (white) rather than wrapping round to a dark 14. Fixed-point numbersCommon in microcontrollers, DSPs and finance software · Format · Current · Intermediate Integers with an imagined decimal point, giving fractions without floating-point hardware. Storing prices in pence (1299 means £12.99) keeps accounting totals exact. Year 2038 problemAffects systems using a signed 32-bit Unix time_t · Concept · Current · Intermediate Clocks stored as signed 32-bit seconds since 1970 overflow on 19 January 2038 at 03:14:07 UTC. Old embedded devices and file formats are being moved to 64-bit timestamps so dates don't jump back to 1901. Integer overflow vulnerability (CWE-190)MITRE Common Weakness Enumeration · Concept · Current · Advanced A security weakness where an overflow produces a wrong size or index, leading to memory corruption. A size calculation wraps to a tiny number, the program allocates too little memory, and an attacker overruns the buffer. Sign extension and zero extensionx86 MOVSX/MOVZX; Arm SXTB/UXTB; RISC-V LB vs LBU loads · Concept · Current · Intermediate Widening a number to more bits: sign extension copies the top bit so negatives stay negative; zero extension pads unsigned values with zeros. Loading the byte 0xFB with sign extension gives −5 as a 32-bit integer; with zero extension it gives 251.

docs.title: 1.6 Real Numbers: Floating Point and IEEE 754
docs.text:
Floating-point numbers are how computers store numbers with fractions, as well as very large and very tiny numbers. They work like scientific notation (6.02 × 10²³), keeping a sign, a fixed number of significant digits and an exponent — but in binary. Because only so many digits fit, most decimal fractions such as 0.1 cannot be stored exactly, so tiny rounding errors appear.

Encoding 6.5 as an FP32 number. The leading 1 is never stored, which buys one extra bit of precision for free.

Think of it like…

Floating point is like writing every number on a small card with room for only seven significant digits plus '× 10 to the power of something': you can write the size of an atom or of a galaxy, but never with unlimited detail.

Real-world example

Priya, a second-year student, types 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 into Python and gets False. The reason: 0.1 and 0.2 are endless repeating fractions in binary (just as 1/3 is 0.333... in decimal), so each is stored very slightly off, and their sum prints as 0.30000000000000004. Her lecturer explains that scientific code compares floats with a tolerance using math.isclose(), while banking code uses decimal types or counts whole pennies.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Write the number in binary scientific notation, for example 6.5 = 1.101 (binary) × 2².
  2. Store the sign bit: 0 for positive, 1 for negative.
  3. Store the exponent with a bias added (127 for FP32, 1023 for FP64) so it is always a positive pattern.
  4. Store the fraction bits after the leading 1; that 1 is implied, which saves a bit.
  5. Round to the nearest value that fits — this rounding is where small errors creep in.
  6. Reserved patterns represent zero, ±infinity, NaN (Not a Number) and tiny 'subnormal' numbers.

Who uses it

Scientific programmers, game and graphics developers, data scientists, AI engineers (who use FP16, BF16 and FP8) and anyone handling money must understand floating-point limits.

Key takeaway

Never compare floats with ==; use a tolerance such as math.isclose(), and remember FP64 gives about 15-16 significant decimal digits and FP32 about 7.

Going deeper

  • Precision is relative, not absolute: FP64 values near 1 are about 2.2 × 10^-16 apart, but near 10^16 neighbouring doubles are 2 apart, so adding 1 to 10^16 changes nothing.
  • Whole numbers are exact in FP64 only up to 2^53 (about 9 × 10^15) — which is why JavaScript defines Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER and BigInt, and why 64-bit IDs in JSON are often sent as strings.
  • Subnormal numbers fill the gap next to zero so underflow is gradual, but many processors handle them far more slowly; performance code sometimes enables flush-to-zero modes (FTZ/DAZ) to avoid that cost.
  • The default IEEE 754 rounding is round-to-nearest with ties to even, which avoids systematic bias; directed modes (towards +∞, −∞ or zero) support interval arithmetic and error analysis.
  • Floating-point addition is not associative — (a + b) + c can differ from a + (b + c) — so parallel reductions, -ffast-math and different GPU thread orders can change results slightly between runs.
  • AI moved to narrow formats because moving data dominates cost: going from FP32 to BF16 halves memory traffic and roughly doubles tensor-core throughput, and FP8 or FP4 with scaling factors push further.
  • Besides IEEE 754-2019, a separate IEEE working group (P3109) and the industry OCP FP8 and microscaling (MX) specifications define the 8-bit and smaller formats used in machine learning.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Comparing floats with ==: use a relative or absolute tolerance (math.isclose, numpy.allclose), because tiny rounding differences are normal.
  • Using binary floats for currency: 0.10 cannot be stored exactly, so use whole cents or a decimal type for money.
  • Believing more printed decimal places means more accuracy: FP32 carries only about 7 significant digits whatever print() displays.
  • Expecting bit-identical results across machines with -ffast-math or different summation orders; reproducibility needs a fixed order and strict IEEE settings.

docs.title: Try it: Look inside a float with Python's struct module
docs.text:
import struct, math
print(0.1 + 0.2)                     # 0.30000000000000004
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))  # True
bits = struct.unpack('>I', struct.pack('>f', 6.5))[0]
print(f'{bits:032b}')
# 0 10000001 10100000000000000000000
# sign | exponent (127+2) | fraction (.101)
print(float('inf'), float('nan'), 1e308 * 10)   # inf nan inf

docs.title: Key chips, architectures, standards, tools & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example IEEE 754IEEE (754-1985, revised 2008 and 2019) · Standard · Current · Beginner The standard defining binary floating-point formats, rounding rules and special values, used by almost every processor. Because CPUs and GPUs follow IEEE 754, the same FP64 calculation done in the same order gives identical results on Intel, AMD and Arm. FP64 (double precision)IEEE 754 binary64 · Format · Current · Beginner 64 bits: 1 sign, 11 exponent and 52 fraction bits; about 15-16 decimal digits, values up to about 10^308. Python floats and JavaScript numbers are FP64, and supercomputer rankings measure FP64 speed. FP32 (single precision)IEEE 754 binary32 · Format · Current · Beginner 32 bits: 1 sign, 8 exponent and 23 fraction bits; about 7 decimal digits, values up to about 3.4 × 10^38. Games store 3D vertex positions in FP32, halving memory use compared with FP64. FP16 (half precision)IEEE 754 binary16 · Format · Current · Intermediate 16 bits: 1 sign, 5 exponent and 10 fraction bits; about 3 decimal digits and a maximum value of 65,504. AI inference and graphics shaders use FP16 to save memory and run faster on GPUs. bfloat16 (BF16)Google Brain; now supported by most CPUs, GPUs and AI chips · Format · Current · Intermediate 16 bits with FP32's 8-bit exponent but only 7 fraction bits: huge range, low precision — well suited to AI training. Large language models are commonly trained in BF16 on GPUs and TPUs. FP8 (E4M3 and E5M2)OCP 8-bit floating point specification (NVIDIA, Arm, Intel, AMD and others) · Format · Current · Advanced 8-bit floats used to speed up AI; E4M3 favours precision, E5M2 favours range. Covered more in the accelerator chapter. NVIDIA's Hopper and Blackwell GPU generations run FP8 matrix maths for faster training and inference. Sign, exponent and significand (mantissa)IEEE 754 terminology · Concept · Current · Beginner The three fields of a float: a sign bit, a power-of-two exponent stored with a bias, and the fraction digits. −0.75 = −1.1 (binary) × 2^−1: sign 1, exponent −1 (stored as 126 in FP32), fraction .1. Machine epsilonNumerical analysis; IEEE 754 formats · Metric · Current · Intermediate The gap between 1.0 and the next representable number: 2^−52, about 2.2 × 10^−16, for FP64. In Python, sys.float_info.epsilon prints 2.220446049250313e-16. NaN and infinityIEEE 754 special values · Concept · Current · Beginner Special values for undefined results (NaN, e.g. 0/0) and results too big to hold (±infinity); NaN is not even equal to itself. In a data-cleaning script float('nan') == float('nan') is False, so math.isnan() is used to find missing values. Rounding errorNumerical analysis · Concept · Current · Beginner The small difference between a real number and the nearest float, which can build up over many operations. Adding 0.1 to a total ten times in a loop gives 0.9999999999999999, not exactly 1.0. Catastrophic cancellationNumerical analysis · Concept · Current · Advanced Losing most significant digits when subtracting two nearly equal floats, leaving mostly rounding noise. In FP32, 1.0000001 − 1.0 gives about 1.19e-7 instead of 1e-7 — a 19% error from one subtraction. Kahan (compensated) summationWilliam Kahan; Python's math.fsum and sum() (3.12+) use compensated methods · Technology · Current · Advanced An algorithm that tracks the tiny bits lost in each addition, greatly reducing error when summing many floats. math.fsum([0.1] * 10) returns exactly 1.0, unlike a simple running-total loop. Decimal floating pointIEEE 754-2008 decimal formats; Python decimal, Java BigDecimal · Format · Current · Intermediate Stores digits in base 10 so values like 0.1 are exact; preferred for money. In Python, Decimal('0.1') + Decimal('0.2') == Decimal('0.3') is True. Patriot missile timing error (1991)US GAO report IMTEC-92-26 · Concept · Legacy · Intermediate A rounding error in storing 0.1 seconds in binary built up over 100 hours, throwing tracking off by about a third of a second. In February 1991 a Patriot battery in Dhahran failed to intercept a Scud missile; 28 US soldiers died — a classic lesson in numeric precision. Subnormal (denormal) numbersIEEE 754 · Concept · Current · Advanced Tiny values below the smallest normal number, stored without the hidden leading 1, so results fade gradually towards zero instead of jumping. In FP32 the smallest normal value is about 1.18 × 10^-38, but subnormals reach down to about 1.4 × 10^-45. Rounding modes (round half to even)IEEE 754 (default: round to nearest, ties to even) · Concept · Current · Intermediate Rules for picking the nearest representable value; by default exact ties go to the even neighbour, avoiding systematic upward bias. Python's round(2.5) returns 2 and round(3.5) returns 4, applying the same ties-to-even rule.

docs.title: 1.7 Text, Images and Sound as Numbers
docs.text:
Computers only store numbers, so text, pictures and sounds have to be turned into numbers using agreed codes. For text, each character gets a number (a code point) from a huge shared table called Unicode, and an encoding such as UTF-8 turns that number into bytes. Pictures become grids of coloured dots called pixels, and sound becomes thousands of volume measurements per second.

Same characters, three Unicode encodings (bytes in hex)

UTF-8 UTF-16 (BE) UTF-32 (BE) A (U+0041) 41 00 41 00 00 00 41 é (U+00E9) C3 A9 00 E9 00 00 00 E9 € (U+20AC) E2 82 AC 20 AC 00 00 20 AC Emoji (U+1F600) F0 9F 98 80 D8 3D DE 00 00 01 F6 00

UTF-8 keeps ASCII to one byte, while characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane need four bytes in every encoding.

Think of it like…

Character encoding is like a codebook shared by two spies: if both use the same book the message is clear, but with different books it turns into nonsense.

Real-world example

Kofi exports a customer list from an old accounting program, and names like 'José' appear as 'JosÃ©'. The file was saved in UTF-8 but opened as Windows-1252, so the two bytes of 'é' showed up as two wrong characters — this garbling is called mojibake. Re-opening the file as UTF-8 fixes it. The same week he notices a 3-minute song is about 32 MB as a CD-quality WAV file but only about 7 MB as a 320 kbit/s MP3, because MP3 throws away sounds people barely hear.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Each character is given a number called a code point: 'A' = U+0041, '€' = U+20AC, '😀' = U+1F600.
  2. An encoding turns code points into bytes: UTF-8 uses 1-4 bytes per character, UTF-16 uses 2 or 4.
  3. Images are grids of pixels; each pixel usually stores red, green and blue values from 0 to 255 (24 bits).
  4. Sound is sampled: the wave's height is measured many times a second (44,100 for CD audio) and each sample stored as a number.
  5. Compression shrinks files: lossless (PNG, FLAC, ZIP) keeps every bit, lossy (JPEG, MP3, AAC) discards detail people barely notice.

Who uses it

Web and app developers, data engineers, localisation teams, multimedia and game developers, and digital forensics analysts all work with encodings and media formats.

Key takeaway

Use UTF-8 everywhere (files, databases, web pages), and remember that a raw image needs width × height × bytes per pixel of memory.

Going deeper

  • UTF-8 is self-synchronising: lead bytes begin 0, 110, 1110 or 11110 and continuation bytes begin 10, so a decoder can find character boundaries even after jumping into the middle of a stream.
  • One visible character can be several code points: 'é' may be U+00E9 or 'e' plus the combining accent U+0301, and family emoji join several code points with zero-width joiners — such units are called grapheme clusters.
  • Uncompressed media sizes are simple products: image = width × height × bytes per pixel; audio = sample rate × bytes per sample × channels × seconds; raw video multiplies one frame by frames per second.
  • Images often add a fourth alpha (transparency) channel, giving 32-bit RGBA pixels, and HDR video uses 10 or 12 bits per colour channel to avoid visible banding in smooth gradients.
  • Lossy codecs exploit human perception: JPEG uses the discrete cosine transform and quantisation, MP3 and AAC use psychoacoustic models, and video codecs such as H.264, HEVC and AV1 mostly encode changes between frames.
  • Dedicated media engines in CPUs, GPUs and phone SoCs encode and decode H.264, HEVC and AV1 in hardware, using a small fraction of the power that software decoding on general cores would need.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming one character equals one byte: in UTF-8 'naïve' is 6 bytes for 5 characters, so byte-length limits can cut a character in half.
  • Relying on the system default encoding: always pass encoding='utf-8' (or the correct encoding) when reading and writing text files in code.
  • Re-saving lossy files repeatedly: each JPEG or MP3 re-encode loses more detail, so keep a lossless master and export copies from it.
  • Treating Base64 as encryption: it is only an encoding, and anyone can decode it instantly.

docs.title: Try it: Peek at how text becomes bytes in Python
docs.text:
>>> 'A'.encode('utf-8'), 'é'.encode('utf-8'), '€'.encode('utf-8')
(b'A', b'\xc3\xa9', b'\xe2\x82\xac')
>>> ord('A'), hex(ord('😀'))
(65, '0x1f600')
>>> len('😀'.encode('utf-8')), len('😀'.encode('utf-16-le'))
(4, 4)
>>> 1920 * 1080 * 3 / 1e6   # MB for one uncompressed Full HD image
6.2208

docs.text: Name What it does Example ASCIIANSI X3.4 (first published 1963) · Standard · Current · Beginner A 7-bit code with 128 characters: English letters, digits, punctuation and control codes; Unicode's first 128 code points match it. 'A' is 65, 'a' is 97, a space is 32 and a newline (LF) is 10. Code pages (extended ASCII)ISO/IEC 8859 series; Microsoft Windows-1252 · Standard · Legacy · Intermediate 8-bit tables using values 128-255 for accented or local letters; different regions used incompatible tables. Byte 0xE9 meant 'é' in Western European code pages but a completely different letter in Cyrillic or Greek ones. UnicodeUnicode Consortium (kept in step with ISO/IEC 10646) · Standard · Current · Beginner One universal character set giving every character in every writing system its own number; version 18.0 (2026) covers over 170,000 characters. Latin, Arabic, Devanagari, Chinese characters and emoji can all appear together in one Unicode document. Code pointUnicode Consortium · Concept · Current · Beginner The number Unicode assigns to a character, written as U+ followed by hexadecimal digits. U+0041 is 'A', U+00E9 is 'é' and U+1F600 is the grinning-face emoji. UTF-8Ken Thompson and Rob Pike (1992); IETF RFC 3629 · Format · Current · Beginner Variable-length encoding using 1-4 bytes per character, with plain ASCII text unchanged; by far the most common encoding on the web. 'A' takes 1 byte, 'é' 2 bytes, '€' 3 bytes and '😀' 4 bytes. UTF-16Unicode Consortium; IETF RFC 2781 · Format · Current · Intermediate Uses 2 bytes for most characters and 4 bytes (a 'surrogate pair') for the rest; used inside Windows, Java and JavaScript. JavaScript reports '😀'.length as 2 because the emoji is stored as a surrogate pair of two 16-bit units. UTF-32Unicode Consortium · Format · Current · Intermediate Uses a fixed 4 bytes for every code point: simple to index but wasteful of space. Some text-processing libraries convert to UTF-32 internally so the nth character always starts at byte 4 × n. Byte Order Mark (BOM)Unicode Consortium (U+FEFF) · Concept · Current · Intermediate An optional invisible character at the start of a file that signals the encoding and byte order. Some Windows editors put the bytes EF BB BF at the start of UTF-8 files, which can break the first line of a Linux shell script. MojibakeJapanese term for garbled text · Concept · Current · Beginner Scrambled text produced when bytes are decoded using the wrong encoding. 'Café' saved in UTF-8 but opened as Windows-1252 shows up as 'CafÃ©'. Base64IETF RFC 4648 · Format · Current · Beginner Encodes any binary data as 64 safe text characters so it can pass through text-only systems; output is about a third larger. Email attachments and small images embedded directly in web pages (data: URLs) are Base64-encoded. Pixels and colour depth (RGB)General imaging concept · Concept · Current · Beginner An image is a grid of pixels; 24-bit colour stores 8 bits each of red, green and blue — about 16.7 million colours. An uncompressed 1920 × 1080 image needs 1920 × 1080 × 3 bytes, about 6.2 MB. PNG, JPEG, WebP and AVIFPNG: W3C / ISO/IEC 15948; JPEG: ISO/IEC JPEG committee; WebP: Google; AVIF: AOMedia · Format · Current · Beginner Common image file formats: PNG is lossless (logos, screenshots), JPEG is lossy (photos), WebP and AVIF give smaller files for the web. A 6 MB uncompressed photo typically shrinks to well under 1 MB as a good-quality JPEG with little visible difference. Audio sampling (PCM)Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem · Concept · Current · Intermediate Sound is measured many times per second; the rate must exceed twice the highest frequency, so CDs use 44.1 kHz at 16 bits. One minute of CD-quality stereo is 44,100 × 2 bytes × 2 channels × 60 ≈ 10.6 MB. Lossless vs lossy compressione.g. ZIP, PNG, FLAC (lossless); JPEG, MP3, AAC, H.264, AV1 (lossy) · Concept · Current · Beginner Lossless compression rebuilds the original exactly; lossy compression discards less-noticeable detail to make files far smaller. Streaming services send video in lossy formats such as H.264, H.265 or AV1 because raw video would need gigabits per second. Unicode normalisation (NFC, NFD)Unicode Standard Annex #15 · Standard · Current · Intermediate Rules that convert equivalent character sequences into one standard form, so strings that look identical also compare as equal. Before comparing usernames, a site normalises to NFC so 'é' typed as one code point matches 'e' followed by a combining accent.

docs.title: 1.8 Logic Gates, Boolean Algebra and Transistors
docs.text:
A logic gate is a tiny circuit that takes one or more bits in and gives one bit out according to a simple rule, such as 'output 1 only if both inputs are 1' (AND). Gates are built from transistors, which are electrically controlled switches. The maths for combining true and false values is called Boolean algebra, and with enough gates you can build every calculation a computer does.

Truth table for three key gates

AND OR XOR A=0, B=0 0 0 0 A=0, B=1 0 1 1 A=1, B=0 0 1 1 A=1, B=1 1 1 0

XOR is 1 only when its inputs differ — exactly the sum bit of a one-bit adder.

Think of it like…

Gates are like rules for opening a door: an AND door needs a key and a passcode, an OR door opens with either one, and a NOT door does the opposite of whatever you tell it.

Real-world example

Jade designs an alarm for a fictional bike shop, Spoke & Sprocket: the siren should sound if the system is armed AND (the door opens OR the window breaks). In Boolean algebra that is Siren = Armed · (Door + Window). She writes its truth table (8 rows for 3 inputs), builds it in the free simulator Logisim-evolution with one OR gate and one AND gate, and checks every row before soldering the real circuit.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Represent true/false as 1/0, which inside a chip means a high or low voltage.
  2. Basic gates: NOT flips a bit, AND outputs 1 only if all inputs are 1, OR outputs 1 if any input is 1.
  3. Derived gates: NAND and NOR are AND and OR followed by NOT; XOR outputs 1 when its inputs differ.
  4. A truth table lists the output for every input combination — 2^n rows for n inputs.
  5. Boolean algebra rules, including De Morgan's laws, simplify an expression so it needs fewer gates.
  6. On a chip each gate is a handful of CMOS transistors switching billions of times per second.

Who uses it

Digital design, FPGA and chip (ASIC) engineers, embedded developers and computer science students use gates and Boolean logic; every programmer uses the same logic in if-statements.

Key takeaway

Remember that NAND (or NOR) on its own can build every other gate, and De Morgan's law: NOT(A AND B) = (NOT A) OR (NOT B).

Going deeper

  • A CMOS gate pairs a pull-up network of p-type transistors with a pull-down network of n-type transistors; for any input only one network conducts, so almost no current flows while the gate is not switching.
  • Dynamic power in CMOS is roughly activity × capacitance × voltage² × frequency, which is why lowering the supply voltage saves so much energy and why chips switch off the clock to idle blocks (clock gating).
  • NAND is the natural CMOS gate: it needs 4 transistors, while AND needs 6 (a NAND plus an inverter), so standard-cell libraries build most logic from NAND, NOR and other inverting gates.
  • Every gate has a propagation delay measured in picoseconds; the slowest chain of gates between two flip-flops, the critical path, sets the maximum clock frequency of the whole design.
  • Any Boolean function can be written as a sum of products (an OR of ANDs) taken straight from the truth table's 1-rows; Karnaugh maps by hand, or tools such as Espresso, then minimise it.
  • Real chips are not drawn gate by gate: logic-synthesis tools from Synopsys, Cadence and the open-source Yosys project turn hardware-description code into optimised gate netlists.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Confusing logical and bitwise operators in code: && and || work on whole true/false values, while & and | act on every bit separately.
  • Applying De Morgan's law halfway: negate each input and also swap AND for OR — NOT(A AND B) equals NOT A OR NOT B.
  • Thinking gates switch instantly: every gate has a delay, and ignoring delays causes glitches and timing failures in real circuits.

docs.title: Try it: Print truth tables with a tiny Python script
docs.text:
from itertools import product
gates = {
    'AND':  lambda a, b: a & b,
    'OR':   lambda a, b: a | b,
    'NAND': lambda a, b: 1 - (a & b),
    'XOR':  lambda a, b: a ^ b,
}
print('\t'.join(['A', 'B', *gates]))
for a, b in product([0, 1], repeat=2):
    print('\t'.join(map(str, [a, b, *(f(a, b) for f in gates.values())])))

docs.title: Key chips, architectures, standards, tools & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example Boolean algebraGeorge Boole, 'The Laws of Thought' (1854) · Concept · Current · Beginner The algebra of true/false values using AND, OR and NOT; the mathematical basis of all digital circuits. The expression A·B + A·C simplifies to A·(B + C), saving one gate. Switching theoryClaude Shannon, MIT master's thesis (1937) · Concept · Intermediate Shannon showed that circuits of switches and relays can carry out Boolean algebra, linking logic to electronics. Thanks to this idea, an engineer can turn any truth table into a working circuit of switches. Truth tableStandard notation in logic and digital design · Tool · Current · Beginner A table listing a circuit's output for every possible combination of its inputs. A 2-input AND gate's truth table has 4 rows, and only the row A=1, B=1 outputs 1. AND gateSymbols defined in IEEE Std 91 and IEC 60617 · Component · Current · Beginner Outputs 1 only when all of its inputs are 1. A car's engine starts only if the brake is pressed AND the key fob is detected. OR gateSymbols defined in IEEE Std 91 and IEC 60617 · Component · Current · Beginner Outputs 1 when at least one of its inputs is 1. A hallway light comes on if the wall switch OR the motion sensor is active. NOT gate (inverter)Symbols defined in IEEE Std 91 and IEC 60617 · Component · Current · Beginner Has a single input and outputs the opposite value. A 'door closed' sensor signal is inverted to produce a 'door open' warning. NAND and NOR gatesSymbols defined in IEEE Std 91 and IEC 60617 · Component · Current · Beginner AND or OR followed by NOT; each is 'universal', meaning any other gate can be built from it alone. The free Nand2Tetris course builds an entire working computer starting from nothing but NAND gates. XOR and XNOR gatesSymbols defined in IEEE Std 91 and IEC 60617 · Component · Current · Beginner XOR outputs 1 when its inputs differ; XNOR outputs 1 when they match. Key to adders, parity checks and encryption. A parity check XORs all the bits of a byte together to detect a single bit flipped during transmission. De Morgan's lawsAugustus De Morgan (19th century) · Concept · Current · Beginner NOT(A AND B) = NOT A OR NOT B, and NOT(A OR B) = NOT A AND NOT B. 'Not (raining and cold)' means 'not raining or not cold'; designers use this to rebuild circuits from NAND gates only. Karnaugh mapMaurice Karnaugh, Bell Labs (1953) · Tool · Current · Intermediate A grid method for simplifying Boolean expressions by circling neighbouring groups of 1s. Students reduce a 4-input truth table to a two-term expression with a K-map in digital logic exams. Transistor (MOSFET)Bell Labs (first transistor 1947 by Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley; MOSFET 1959) · Component · Current · Beginner A tiny electrically controlled switch: a voltage on its gate lets current flow or blocks it. Billions make up every chip. NVIDIA's B200 GPU contains 208 billion transistors across its two dies. CMOS (Complementary MOS)Frank Wanlass, Fairchild Semiconductor (1963) · Technology · Current · Intermediate Pairs of n-type and p-type transistors that use power mainly while switching, so nearly all modern chips use CMOS. A CMOS NOT gate needs just two transistors, and a 2-input NAND gate needs four. Logic simulators (Logisim-evolution, Digital)Open-source community projects · Tool · Current · Beginner Free programs for drawing and testing gate circuits on your computer before building real hardware. A class builds and tests a 4-bit adder in Logisim-evolution in a single lab session. Propagation delayDigital design fundamentals; quoted in standard-cell datasheets · Metric · Current · Intermediate The time a gate's output takes to respond after an input changes — picoseconds on modern chips — and delays add up along each path. If the longest path between two registers takes 200 ps, the clock cannot tick faster than 5 GHz.

docs.title: 1.9 Circuit Building Blocks: Combinational and Sequential Logic
docs.text:
Gates are combined into bigger building blocks. Combinational circuits — adders, multiplexers, decoders and the ALU — produce outputs that depend only on their inputs right now, like a calculator. Sequential circuits — latches, flip-flops, registers and counters — also have memory, so their output depends on what happened before, and a clock signal keeps them all in step.

From transistors to a CPU core. Each layer is built only from the layer beneath it — the core idea of digital abstraction.

Think of it like…

A combinational circuit is like a vending machine's price display, which just reacts to the button you press now; a sequential circuit is like its coin counter, which remembers how much you have already put in.

Real-world example

For a lab, Tomás builds a 4-bit adder by chaining four full adders, each passing its carry to the next, so 0110 (6) + 0111 (7) gives 1101 (13). He then adds a 4-bit register made of D flip-flops to hold a running total, and a push-button clock: each press adds the input to the stored value. Without realising it, he has built the heart of a CPU — an ALU, a register and a clock.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A half adder uses XOR for the sum bit and AND for the carry; a full adder also accepts a carry in.
  2. Chaining full adders makes a multi-bit adder; faster designs work out the carries in advance (carry-lookahead).
  3. Multiplexers pick one of several inputs; decoders turn a binary number into a single active output line.
  4. An ALU combines adders and logic gates with a multiplexer that chooses which operation's result to output.
  5. Feedback loops create memory: a latch holds a bit, and a flip-flop captures its input only at a clock edge.
  6. Registers, counters and finite state machines are flip-flops plus logic, all synchronised by the clock.

Who uses it

Digital designers, FPGA and ASIC engineers, verification engineers and computer architecture students work with these blocks daily, usually written in a hardware description language.

Key takeaway

Combinational = no memory, output depends only on present inputs; sequential = memory plus a clock. Also learn the full adder: Sum = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin, Cout = AB + Cin(A ⊕ B).

Going deeper

  • Synchronous designs work because every flip-flop updates on the same clock edge: the combinational logic between two registers must settle within one clock period, minus setup time and clock skew.
  • Setup and hold times are a flip-flop's timing contract: data must be stable just before (setup) and just after (hold) the clock edge, or the flip-flop can become metastable and output garbage.
  • Carry-lookahead adders compute generate (G = A·B) and propagate (P = A ⊕ B) signals so all carries are ready after about log2(n) gate levels instead of n, letting 64-bit addition fit in a fraction of a nanosecond.
  • Finite state machines come in two styles: Moore machines' outputs depend only on the current state, while Mealy machines' outputs also depend on the current inputs and often need fewer states.
  • FPGAs build these blocks from lookup tables (LUTs), which can mimic any small combinational function, plus flip-flops — so the same Verilog can run on an FPGA prototype or become a custom chip.
  • Signals crossing between unrelated clock domains need synchronisers, typically two flip-flops in series, to make metastability vanishingly rare — a classic source of intermittent, hard-to-reproduce hardware bugs.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Confusing latches and flip-flops: a latch is transparent the whole time it is enabled, while a flip-flop samples only at a clock edge.
  • Writing HDL like software: Verilog describes parallel hardware, so every always block runs at the same time rather than line by line.
  • Assuming ripple-carry adders are good enough for wide numbers: the carry delay grows with width, so CPUs use lookahead or prefix adders.

docs.title: Try it: A full adder and a 4-bit ripple-carry adder in Python
docs.text:
def full_adder(a, b, cin):
    s = a ^ b ^ cin
    cout = (a & b) | (cin & (a ^ b))
    return s, cout

def add4(x, y):
    carry, result = 0, 0
    for i in range(4):
        s, carry = full_adder((x >> i) & 1, (y >> i) & 1, carry)
        result |= s << i
    return result, carry

print(add4(6, 7))   # (13, 0)
print(add4(9, 9))   # (2, 1)  -> overflow: 18 = 16 + 2

docs.text: Name What it does Example Combinational logicDigital design fundamentals · Concept · Current · Beginner Circuits whose outputs depend only on their current inputs, with no memory. A 7-segment display decoder lights the right segments straight away for whatever digit is fed in. Sequential logicDigital design fundamentals · Concept · Current · Beginner Circuits whose outputs depend on current inputs and stored past state, usually synchronised by a clock. A traffic-light controller remembers it is on green and moves to amber after a set number of clock ticks. Adding 1 + 1 in a half adder gives sum 0 and carry 1 — that is 10 in binary. Ripple-carry and carry-lookahead addersDigital design fundamentals · Architecture · Current · Intermediate Ripple-carry passes the carry along bit by bit (simple, slow); carry-lookahead works out carries in parallel (faster, more gates). A 64-bit CPU adder uses lookahead-style tricks so an addition fits inside a clock cycle lasting a fraction of a nanosecond. Multiplexer (MUX) and demultiplexerDigital design fundamentals · Component · Current · Beginner A MUX uses select lines to route one of several inputs to a single output; a DEMUX does the reverse. An ALU uses a multiplexer to choose whether the adder's, the AND's or the OR's result goes to the output. Decoder and encoderDigital design fundamentals · Component · Current · Beginner A decoder turns an n-bit number into one of 2^n active lines; an encoder does the opposite. A memory chip's address decoder switches on exactly one row of cells for each address. ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit)Part of every CPU and GPU core · Component · Current · Beginner The block that does arithmetic (add, subtract) and logic (AND, OR, XOR, shifts) and sets status flags. For a SUB instruction the ALU adds the two's complement of the second number and sets the zero flag if the answer is 0. SR latch and D latchDigital design fundamentals · Component · Current · Intermediate The simplest memory elements, built from gates feeding back into each other; a D latch copies its input while 'enable' is on. Two cross-coupled NOR gates form an SR latch that remembers whether a reset button was pressed. D flip-flopDigital design fundamentals · Component · Current · Beginner Stores one bit and updates only at the rising (or falling) edge of the clock; the basic memory cell of synchronous designs. Each stage of a CPU pipeline ends in a row of D flip-flops that capture results at every clock tick. An x86-64 CPU's RAX register holds a 64-bit value used by arithmetic instructions. A microcontroller timer counts clock ticks to trigger an interrupt exactly every millisecond. Timing analysis reports a 250 ps critical path, so engineers split the multiplier across two pipeline stages to reach a 4 GHz target.

docs.title: 1.10 Computer Architecture Models: von Neumann vs Harvard
docs.text:
Almost every computer follows a plan written down in 1945: a processor, one memory that holds both the program and its data, and input/output, all joined by shared wires called buses. This is the von Neumann, or stored-program, architecture. The Harvard architecture instead keeps instructions and data in separate memories so both can be fetched at once, and most modern chips mix the two ideas.

Three ways to connect processor and memory

von Neumann Harvard Modified Harvard Memories One, for code and data Separate code and data One shared main memory Paths to CPU One shared bus Two independent buses Split L1i and L1d caches Code + data fetched together? No, they take turns Yes Yes, from the L1 caches Typical use Classic textbook model DSPs, small MCUs (AVR) PCs, phones, servers

Most modern chips are von Neumann outside the core and Harvard inside it.

Think of it like…

Von Neumann is a chef with one bookshelf holding both recipes and ingredients, walking up and down one corridor; Harvard gives the chef two shelves and two corridors, so a recipe and an ingredient can arrive at the same time.

Real-world example

Noor compares her laptop with the microcontroller in her robotics club's line-following robot. The laptop's CPU loads programs and data from the same RAM (von Neumann), but inside the chip it has separate level-1 caches for instructions and data — a 'modified Harvard' design. The robot's microcontroller keeps its program in flash and its variables in separate SRAM, much closer to pure Harvard. Both still slow down when the processor has to wait for memory: the von Neumann bottleneck.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The control unit fetches the next instruction from memory, using the program counter to know where it is.
  2. Addresses travel on the address bus, values on the data bus, and read/write commands on the control bus.
  3. The ALU and registers carry out the instruction, and results go back to registers or memory.
  4. In a von Neumann design one path carries both instructions and data, so they must take turns.
  5. In a Harvard design separate paths let an instruction and a piece of data be fetched in the same cycle.
  6. Modern CPUs add caches, including split L1 instruction and data caches, to soften the memory bottleneck.

Who uses it

Computer architects, embedded and firmware engineers, performance engineers and students sitting computer architecture exams all rely on this model.

Key takeaway

Know the von Neumann bottleneck by name: processors became far faster than memory, which is why caches, prefetching and high-bandwidth memory exist.

Going deeper

  • Von Neumann's 1945 EDVAC report described five parts — arithmetic, control, memory, input and output — plus binary stored programs, a blueprint that almost every later general-purpose computer followed.
  • Because code is just data, programs can create other programs (compilers, JITs, loaders), but attackers can also inject code — which is why CPUs now mark data pages as non-executable (the NX bit).
  • Processor speed rose far faster than DRAM latency for decades (the 'memory wall'), so a modern core waits hundreds of cycles on a DRAM miss and depends on caches and prefetching to stay busy.
  • Separate instruction and data paths pay off in small chips: an AVR microcontroller fetches its next instruction from flash while the current one accesses SRAM, so most instructions complete in a single cycle.
  • Because L1i and L1d are separate, freshly written code (JIT output, self-modifying code) needs cache-maintenance or synchronisation steps before it runs — explicit instructions on Arm, mostly automatic on x86.
  • Alternatives to the von Neumann model — dataflow machines, systolic arrays as in Google's TPUs, neuromorphic chips and processing-in-memory — all aim to cut the cost of moving data to a central processor.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Calling modern PCs 'Harvard' because they have split L1 caches: main memory is still shared, so they are modified Harvard machines.
  • Believing a faster clock fixes the von Neumann bottleneck: if data cannot arrive faster, a faster core simply waits longer.
  • Confusing address-bus width with data-bus width: the first limits how much memory can be addressed, the second how much moves per transfer.
