docs.text:
# Linux
lscpu | grep -i cache
#   L1d cache: 384 KiB (8 instances)   <- data
#   L1i cache: 256 KiB (8 instances)   <- instructions
#   L2 cache: ...   L3 cache: ...      <- shared by both

# Windows (PowerShell)
Get-CimInstance Win32_CacheMemory | Select-Object Purpose, InstalledSize

docs.title: Key chips, architectures, standards, tools & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example von Neumann architectureJohn von Neumann, 'First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC' (1945) · Architecture · Current · Beginner Stored-program design in which instructions and data share one memory and one pathway to the processor. Your PC loads a game's code and its level data into the same RAM. Stored-program conceptEckert, Mauchly, von Neumann and Turing (1940s) · Concept · Current · Beginner Programs are kept in memory as numbers, just like data, so a computer can be reprogrammed without rewiring. Installing an app just copies bytes into storage — unlike ENIAC in 1946, which was reprogrammed by moving cables and switches. Harvard architectureNamed after the Harvard Mark I (1944) · Architecture · Current · Intermediate Separate memories and buses for instructions and data, so both can be accessed at the same time. Many digital signal processors and small microcontrollers, such as Microchip's AVR family, keep program flash and data RAM separate. Modified Harvard architectureUsed by Intel, AMD, Apple, Arm and RISC-V core designs · Architecture · Current · Intermediate One shared main memory, but separate instruction and data caches or paths close to the CPU; how most modern processors work. A laptop CPU core has its own L1 instruction cache and L1 data cache, backed by unified L2 and L3 caches. von Neumann bottleneckTerm popularised by John Backus, 1977 Turing Award lecture · Concept · Current · Beginner The limited data rate between processor and memory, which leaves fast CPUs waiting for data. A program summing a huge array runs at memory speed, not CPU speed, because each value must be fetched from RAM. Control unitPart of every CPU · Component · Current · Beginner The part of the CPU that decodes instructions and sends control signals to the ALU, registers and memory. On decoding 'LOAD R1, [address]', the control unit tells memory to read and routes the value into register R1. Program counter (instruction pointer)Part of every CPU (called RIP on x86-64, PC on Arm) · Component · Current · Beginner A register holding the memory address of the next instruction; jumps, branches and calls change it. A function call saves the program counter so the CPU knows where to return when the function finishes. Instruction registerClassic CPU model · Component · Current · Beginner Holds the instruction currently being decoded and executed. After a fetch, the bytes for 'ADD R1, R2' sit in the instruction register while the control unit decodes them. MAR and MDRClassic textbook CPU model · Component · Current · Beginner The memory address register holds the address being accessed; the memory data register holds the value being read or written. To read address 0x1000 the CPU places 0x1000 in the MAR, and the value from memory arrives in the MDR. System buses (address, data, control)Classic computer organisation model · Interface · Current · Beginner Sets of wires: the address bus says where, the data bus carries the value, and the control bus says read or write. A 32-bit address bus can name 2^32 bytes, which is why old 32-bit PCs topped out at 4 GB of memory. Memory-mapped I/OCommon in Arm, RISC-V and x86 systems · Concept · Current · Intermediate Devices appear at memory addresses, so the CPU controls hardware with ordinary load and store instructions. Writing to a GPIO register address on a Raspberry Pi Pico switches an LED on. Cache memoryBuilt into every modern CPU and GPU · Component · Current · Beginner Small, fast SRAM beside the processor holding recently used instructions and data — the main fix for the von Neumann bottleneck (see the processors chapter). After a loop's first pass its instructions sit in the L1 cache, so later passes fetch them in about a nanosecond. Non-von Neumann architecturesDataflow, systolic arrays, neuromorphic chips, processing-in-memory (research and industry) · Architecture · Emerging · Advanced Designs that abandon fetching instructions and data from one shared memory, aiming to cut data movement, for example by computing inside or beside memory. Google's TPU uses a systolic array: data flows between thousands of multiply units without returning to memory between steps. Little Man ComputerStuart Madnick, MIT (1965); many free online simulators · Resource · Current · Beginner A teaching model of a von Neumann computer with 100 numbered mailboxes, an accumulator and about ten instructions. Students write a Little Man Computer program that inputs two numbers and outputs the larger, watching the program counter step through mailboxes.

docs.title: 1.11 How a Program Runs: From Source Code to Machine Code
docs.text:
Programs are written in human-readable languages like C or Python, but the CPU only understands machine code — numbers that encode simple instructions such as 'add these two registers'. Tools translate one into the other: a compiler converts the whole program ahead of time, while an interpreter translates and runs it piece by piece. The operating system then loads the program into memory and the CPU runs it with an endless fetch-decode-execute loop.

From hello.c to a running process. The first four steps happen once at build time; loading and execution happen every time the program starts.

Think of it like…

Compiling is like translating a whole novel before it is published; interpreting is like a live interpreter translating a speech sentence by sentence as it is spoken.

Real-world example

Ravi writes hello.c and runs gcc hello.c -o hello. The preprocessor pulls in stdio.h, the compiler turns C into x86-64 assembly, the assembler turns that into machine code in an object file, and the linker joins it with the C library to make an executable. When he types ./hello, the operating system's loader maps the file into memory, sets up a stack and jumps to the start, and the CPU starts fetching instructions. His friend's Python script takes a different route: CPython compiles it to bytecode and an interpreter loop runs that bytecode.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Write source code in a high-level language such as C, Rust, Java or Python.
  2. Compile it: translate to assembly or straight to machine code (or to bytecode for a virtual machine).
  3. Assemble and link: turn assembly into object files and join them with libraries into one executable.
  4. Load: the operating system maps the executable into memory, creates a process and jumps to its entry point.
  5. Execute: the CPU repeats fetch (get the instruction at the program counter), decode (work out what it means), execute (do it) and write back the result.

Who uses it

Software developers, compiler and toolchain engineers, reverse engineers, malware analysts and performance engineers all need to know what happens between source code and silicon.

Key takeaway

Use Compiler Explorer (godbolt.org) or gcc -S to see the assembly your code becomes — it is the quickest way to understand what the CPU really does.

Going deeper

  • Modern compilers have three layers: a front end parses the language into an intermediate representation (LLVM IR, GCC GIMPLE), a middle end optimises it and a back end emits code for each ISA — one optimiser serves many languages and chips.
  • Optimisation levels trade build time and debuggability for speed: -O0 keeps code close to the source for debugging, -O2 is the usual release setting, and -O3 adds more aggressive inlining and vectorisation.
  • Dynamic linking (.so, .dll, .dylib files) lets programs share one library copy and receive security fixes without relinking; static linking makes self-contained binaries, popular for containers and Go programs.
  • Before main() runs, start-up code (_start, from crt files) sets up the stack, arguments and environment, initialises the C library and runs constructors; returning from main calls exit(), which flushes output buffers.
  • Address space layout randomisation (ASLR) makes the loader place code, stack, heap and libraries at random addresses on each run, so attackers cannot rely on fixed locations; position-independent executables (PIE) make it possible.
  • Most runtimes are hybrids: Java and .NET start by interpreting or quickly compiling and JIT-compile hot methods, Android's ART mixes ahead-of-time and JIT compilation, and CPython 3.13 added an experimental JIT.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Saying Python is 'not compiled': CPython compiles source to bytecode first, and it is the bytecode that is interpreted.
  • Shipping binaries built with -march=native: they can crash with 'illegal instruction' on older CPUs that lack the same extensions.
  • Confusing compiler errors with linker errors: 'undefined reference' comes from the linker and usually means a missing library or object file, not bad syntax.
  • Timing debug (-O0) builds and drawing performance conclusions; always measure optimised release builds.

docs.title: Try it: See the assembly and bytecode your code turns into
docs.text:
/* square.c */
int square(int x) { return x * x; }

$ gcc -O2 -S square.c -o -      # print x86-64 assembly
# typical output (AT&T syntax), lines starting with '.' omitted:
square:
        imull   %edi, %edi
        movl    %edi, %eax
        ret

$ python -c "import dis; dis.dis(lambda x: x * x)"   # CPython bytecode

A 3 GHz core averaging 4 instructions per cycle completes about 12 billion instructions a second, overlapping many in a pipeline. Compiler Explorer (godbolt.org)Matt Godbolt (open source) · Tool · Current · Beginner A website that shows, as you type, the assembly produced by many different compilers for your code. docs.title: 1.12 Measuring Performance: Clock Speed, IPC, FLOPS and Amdahl's Law
docs.text:
'Fast' can mean two things: how long one task takes (latency) or how many tasks are finished per second (throughput). A processor's speed on a program depends on how many instructions it needs, how many clock cycles each takes on average, and how fast the clock ticks. Laws such as Amdahl's law show that adding more processors only helps as much as the work can be split up.

Amdahl's law when 90% of the work is parallel. Speed-up flattens towards 10× however many cores you add, because the serial 10% never shrinks.

Think of it like…

Latency is how long one pizza takes to bake; throughput is how many pizzas the shop sells per hour — a bigger oven raises throughput without baking any single pizza faster.

Real-world example

Mei's video-render script takes 100 seconds: 90 seconds of work can run in parallel, but 10 seconds must run on one core. On 10 cores, Amdahl's law predicts 10 + 90 ÷ 10 = 19 seconds, about a 5.3× speed-up — and even with unlimited cores it can never beat 10 seconds (10×). Her teammate points out Gustafson's view: with 10 cores they could render a scene about ten times bigger in roughly the same time. Mei also realises that halving the instructions in the serial part would help as much as a faster clock.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Clock rate is cycles per second (GHz); one cycle at 4 GHz lasts 0.25 ns.
  2. CPI (cycles per instruction), or its inverse IPC, shows how much work each cycle does.
  3. CPU time = instruction count × CPI ÷ clock rate — improving any of the three makes a program faster.
  4. Latency measures time per task, throughput measures tasks per second, and bandwidth measures data moved per second.
  5. Amdahl's law: speed-up = 1 ÷ ((1 − p) + p ÷ n), where p is the parallel fraction and n the number of processors.
  6. Benchmarks such as SPEC CPU, Geekbench and HPL give comparable scores on standard workloads.

Who uses it

Performance engineers, HPC specialists, game developers, cloud architects sizing servers and anyone buying hardware rely on these measures.

Key takeaway

Clock speed alone does not decide performance — think instruction count × CPI ÷ clock rate, and apply Amdahl's law before parallelising anything.

Going deeper

  • The 'iron law' splits CPU time into instruction count (set by algorithm, compiler and ISA), CPI (set by microarchitecture and memory behaviour) and cycle time (set by circuit design and process) — every optimisation targets one factor.
  • Wall-clock (elapsed) time includes waiting for disks, networks and other programs, while CPU time counts only cycles spent running your code; users feel wall-clock time, so report both.
  • Peak FLOPS = cores × clock × FLOPs per cycle per core: a core with two 512-bit FMA units performs 2 units × 16 FP32 lanes × 2 operations = 64 FP32 FLOPs per cycle, which real code rarely sustains.
  • Supercomputer lists report Rpeak (theoretical) and Rmax (achieved on HPL); large GPU systems typically reach roughly 60-80% of peak on HPL, and real applications usually achieve much less.
  • Benchmark suites summarise many tests with a geometric mean of speed ratios (as SPEC does) so no single test dominates; for interactive services, tail-latency percentiles such as p99 matter more than averages.
  • SPEC CPU 2026, released in May 2026 with 52 benchmarks in four suites, succeeds SPEC CPU 2017 and adds an optional energy metric, so expect vendors to quote both suites for a while.
  • Gustafson's scaled speed-up, (1 − p) + p × n, explains why machines with millions of cores are useful: scientists grow the problem size with the machine instead of shrinking the run time.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Comparing CPUs by GHz alone: a 3.5 GHz chip with higher IPC can beat a 5 GHz chip, so compare benchmarks on your own workload.
  • Reporting only average latency: a service averaging 20 ms may still make 1 in 100 users wait seconds, so track percentiles too.
  • Ignoring Amdahl's law: buying four times the cores rarely gives four times the speed when part of the job is serial or I/O-bound.
  • Mixing up throughput and latency: adding servers raises requests per second but does not make any single request faster.

docs.title: Try it: Amdahl's law calculator in Python
docs.text:
def amdahl(p, n):
    return 1 / ((1 - p) + p / n)

for n in (2, 4, 8, 16, 64, 1_000_000):
    print(f'{n:>9} cores -> {amdahl(0.9, n):5.2f}x')
# 2 -> 1.82x, 8 -> 4.71x, 64 -> 8.77x ... never more than 10x
# when 10% of the work must run serially

docs.title: Key chips, architectures, standards, tools & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example Clock rate (frequency)Measured in hertz (MHz, GHz) · Metric · Current · Beginner Clock cycles per second; higher means more steps per second, but says nothing about how much work each step does. A 5.0 GHz desktop CPU completes 5 billion cycles per second, each lasting 0.2 ns. CPI and IPCHennessy and Patterson terminology · Metric · Current · Intermediate Cycles Per Instruction and Instructions Per Cycle (IPC = 1 ÷ CPI); modern cores average several instructions per cycle. A core reaching an IPC of 4 at 3 GHz retires about 12 billion instructions per second on that code. CPU performance equationHennessy and Patterson, 'Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach' · Concept · Current · Intermediate CPU time = instruction count × CPI × clock cycle time; shows how compilers, chip design and clock speed each contribute. 2 billion instructions × CPI 0.5 ÷ 4 GHz = 0.25 seconds of CPU time. MIPS (the metric)Millions of Instructions Per Second · Metric · Legacy · Intermediate An easy-to-quote speed figure that misleads, because instructions do different amounts of work on different processors. A CPU with very simple instructions can post a higher MIPS figure yet finish a real program more slowly. FLOPSFloating-point operations per second · Metric · Current · Beginner Floating-point operations per second; used for scientific and AI performance, quoted in giga-, tera-, peta- or exaFLOPS. An exascale supercomputer sustains at least 10^18 FP64 operations per second on the HPL benchmark. LatencyGeneral performance concept · Metric · Current · Beginner The time to complete one operation from start to finish, such as nanoseconds for memory or milliseconds for a web request. A web page that takes 200 ms to appear has a latency of 200 ms as the user experiences it. Throughput and bandwidthGeneral performance concepts · Metric · Current · Beginner Throughput is work completed per second; bandwidth is the maximum rate at which a link or memory can move data. A web server handling 20,000 requests per second has high throughput even if each request takes 50 ms. Speed-upGeneral performance concept · Metric · Current · Beginner The ratio of the old running time to the new running time after an improvement. Cutting a job from 60 seconds to 15 seconds is a 4× speed-up. Amdahl's lawGene Amdahl (1967) · Concept · Current · Beginner The overall speed-up is limited by the part of the work that cannot be improved or run in parallel. If 5% of a program must run serially, no number of processors can make it more than 20× faster. Gustafson's lawJohn Gustafson (1988) · Concept · Current · Intermediate With more processors people usually tackle bigger problems in the same time, so scaled speed-up grows almost in line with processor count. A weather centre doubles its cores and runs a forecast with twice as many grid points in the same time window. Performance per wattTracked for supercomputers by the Green500 list · Metric · Current · Beginner Useful work per unit of energy; now as important as raw speed for phones, laptops, data centres and supercomputers. The Green500 list ranks supercomputers by gigaFLOPS per watt rather than by total speed. SPEC CPUSPEC (Standard Performance Evaluation Corporation) · Benchmark · Current · Intermediate Industry-standard suites of real programs measuring CPU, memory and compiler performance; SPEC CPU 2026 (released May 2026) succeeds SPEC CPU 2017. Server makers publish SPEC CPU results so buyers can compare processors on the same workloads. Geekbench and CinebenchPrimate Labs (Geekbench), Maxon (Cinebench) · Benchmark · Current · Beginner Popular consumer benchmarks giving single-core and multi-core scores for PCs, Macs and phones. Laptop reviewers quote Geekbench and Cinebench single- and multi-core scores when comparing new chips. HPL (High-Performance LINPACK)Jack Dongarra and colleagues; used by TOP500 · Benchmark · Current · Intermediate Solves a huge dense system of linear equations in FP64; the yardstick for the TOP500 supercomputer ranking. Frontier's HPL result of about 1.1 exaFLOPS in May 2022 made it the first officially ranked exascale computer. Wall-clock time vs CPU timeReported by the Unix time command, perf stat and profilers · Metric · Current · Beginner Wall-clock time is real elapsed time; CPU time is time actually spent executing on cores, summed across all threads. time make -j8 reports real 1m10s but user 7m40s, showing that eight cores were busy for most of the build. Peak vs sustained performance (Rpeak vs Rmax)TOP500 terminology; vendor datasheets · Metric · Current · Intermediate Peak is the theoretical maximum from the spec sheet; sustained is what a real benchmark or application achieves, usually much lower. On the June 2026 TOP500 list, El Capitan's measured Rmax of about 1.8 exaFLOPS is well below its theoretical Rpeak.

docs.title: 1.13 Moore's Law, Dennard Scaling and Process Nodes
docs.text:
In 1965 Gordon Moore noticed that the number of transistors on a chip was doubling at a steady pace — later settled at about every two years — and this 'Moore's law' held for decades. For a long time, smaller transistors were also faster and more power-efficient (Dennard scaling), but that bonus ended in the mid-2000s, so clock speeds stopped climbing and chips gained more cores instead. Chips are made in factories called fabs using generations of technology called process nodes, such as '3 nm' or '2 nm' — names that are now marketing labels rather than real measurements.

Transistors per chip, 1971-2024 (log scale). On a log scale about 26 doublings in 53 years look like steady growth — Moore's law in one picture.

Think of it like…

Moore's law is like fitting ever more houses into the same town by making each one smaller; Dennard scaling was the bonus that smaller houses also needed less heating — until the walls got so thin that heat leaked everywhere.

Real-world example

Students at a fictional college, Westbrook Tech, line up three chips: the Intel 4004 from 1971 with about 2,300 transistors, a 2005 dual-core desktop processor with a few hundred million, and a 2024 AI GPU with over 200 billion. That is roughly a 100-million-fold increase in about 50 years. They also notice clock speeds climbed from 740 kHz to around 3-4 GHz by the mid-2000s and then barely moved — the point where Dennard scaling broke down.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Fabs print transistors onto silicon wafers using lithography: light projects circuit patterns onto light-sensitive coatings.
  2. Shrinking features fits more transistors per square millimetre, lowering the cost of each transistor.
  3. Under Dennard scaling, smaller transistors used proportionally less power, so clocks could rise without overheating.
  4. Around 2005-2006 leakage current stopped voltages falling, so heat — the 'power wall' — became the main limit.
  5. The industry responded with multicore chips, specialised accelerators, 3D transistor shapes (FinFET, then gate-all-around) and chiplets.
  6. In 2026 the leading foundries (TSMC, Samsung, Intel) are shipping 2 nm-class nodes, and backside power delivery is arriving.

Who uses it

Semiconductor process engineers, chip designers, hardware analysts and anyone choosing or buying processors should understand nodes and scaling trends.

Key takeaway

A '2 nm' node contains no feature that is literally 2 nm wide — compare nodes by transistor density, performance and power, not by their names.

Going deeper

  • Moore's 1965 article predicted the number of components per chip would double every year; in 1975 he revised it to about every two years, a pace the industry roughly kept until the 2010s before slowing.
  • Dennard scaling ended because supply voltage stopped falling: near and below about 1 V, threshold-voltage limits and leakage current meant smaller transistors kept wasting power even when idle.
  • Transistor shapes changed to keep leakage under control: planar devices until about 22 nm, FinFETs (Intel 2011-12, TSMC 16 nm in 2015), gate-all-around nanosheets (Samsung 2022, TSMC N2 and Intel 18A from 2025), with stacked CFETs next on roadmaps.
  • Leading-edge fabs cost tens of billions of dollars, so only TSMC, Samsung and Intel compete at the frontier; Japan's Rapidus is aiming for 2 nm-class mass production around 2027.
  • SRAM cells have shrunk much more slowly than logic at recent nodes, one reason designers move large caches onto separate stacked dies, as in AMD's 3D V-Cache.
  • Cost per transistor stopped falling quickly after roughly the 28 nm era, so 'More than Moore' approaches — chiplets, advanced packaging and specialised accelerators — now deliver much of the progress.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Reading 'Moore's law is dead' as 'no more progress': density still rises, just more slowly and at a higher cost per wafer.
  • Comparing node names across foundries: Intel 18A, TSMC N2 and Samsung SF2 differ in density and power, so compare published data instead.
  • Confusing Moore's law with clock speed: transistor counts kept climbing after 2005 even though clock frequencies stalled.

docs.title: Try it: Check Moore's law yourself with two data points
docs.text:
import math
start, end = 2_300, 208_000_000_000   # Intel 4004 (1971) vs NVIDIA B200 (2024)
doublings = math.log2(end / start)
print(round(doublings, 1))                   # ~26.4 doublings
print(round((2024 - 1971) / doublings, 2))   # ~2.0 years per doubling

docs.title: 1.14 Orders of Magnitude: Prefixes and Latency Numbers
docs.text:
Computing covers enormous ranges: one CPU step takes a fraction of a nanosecond, while a message to another continent takes hundreds of millions of times longer. Engineers use prefixes such as nano, micro, milli, kilo, mega and giga to talk about these scales, and memorise rough 'latency numbers' so they can quickly judge whether a design will be fast. Getting the order of magnitude (the power of ten) right matters far more than being exact.

How long things take (log scale). Each step to the right is roughly 10-1,000× slower — design around the big gaps, not the small ones.

Think of it like…

If one CPU cycle (about 0.3 ns) were stretched to one second, reading main memory would take about five minutes, an SSD read about four days, and a packet to another continent about fifteen years.

Real-world example

Jonas, a junior developer at a fictional delivery app called Parcelpath, must decide where to keep user sessions. Main memory answers in about 100 ns, a local NVMe SSD in roughly 100 µs (1,000× slower), and a database in another region in about 50-150 ms (another 1,000× slower). Each page load needs 20 session reads, so the cross-region design would add up to around two seconds, while an in-memory cache adds only microseconds. A quick back-of-the-envelope estimate settles the debate before anyone writes code.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Learn the SI prefixes in steps of 1000: nano (10^-9), micro (10^-6), milli (10^-3), kilo (10^3), mega (10^6), giga (10^9), tera, peta, exa, zetta.
  2. Memorise rough latencies: cache ~1-10 ns, RAM ~100 ns, SSD ~10-100 µs, hard disk ~5-10 ms, intercontinental ~100-150 ms or more.
  3. Multiply counts by costs for a back-of-the-envelope estimate (number of operations × time per operation).
  4. Compare options by ratio: a 1000× gap always matters, a 10% gap rarely does at the design stage.
  5. Measure afterwards to confirm, because real hardware varies by generation and workload.

Who uses it

Software and systems engineers, site reliability engineers, cloud architects and candidates in system-design interviews use these numbers all the time.

Key takeaway

In system-design interviews, say approximate latencies and do quick estimates out loud — interviewers care about the right order of magnitude, not exact figures.

Going deeper

  • Powers of two approximate powers of ten: 2^10 ≈ 10^3, so 2^20 is about a million, 2^30 about a billion and 2^40 about a trillion — handy for quick memory and address-space estimates.
  • A day has 86,400 seconds (≈ 10^5) and a year about 31.5 million (≈ π × 10^7); dividing a daily total by 10^5 gives a quick average per-second rate.
  • Little's law (items in the system = arrival rate × time each spends there) turns latency into capacity: 1,000 requests per second taking 50 ms each means about 50 requests in flight at once.
  • Bandwidth and latency are independent: a van full of hard drives has huge bandwidth but terrible latency, and the bandwidth-delay product tells you how much data must be in flight to keep a link busy.
  • Since the classic latency list was written, DRAM latency has barely improved, SSDs have become roughly 100× faster than disks, and RDMA networks have cut in-data-centre messages to a few microseconds.
  • Energy follows orders of magnitude too: fetching 64 bits from DRAM costs about a hundred times or more the energy of a 64-bit floating-point operation, so data movement dominates chip power budgets.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Mixing ms, µs and ns in one estimate: convert everything to a single unit first, because a 1,000× slip reverses conclusions.
  • Assuming network calls are free because the LAN is fast: half a millisecond per call adds up when a page makes hundreds of sequential calls.
  • Treating memorised latency numbers as exact: they shift with each hardware generation, so use them for orders of magnitude and measure real systems.

docs.title: Try it: Turn nanoseconds into human time
docs.text:
latency_ns = {
    'L1 cache hit': 1,
    'Main memory (DRAM)': 100,
    'NVMe SSD random read': 100_000,
    'Hard disk seek': 5_000_000,
    'Packet to another continent': 150_000_000,
}
# pretend one 0.3 ns CPU cycle lasts 1 second
for name, ns in latency_ns.items():
    secs = ns / 0.3
    print(f'{name:30} {secs:>14,.0f} s  (~{secs / 86400:,.1f} days)')

Supercomputer speed is now measured in exaFLOPS, and global yearly data in zettabytes. Small SI prefixes (milli to pico)BIPM — International System of Units · Standard · Current · Beginner milli (10^-3), micro (10^-6), nano (10^-9) and pico (10^-12); used for times, voltages and sizes. A 3 GHz clock cycle lasts about 333 picoseconds, or 0.33 nanoseconds. NanosecondOne billionth (10^-9) of a second · Metric · Current · Beginner One billionth of a second; light in a vacuum travels only about 30 cm in that time. Computing pioneer Grace Hopper handed out 30 cm lengths of wire to show audiences what a nanosecond looks like. Latency numbers every programmer should knowPopularised by Jeff Dean and Peter Norvig · Resource · Current · Intermediate A list of approximate times for common operations, from a cache hit to a cross-continent round trip, used for quick estimates. Engineers recall that RAM is about 100× slower than L1 cache and about 1,000× faster than an SSD read. Cache latency (L1, L2, L3)Varies by CPU generation · Metric · Current · Intermediate Roughly 1 ns for L1, a few nanoseconds for L2 and about 10-20 ns for L3 on modern processors. A loop over a small array that fits in L1 runs many times faster than one scanning gigabytes of RAM. DRAM access latencyVaries by memory type and platform · Metric · Current · Intermediate About 80-120 ns for the CPU to fetch from main memory — hundreds of CPU clock cycles. A cache miss to DRAM on a 4 GHz core costs around 400 cycles, during which that work may stall. SSD and hard-disk latencyVaries by device · Metric · Current · Beginner NVMe SSD reads take tens of microseconds to about a tenth of a millisecond; hard-disk seeks take several milliseconds. Swapping a boot hard disk for an SSD turns a one-minute start-up into seconds because thousands of small reads become about 100× faster. Network round-trip time (RTT)Measured with ping and similar tools · Metric · Current · Beginner The time for a packet to reach a destination and come back: well under 1 ms inside a data centre, roughly 70-300 ms between continents. A ping from London to New York typically shows around 70-80 ms. A 6,000 km fibre route adds at least 30 ms each way, however fast the routers are. Throughput scales (Gbit/s, GB/s, TB/s)General performance units · Metric · Current · Beginner Data rates range from megabits per second on mobile links to terabytes per second inside AI accelerators. Home broadband might give 1 Gbit/s, a fast NVMe SSD over 10 GB/s, and an AI GPU's HBM memory several TB/s. Back-of-the-envelope estimationEngineering practice · Concept · Current · Beginner Quickly multiplying rough counts by rough costs to judge whether something is feasible before building it. 1 million users × 10 requests a day ≈ 116 requests per second on average — easy for one modest server. Logarithmic scaleMathematics · Concept · Current · Beginner A scale where each step is a multiple (such as ×10), making huge ranges readable on one chart. Moore's law is plotted on a log scale, so 50 years of doubling appear as a nearly straight line. Exascale10^18 FLOPS; first reached on the TOP500 by Frontier (2022) · Metric · Current · Beginner Computing at 10^18 — a billion billion — floating-point operations per second. An exascale machine does in one second what a person doing one sum per second would need about 31.7 billion years to finish. Powers-of-two rule (2^10 ≈ 10^3)Engineering rule of thumb · Concept · Current · Beginner Because 1,024 is close to 1,000, every extra 10 bits multiplies a count by about a thousand, making binary sizes easy to estimate. A 10 Gbit/s link with an 80 ms round trip needs about 100 MB in flight, so TCP windows must grow very large.

docs.title: 1.15 A Short History of Computing: From Babbage to Exascale
docs.text:
Modern computers are the result of about two centuries of ideas and inventions, from mechanical calculating engines to chips with hundreds of billions of transistors. Each step — theory, vacuum tubes, transistors, integrated circuits, microprocessors, personal computers, smartphones and AI accelerators — made computing smaller, cheaper and more powerful. Knowing the timeline helps you understand why today's machines look the way they do.

Milestones from Babbage to exascale. Each milestone made computing smaller, cheaper or faster — usually all three.

Think of it like…

Computing history is like a relay race: Babbage and Lovelace drew the map, Turing and von Neumann wrote the rules, and each generation of engineers took the baton and ran faster with smaller, cheaper parts.

Real-world example

For a history poster, Aisha picks five milestones: ENIAC (1945), a room-sized machine with about 18,000 vacuum tubes drawing roughly 150 kW; the Intel 4004 (1971), a whole CPU on one chip with about 2,300 transistors; the IBM PC (1981), which made the personal computer an everyday business tool; the iPhone (2007), which put a powerful computer in millions of pockets; and Frontier (2022), the first officially ranked exascale supercomputer. In under 80 years computers went from filling a room to fitting in a palm, while becoming trillions of times faster.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. 1800s: mechanical ideas — Babbage designs the Analytical Engine and Ada Lovelace publishes an algorithm for it.
  2. 1930s-40s: theory and electronics — Turing's universal machine (1936), Shannon's switching circuits, Colossus, ENIAC and the first stored-program computers.
  3. 1947-1971: the transistor, the integrated circuit and the first microprocessor (Intel 4004) shrink computers dramatically.
  4. 1970s-1990s: personal computers (Apple II, IBM PC), Arm's low-power RISC chips and the first GPUs.
  5. 2000s: multicore processors, smartphones (iPhone 2007, Android 2008) and cloud computing.
  6. 2010s-2020s: GPUs power deep learning, exascale supercomputers arrive (Frontier, 2022) and generative AI goes mainstream.

Who uses it

Students, teachers, technology journalists, and anyone asked in an interview or exam to explain how computing evolved will find this timeline useful.

Key takeaway

Memorise a handful of anchor dates: 1936 Turing, 1945 ENIAC, 1947 transistor, 1971 Intel 4004, 1981 IBM PC, 2007 iPhone, 2022 Frontier exascale.

Going deeper

  • Computer generations are often grouped by switching technology: vacuum tubes (1940s-50s), discrete transistors (late 1950s-60s), integrated circuits (1960s-70s) and microprocessors (1970s onwards).
  • Colossus stayed secret until the 1970s, which is partly why ENIAC was long called the first electronic computer; the Manchester Baby of 1948 was the first to run a program stored in its own memory.
  • IBM's System/360 (1964) offered one instruction set across a family of compatible machines of different speeds — separating architecture from implementation, the idea that x86 and Arm still follow.
  • Software milestones matter as much as hardware: FORTRAN (1957) made compilers practical, UNIX and C (early 1970s) made operating systems portable, and Linux (1991) now runs most servers and every TOP500 supercomputer.
  • Clock speeds rose roughly a thousandfold from the 1970s to the mid-2000s and then flattened around 3-5 GHz; since then gains have come from more and wider cores, accelerators and smaller number formats.
  • On the June 2026 TOP500 list China's LineShine took first place at about 2.2 exaFLOPS, ending El Capitan's run at the top and becoming the fifth exascale system on the list.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Calling ENIAC 'the first computer' without qualification: Colossus, the Atanasoff-Berry Computer and Zuse's Z3 came earlier in different forms, so precise claims need qualifiers.
  • Assuming Ada Lovelace built hardware: she analysed and wrote programs for Babbage's Analytical Engine, which was never completed.
  • Thinking history is irrelevant to the job: x86's 1978 roots explain its variable-length instructions and legacy modes that engineers still handle today.

docs.title: Try it: Compare then and now with quick arithmetic
docs.text:
eniac_adds_per_s = 5_000      # ENIAC (1945), about 5,000 additions per second
frontier_flops = 1.1e18       # Frontier HPL result (2022)
print(f'{frontier_flops / eniac_adds_per_s:.1e}x faster')    # ~2.2e+14
print(f'{208e9 / 2300:,.0f}x more transistors (4004 -> B200)')

Presper Eckert and John Mauchly (ENIAC, 1945) · System · Legacy · Beginner Early electronic computers built from vacuum tubes: Colossus helped break wartime codes at Bletchley Park; ENIAC was general-purpose. Intel 4004 (1971)Intel (Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff, Stan Mazor) with Busicom's Masatoshi Shima · Processor · Legacy · Beginner The first commercial single-chip microprocessor: 4-bit, about 2,300 transistors, running at up to 740 kHz. IBM PC (1981)IBM (model 5150) · System · Legacy · Beginner A personal computer with an Intel 8088 CPU and Microsoft's MS-DOS; its open design created the 'PC compatible' industry. Today's Windows PCs still descend from the IBM PC's x86 architecture. The first ARM1 chip ran in 1985; today Apple's M-series Macs and AWS Graviton servers use Arm-based processors. GPU (1999 onwards)NVIDIA GeForce 256, marketed as the first 'GPU' · Accelerator · Current · Beginner Graphics chips with many parallel units; they became programmable for general maths (CUDA, 2006-07) and now drive AI. AlexNet's 2012 image-recognition win, trained on two NVIDIA gaming GPUs, kicked off the deep-learning boom. Multicore processors (2000s)IBM POWER4 (2001); AMD and Intel desktop dual-cores (2005) · Processor · Current · Beginner Several CPU cores on one chip, adopted once the power wall stopped clock speeds rising. In 2005 AMD's Athlon 64 X2 and Intel's Pentium D brought dual-core chips to home PCs. Smartphone era (2007 onwards)Apple iPhone (2007); Google Android (2008) · System · Current · Beginner Phones became general-purpose pocket computers built on Arm system-on-chips — the most widespread computers ever made. A mid-range phone today packs a multi-core CPU, a GPU and an AI engine onto one chip smaller than a fingernail. Exascale and the AI era (2020s)Frontier (ORNL, 2022); El Capitan (LLNL); LineShine (NSCS Shenzhen) · System · Current · Beginner Supercomputers passed 10^18 FLOPS, and AI clusters with tens of thousands of GPUs now train generative models. Commands like ls and cat that students type in a Linux terminal today descend directly from 1970s Bell Labs UNIX. In 2006 a start-up could launch EC2 virtual servers with a credit card instead of buying and racking its own machines.

docs.title: Glossary of Terms
A
docs.text: Accelerator A specialised chip (GPU, TPU, NPU, FPGA) that runs certain workloads much faster or more efficiently than a general CPU. ALU Arithmetic Logic Unit — the part of a processor that does maths and logic operations. Amdahl's law The speed-up from parallelism is limited by the part of the program that must stay serial. APU Accelerated Processing Unit — AMD's name for a chip combining CPU cores and a capable GPU that share memory. ASIC Application-Specific Integrated Circuit — a chip designed for one fixed job; most efficient, but costly to design and unchangeable. Assembly language The human-readable text form of a processor's machine instructions, one line per instruction, specific to each instruction set.

docs.title: B
docs.text: Bandwidth How much data can be moved per second, e.g. a memory system delivering 100 GB/s. Binary The base-2 number system using only 0 and 1, which computers use internally. BIOS / UEFI Firmware that starts a PC, tests hardware and hands control to the operating system; UEFI is the modern replacement for BIOS. Bit / Byte A bit is one binary digit; a byte is 8 bits. Branch prediction The CPU guessing which way an if-statement will go so it can keep its pipeline full.

docs.title: C
docs.text: Cache Small, very fast memory close to the CPU that keeps copies of recently used data. Chiplet A small die combined with others in one package to build a larger processor. Clock speed How many cycles per second a processor runs, measured in gigahertz (GHz). Cloud computing Renting computing power, storage and services over the Internet, paying for what you use. Compiler A program that translates source code (e.g. C) into machine code a CPU can run. Container A lightweight package of an app and its dependencies that shares the host's OS kernel. Core An independent processing unit inside a CPU; modern chips have many cores. CPI / IPC Cycles Per Instruction and its inverse, Instructions Per Cycle — measures of CPU efficiency. CPU Central Processing Unit — the general-purpose processor that runs programs. CUDA NVIDIA's platform and programming model for running general code on its GPUs. CXL Compute Express Link — an open interconnect built on PCIe for sharing and expanding memory between processors and devices.

docs.title: D
docs.text: DDR5 The fifth generation of Double Data Rate DRAM used as main memory in PCs and servers. Die A single piece of silicon cut from a wafer containing a chip's circuits. DMA Direct Memory Access — a device copying data to or from main memory by itself, without the CPU moving each byte. DPU Data Processing Unit — a network card with its own processor cores that runs networking, storage and security services for a server. DRAM Dynamic RAM — dense main memory that stores bits as charge in capacitors and must be refreshed. DSP Digital Signal Processor — a processor optimised for fast multiply-accumulate maths on audio, radio and sensor signals.

docs.title: E
docs.text: ECC Error-Correcting Code — extra check bits stored with data so memory can detect and automatically fix bit errors. Edge computing Processing data close to where it is created (factories, shops, phones) instead of a distant data centre.

docs.title: F
docs.text: Firmware Low-level software stored in a chip that controls hardware, such as UEFI or an SSD controller's code. Floating point A way of storing real numbers with a sign, exponent and fraction, standardised by IEEE 754. FLOPS Floating-point operations per second — a measure of maths throughput (e.g. teraFLOPS, exaFLOPS). FPGA Field-Programmable Gate Array — a chip whose logic can be rewired after manufacture.

docs.title: G
docs.text: Garbage collection Automatic memory management that frees objects a program can no longer reach, used by Java, C#, Go, JavaScript and Python. GPU Graphics Processing Unit — a massively parallel processor used for graphics, AI and scientific computing.

docs.title: H
docs.text: HBM High Bandwidth Memory — stacked DRAM placed beside a GPU or accelerator for very high bandwidth. Hexadecimal Base-16 numbers (0-9, A-F); one hex digit equals four bits. HPC High-Performance Computing — using supercomputers and clusters to solve very large problems. Hypervisor Software that creates and runs virtual machines, such as KVM, ESXi or Hyper-V.

docs.title: I
docs.text: Instruction set architecture (ISA) The contract between software and hardware: the instructions, registers and rules a CPU understands, e.g. x86-64, Arm, RISC-V. Interrupt A signal that makes the CPU pause its current work to handle an urgent event. ISP Image Signal Processor — hardware that turns raw camera-sensor data into finished photos and video.

docs.title: K
docs.text: Kernel The core of an operating system that manages CPU time, memory and devices. Kubernetes An open-source system for deploying, scaling and managing containers across many machines.

docs.title: L
docs.text: Latency The time one operation takes from start to finish, e.g. nanoseconds for a cache hit. Logic gate A tiny circuit (AND, OR, NOT, NAND...) that computes a Boolean function on bits.

docs.title: M
docs.text: Microcontroller (MCU) A small, low-power chip with a CPU, memory and I/O on one die, used in embedded devices. Moore's law Gordon Moore's observation that transistor counts on chips roughly double about every two years. MPI Message Passing Interface — the standard for programs that communicate across nodes of a cluster. MPU Microprocessor / application processor — a CPU chip with an MMU and external memory that can run a full OS such as Linux.

docs.title: N
docs.text: NPU Neural Processing Unit — a block on a chip designed to run AI models efficiently. NVMe Non-Volatile Memory Express — the fast protocol SSDs use to talk to a computer over PCIe.

docs.title: O
docs.text: Operating system (OS) Software that manages hardware and provides services to programs, e.g. Linux, Windows, macOS. Out-of-order execution A CPU technique that runs instructions as soon as their inputs are ready, not strictly in program order.

docs.title: P
docs.text: Paging Dividing memory into fixed-size pages so the OS can map virtual addresses to physical memory. PCIe PCI Express — the high-speed serial bus connecting GPUs, SSDs and network cards to the CPU. Pipeline Splitting instruction processing into stages so several instructions are in progress at once. Process A running program with its own memory space, managed by the operating system.

docs.title: Q
docs.text: Qubit A quantum bit that can be in a superposition of 0 and 1; the basic unit of quantum computing.

docs.title: R
docs.text: RAID Redundant Array of Independent Disks — combining drives for speed, capacity or protection. Register The fastest storage in a CPU, holding the values an instruction is working on right now. RISC / CISC Reduced vs Complex Instruction Set Computer — two philosophies of ISA design.

docs.title: S
docs.text: Scheduler The part of an OS (or cluster) that decides which work runs where and when. Serverless A cloud model where you upload functions and the provider runs and scales them, billing per use. Side-channel attack Stealing secrets by measuring side effects of computation, such as timing, power use or cache state, instead of exploiting a software bug. SIMD Single Instruction, Multiple Data — one instruction processes a vector of values at once. SoC System on a Chip — CPU, GPU, NPU, memory controllers and I/O integrated on one chip. SRAM Static RAM — fast memory built from transistor latches, used for caches. SSD Solid-State Drive — storage built from NAND flash with no moving parts. Supercomputer One of the world's fastest computers, ranked twice a year on the TOP500 list. System call A request from a program to the operating system kernel, e.g. to open a file.

docs.title: T
docs.text: TDP Thermal Design Power — the heat (in watts) a cooling system must remove under sustained load. Tensor core A GPU unit that performs small matrix multiply-accumulate operations very quickly for AI. Thread A sequence of instructions within a process that can be scheduled independently. Throughput How much work is completed per unit of time, e.g. requests per second. TLB Translation Lookaside Buffer — a cache of recent virtual-to-physical address translations. TPU Tensor Processing Unit — Google's AI accelerator ASIC (not to be confused with a Trusted Platform Module). Transistor A tiny electronic switch; billions of them form every modern chip.

docs.title: V
docs.text: Virtual machine (VM) A software-emulated computer that runs its own operating system on shared hardware. Virtual memory Giving each process its own private address space, mapped by hardware and the OS onto real memory. von Neumann architecture A design where programs and data share the same memory, fetched by the CPU one instruction at a time.

docs.title: Chapter 4: GPUs & AI Accelerators
docs.text: Modern AI, graphics and science run on chips built to do millions of sums at once: GPUs, TPUs, NPUs, FPGAs and a wave of new AI accelerators. This chapter explains why these chips beat ordinary CPUs at parallel work, how a GPU is organised inside and how it draws graphics, and who makes the key products as of late 2026, from NVIDIA Blackwell and Rubin to AMD Instinct, Google TPUs and laptop NPUs. You will also see how a chip is designed from RTL to tape-out, and learn the number formats, compute maths and networking that turn thousands of accelerators into one AI supercomputer.

docs.title: 4.1 Why Accelerators? CPUs vs GPUs and Specialised Chips
docs.text:
A CPU is a clever all-rounder that finishes one task at a time very quickly, while an accelerator is a chip built to do one kind of job, such as huge piles of multiplications, much faster and with less energy. Graphics, scientific simulation and AI all involve doing the same simple sum on millions of numbers at once, so a chip with thousands of small workers beats a chip with a few brilliant ones. Accelerators exist because ordinary chips stopped getting faster for free, so designers now win speed by specialising.

CPU vs GPU vs AI ASIC

CPU GPU AI ASIC (e.g. TPU) Compute units 8-192 big cores Thousands of simple lanes Large matrix units Optimised for Latency, branchy code Throughput, parallel maths One workload family Memory DDR5, big caches HBM or GDDR, TB/s HBM plus large on-chip SRAM Flexibility Runs anything Parallel programs Mostly neural networks Programming C, Java, Python... CUDA, ROCm, Triton XLA, vendor SDKs AI work per watt Lowest High Highest

Moving right trades flexibility for throughput and energy efficiency on parallel maths.

Think of it like…

A CPU is a few expert chefs who can cook any dish quickly; a GPU is a factory line of hundreds of helpers who can each only chop vegetables, but together they chop a mountain in minutes.

Real-world example

Leo, a physics student, simulates 10 million particles. His 8-core laptop CPU handles about 8 particles at a time and needs 40 minutes per run. His university's GPU runs thousands of particle updates in parallel and finishes in about 90 seconds. But when Leo parses a messy config file with lots of if-statements, the CPU is faster, because that job cannot be split into thousands of identical pieces.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Ask whether the work is the same simple operation repeated on lots of data (parallel) or a long chain of decisions (serial).
  2. Parallel, maths-heavy work (graphics, matrices, AI) goes to a GPU or AI accelerator; branchy, serial work stays on the CPU.
  3. The CPU still runs the operating system, prepares the data and launches work on the accelerator.
  4. Check whether the job is limited by maths speed or by how fast memory can feed data (the roofline idea).
  5. Measure the real speed-up, remembering Amdahl's law: the serial part limits the total gain.

Who uses it

Machine-learning engineers, HPC scientists, game developers, data-centre architects and anyone choosing hardware for AI or simulation meets this trade-off.

Key takeaway

Memorise the one-liner: CPUs are optimised for latency (one task fast), GPUs for throughput (many tasks at once) — and most real systems use both together.

Going deeper

  • Specialisation wins by removing overhead: on a CPU most energy per instruction goes to fetching, decoding, scheduling and moving data, so dedicated datapaths can save tens of times the energy.
  • Roofline formula: attainable FLOPS = min(peak FLOPS, memory bandwidth × arithmetic intensity). Kernels left of the ridge point are memory-bound; those to the right are compute-bound.
  • Dennard scaling ended around 2005 and the power wall held clocks near 3-5 GHz, so performance growth moved to more cores, wider vectors and specialised accelerators.
  • Matrix multiplication dominates AI: an n × n matmul does 2n³ operations on 3n² values, so its arithmetic intensity grows with size, perfect for dense tensor units.
  • Accelerators still need a host CPU for the operating system, I/O and orchestration; system balance (PCIe or NVLink-C2C bandwidth, CPU memory, networking) often decides real speed.
  • TOPS and FLOPS figures are usually quoted at the lowest supported precision and sometimes with sparsity; normalise format (INT8, FP8, FP4) and dense versus sparse before comparing chips.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming a GPU speeds up any program: serial, branch-heavy or small workloads often run faster on the CPU.
  • Comparing peak TFLOPS across vendors or number formats directly: precision, sparsity and achievable utilisation differ widely.
  • Ignoring data transfer: copying data to and from the accelerator can erase the gain for small or one-off computations.

docs.title: Try it: Work out a roofline: is a matrix multiply limited by maths or by memory?
docs.text:
# Roofline back-of-envelope in Python
peak_flops = 989e12      # e.g. H100 SXM dense BF16, FLOP/s
mem_bw     = 3.35e12     # H100 SXM HBM3, bytes/s
ridge = peak_flops / mem_bw
print(f'Ridge point: {ridge:.0f} FLOPs per byte')

n = 4096                 # square matrices, BF16 = 2 bytes
flops = 2 * n**3
bytes_moved = 3 * n * n * 2
ai = flops / bytes_moved
print(f'Matmul intensity: {ai:.0f} FLOPs/byte ->',
      'compute-bound' if ai > ridge else 'memory-bound')

docs.title: Key chips, architectures, standards, tools & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example Domain-specific architecture (DSA)Popularised by Hennessy & Patterson (Turing Lecture, 2018) · Concept · Current · Intermediate A chip designed for one family of tasks, trading flexibility for big gains in speed and energy efficiency. Google's TPU drops features CPUs need for general code and spends the silicon on matrix-multiply units instead. Roofline modelWilliams, Waterman & Patterson, Communications of the ACM, 2009 · Concept · Current · Intermediate A chart showing whether code is limited by peak compute or by memory bandwidth, based on its arithmetic intensity. Plotting a kernel on the roofline shows it sits under the memory slope, so faster memory, not more cores, will help. Arithmetic intensityRoofline model terminology · Metric · Current · Intermediate Number of maths operations performed per byte moved from memory; high intensity means compute-bound, low means memory-bound. Large matrix multiplies reach hundreds of FLOPs per byte; adding two vectors manages well under one. FLOPS and TOPSIndustry metrics · Metric · Current · Beginner FLOPS counts floating-point operations per second; TOPS counts trillions of (usually integer) operations per second, often quoted for NPUs. A laptop NPU rated 50 TOPS at INT8 cannot be compared directly with a GPU's FP16 TFLOPS figure. Heterogeneous computingGeneral architecture concept · Concept · Current · Beginner Using different processor types (CPU, GPU, NPU, FPGA) together in one system, each doing the work it suits best. A phone's CPU runs the app, its GPU draws the interface and its NPU blurs the photo background. Latency-optimised core (CPU style)Intel, AMD, Arm, Apple and other CPU designs · Concept · Current · Beginner A few large cores with out-of-order logic, branch predictors and big caches, spending silicon to finish one thread as fast as possible. A laptop CPU core runs a branchy JSON parser quickly because it predicts branches and reorders instructions on the fly. Throughput-optimised core (GPU style)NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, Apple and other GPU designs · Concept · Current · Beginner Thousands of simple lanes that hide memory delays by switching between many threads, maximising total work rather than single-task speed. A GPU keeps tens of thousands of threads in flight, so while some wait for memory, others compute pixels or matrix tiles. Systolic arrayH. T. Kung and C. E. Leiserson (1978); used in Google TPUs · Architecture · Current · Intermediate A grid of multiply-accumulate cells where data pulses from neighbour to neighbour, reusing each value many times without returning to memory. A 128 × 128 systolic array, as used in TPU matrix units, performs 16,384 multiply-accumulates every clock cycle. Ridge point (machine balance)Roofline model terminology · Metric · Current · Advanced Peak FLOPS divided by memory bandwidth: the arithmetic intensity a kernel needs before compute, rather than memory, limits it. An H100 SXM with 989 dense BF16 TFLOPS and 3.35 TB/s has a ridge point near 295 FLOPs per byte. Offload overheadGeneral heterogeneous-computing concept · Concept · Current · Intermediate Time spent copying data over PCIe and launching work on an accelerator; for small jobs it can exceed the time the accelerator saves. Adding two 1,000-element arrays is slower on a GPU overall, because copying data and launching the kernel outlasts the sum itself. Flexibility-efficiency spectrumGeneral computer-architecture concept · Concept · Current · Beginner Chips range from flexible but less efficient (CPU) through GPU and FPGA to fixed-function but most efficient (ASIC). A start-up prototypes on GPUs, moves a stable video pipeline to an FPGA, then ships an ASIC once the design is final.

docs.title: 4.2 Inside a GPU: SMs, Warps, Tensor Cores and Memory
docs.text:
A GPU is built from dozens or hundreds of identical blocks (NVIDIA calls them Streaming Multiprocessors, AMD calls them Compute Units). Each block runs groups of threads in lockstep, all doing the same instruction on different data. Special units called tensor cores do small matrix multiplications in one step, which is exactly what AI needs, and a stack of very fast memory sits right next to the chip to keep them fed.

GPU memory hierarchy (H100 example). Fast code keeps reused data high in this stack and streams everything else from HBM.

Think of it like…

A GPU is like a huge exam hall split into rooms (SMs); in each room an invigilator reads out one instruction and 32 students (a warp) all do that step on their own question at the same moment.

Real-world example

Aisha writes a kernel that adds two arrays of 1 million numbers. She launches 4,096 blocks of 256 threads; the GPU spreads the blocks across its SMs, and each SM runs its threads in warps of 32. Because neighbouring threads read neighbouring numbers, memory accesses are combined and the job takes well under a millisecond. When she later adds an if-statement that sends half of each warp down a different path, the warps must run both paths one after the other and her kernel slows noticeably.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The CPU copies data to GPU memory and launches a kernel: a grid of thread blocks.
  2. The GPU scheduler hands blocks to SMs (NVIDIA) or CUs (AMD), which split them into warps of 32 or wavefronts of 64 threads.
  3. Each warp executes one instruction across all its threads (SIMT); while one warp waits for memory, the SM switches to another to hide the delay.
  4. Matrix-heavy instructions go to tensor cores (matrix cores on AMD); ray tracing goes to RT cores.
  5. Threads use registers first, then shared memory/L1, then L2 cache, then off-chip HBM or GDDR memory.
  6. Results are written back to GPU memory and copied to the CPU when needed.

Who uses it

CUDA/HIP developers, ML performance engineers, game-engine programmers and computer-architecture students need this mental model to write fast code.

Key takeaway

Learn the ladder registers → shared memory/L1 → L2 → HBM: each step down is larger but slower, and good GPU code keeps reused data as high up the ladder as possible.

Going deeper

  • An H100 SXM has 132 SMs, each with four warp schedulers, 128 FP32 lanes and four tensor cores, and can keep up to 64 warps (2,048 threads) resident per SM.
  • GPUs hide latency instead of avoiding it: when one warp waits hundreds of cycles for memory, the scheduler issues from another ready warp at no switching cost, since every warp's registers stay resident.
  • Tensor cores gained formats each generation: FP16 (Volta), TF32, BF16 and 2:4 sparsity (Ampere), FP8 (Hopper), then FP6 and FP4 with micro-scaling (Blackwell).
  • Hopper added thread-block clusters, distributed shared memory and the Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA) for asynchronous bulk copies, letting data loading overlap tensor-core maths.
  • Occupancy is limited by registers per thread, shared memory per block and threads per block; Nsight Compute shows which resource is the limiter.
  • Single-thread speed is modest: GPU clocks run around 1.5-2.5 GHz, each warp issues in order, and there is no deep branch prediction or speculation like on CPUs.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Equating CUDA cores with CPU cores: a CUDA core is one arithmetic lane, not an independent processor with its own instruction stream.
  • Launching too few threads: a kernel with a handful of blocks leaves most SMs idle; aim for many blocks per SM.
  • Ignoring access patterns: strided or uncoalesced memory access can make a kernel several times slower than its maths suggests.
  • Assuming more registers per thread always helps: heavy register use lowers occupancy and can spill to slow local memory.

docs.title: Try it: Ask your NVIDIA GPU about its SM count, memory and clocks
docs.text:
nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,memory.total,clocks.max.sm,utilization.gpu --format=csv
python -c "import torch;p=torch.cuda.get_device_properties(0);print(p.name,p.multi_processor_count,'SMs',p.total_memory//2**30,'GiB')"

docs.title: Key chips, architectures, standards, tools & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example Streaming Multiprocessor (SM)NVIDIA · Component · Current · Intermediate NVIDIA's basic GPU building block, containing CUDA cores, tensor cores, registers, schedulers and shared memory/L1 cache. An H100 SXM has 132 SMs enabled; a laptop RTX GPU might have around 20-40. Compute Unit (CU)AMD (CDNA, RDNA); Intel uses Xe-cores · Component · Current · Intermediate AMD's equivalent of an SM: a cluster of SIMD units, registers and local data share memory. An AMD Radeon RX 9070 XT has 64 CUs; an Instinct MI300X has 304. Warp / wavefrontNVIDIA (warp, 32 threads); AMD (wavefront, 64 on CDNA, 32 or 64 on RDNA) · Concept · Current · Intermediate A group of threads that the hardware schedules together and that execute the same instruction at the same time. A block of 256 threads on an NVIDIA GPU is run as 8 warps of 32 threads each. SIMT (Single Instruction, Multiple Threads)NVIDIA term (Tesla architecture, 2006) · Architecture · Current · Intermediate Execution model where each thread has its own data and registers, but threads in a warp share one instruction stream. Code is written for one thread, yet the hardware runs it for 32 threads per instruction issued. Warp divergenceGPU programming concept · Concept · Current · Advanced When threads in one warp take different branches, the warp runs each path in turn, wasting lanes and slowing the kernel. An if-statement on odd versus even thread IDs can roughly halve that section's speed. CUDA coreNVIDIA · Component · Current · Beginner Marketing name for one scalar FP32/INT32 arithmetic lane inside an SM; GPUs have thousands of them. The GeForce RTX 5090 is listed with 21,760 CUDA cores. Tensor CoreNVIDIA (first in Volta V100, 2017); AMD calls its versions Matrix Cores · Component · Current · Beginner A unit that multiplies small matrices and adds the result in one operation, giving huge speed-ups for AI. Training in BF16 on tensor cores is many times faster than using the same GPU's ordinary FP32 lanes. RT CoreNVIDIA (first in Turing, 2018); AMD Ray Accelerators · Component · Current · Beginner Hardware that speeds up ray-tracing tests, checking which triangles a light ray hits, for realistic graphics. A game turns on ray-traced reflections; RT cores handle the ray-triangle tests while shader cores colour pixels. GPU register fileAll GPU vendors · Component · Current · Advanced The fastest storage on the GPU, private to each thread; using too many registers per thread reduces how many warps fit. Each H100 SM has a 256 KB register file shared among all the threads it hosts. Shared memory / L1 cacheNVIDIA (shared memory); AMD (LDS, Local Data Share) · Component · Current · Intermediate Small, very fast on-chip memory that threads in a block can share, used to reuse tiles of data. A matrix-multiply kernel loads 64x64 tiles into shared memory so each value is read from HBM only once. GPU L2 cacheAll GPU vendors · Component · Current · Intermediate Large on-chip cache shared by all of a GPU's SMs, catching repeated accesses before they reach HBM or GDDR memory. The H100 has a 50 MB L2 cache; AMD's MI300X adds a 256 MB Infinity Cache. GDDR memoryJEDEC (GDDR6, GDDR7) · Component · Current · Beginner Graphics DRAM soldered around the GPU on the board; cheaper than HBM with lower bandwidth, used in gaming and workstation cards. The RTX 5090 uses 32 GB of GDDR7 on a 512-bit bus. OccupancyNVIDIA / GPU programming term · Metric · Current · Advanced The ratio of active warps on an SM to the maximum possible; higher occupancy helps hide memory delays. Cutting registers per thread from 128 to 64 let twice as many warps run, raising occupancy and speed. GPU memory bandwidthVendor datasheets · Metric · Current · Beginner Bytes per second the GPU can move between its HBM or GDDR memory and the chip; often the true limit for AI inference. An H200's roughly 4.8 TB/s lets it read its entire 141 GB memory about 34 times every second. Memory coalescingCUDA and HIP programming guides · Concept · Current · Intermediate Combining neighbouring threads' memory accesses into a few wide transactions, achieved when consecutive threads read consecutive addresses. Threads 0-31 reading floats 0-31 need one 128-byte transaction; reading every 32nd float needs 32 separate ones.

docs.title: 4.3 NVIDIA GPUs: From V100 to Blackwell, Rubin and GeForce RTX 50
docs.text:
NVIDIA is the biggest maker of AI accelerators, and it releases a new data-centre GPU family roughly every year or two, each named after a scientist: Volta, Ampere, Hopper, Blackwell and now Rubin. Each generation adds more memory, faster links between GPUs and support for smaller, faster number formats. The same architectures also appear, scaled down, in GeForce gaming cards and RTX PRO workstation cards.

NVIDIA data-centre GPU generations. Roughly yearly launches, each adding memory, link bandwidth and a smaller number format.

Think of it like…

NVIDIA's generations are like yearly smartphone models: the shape stays familiar, but each one has more memory, a faster chip and new tricks the previous model lacked.

Real-world example

A fictional AI start-up, Northwind Labs, trained its first model on rented A100s in 2022. In 2024 it moved to H100s, which use FP8 and finished a similar job in roughly a third of the time. In 2025 it reserved part of a GB200 NVL72 rack, where 72 Blackwell GPUs share one NVLink domain and act like one giant GPU. For 2027 it is evaluating Vera Rubin NVL72 cloud capacity, which only began shipping in late 2026.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Volta V100 (2017) introduced tensor cores; Ampere A100 (2020) added TF32, BF16 and Multi-Instance GPU.
  2. Hopper H100 (2022) and H200 (2024) added FP8 and the Transformer Engine, with up to 141 GB of HBM3e.
  3. Blackwell B200/GB200 (2024-25) joined two dies in one package, added FP4 and the 72-GPU NVL72 rack.
  4. Blackwell Ultra B300/GB300 (2025) raised memory to 288 GB HBM3e per GPU.
  5. Vera Rubin (production shipments from August 2026) brings HBM4, NVLink 6 and the Vera CPU; Rubin CPX and Rubin Ultra follow.
  6. GeForce RTX 50 (Blackwell, 2025) and RTX PRO cards bring the same ideas to gamers and workstations.

Who uses it

AI researchers, cloud providers, HPC centres, gamers and anyone renting GPU instances meet these product names daily.

Key takeaway

Learn each generation with one headline feature: V100 = tensor cores, A100 = TF32/MIG, H100 = FP8, B200 = FP4 and NVL72, Rubin = HBM4 and NVLink 6.

Going deeper

  • Data-centre GPUs come as SXM modules on HGX baseboards, for full NVLink bandwidth and higher power, or as PCIe cards that fit standard servers with lower limits.
  • Power per GPU has climbed steeply: about 300 W for V100 SXM, up to 700 W for H100 SXM and roughly 1,000-1,400 W for Blackwell parts, pushing data centres to liquid cooling.
  • The rack is now the product: a GB200 NVL72 draws roughly 120 kW and ships as one liquid-cooled unit with NVLink switch trays, power shelves and cabling.
  • NVIDIA moves whole platforms each generation (GPU, Grace or Vera CPU, NVLink, ConnectX NICs, switches), so buyers plan around platform generations rather than single chips.
  • Software longevity is a selling point: CUDA, cuDNN, NCCL, TensorRT and NGC containers span generations, though new formats such as FP4 need recent drivers and libraries.
  • US export controls restrict the most powerful AI GPUs for some countries, which has led NVIDIA to offer cut-down variants for those markets.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Comparing rack figures with single-GPU figures: check whether quoted petaFLOPS or bandwidth is per GPU, per board or per NVL72 rack.
  • Assuming GeForce gaming cards suit data centres: memory, NVLink, cooling, support and licensing terms differ from data-centre parts.
  • Reading roadmap dates as delivery dates: new parts reach the largest customers first and appear in public clouds months later.

docs.title: 4.4 AMD Instinct and Radeon GPUs
docs.text:
AMD is NVIDIA's main GPU rival. Its Instinct accelerators (based on the CDNA architecture) power supercomputers and AI clouds and are known for carrying lots of memory, while its Radeon cards (RDNA architecture) target gamers and workstations. AMD builds its big chips from several smaller 'chiplets' stacked and joined in one package.

AMD Instinct generations. AMD's lever each generation: more HBM per GPU, then rack-scale systems.

Think of it like…

If NVIDIA is the market-leading car brand, AMD is the strong challenger that often offers a bigger boot (more memory) for the money, and now sells whole buses (rack systems) too.

Real-world example

Marta runs inference for a fictional legal-search firm, Briefwise. Her 405-billion-parameter model in FP8 needs about 405 GB just for weights. Eight MI300X GPUs give 1.5 TB of HBM3 in one server, so the model fits with plenty of room for KV cache. When she upgrades to MI355X (288 GB each), the same server holds about 2.3 TB and can also run FP4.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. CDNA architecture powers Instinct data-centre GPUs; RDNA powers Radeon gaming cards.
  2. MI250X (2021) powered Frontier; MI300X/MI300A (2023) brought 3D-stacked chiplets and 128-192 GB of HBM3.
  3. MI325X (2024) and MI350X/MI355X (2025) raised memory to 256 and 288 GB HBM3E and added FP4/FP6.
  4. MI400 series and the 72-GPU Helios rack (shipping from late 2026) add HBM4 and rack-scale design.
  5. Software runs through ROCm and HIP; PyTorch and vLLM support AMD GPUs directly.

Who uses it

Supercomputer centres, cloud providers, AI labs looking for a second supplier, and gamers buying Radeon cards.

Key takeaway

Remember AMD's selling point in one phrase: 'more HBM per GPU' — and that El Capitan (MI300A) and Frontier (MI250X) are AMD-powered exascale machines.

Going deeper

  • MI300X stacks eight XCD compute chiplets on four I/O dies using 3D hybrid bonding, surrounded by eight HBM3 stacks, a showcase of chiplet design.
  • CDNA runs 64-thread wavefronts (RDNA supports 32 and 64), so code tuned for NVIDIA's 32-thread warps may need changes to reductions, shuffles and occupancy tuning.
  • ROCm now ships faster with broader support: PyTorch, JAX, vLLM and SGLang run on Instinct, though niche CUDA-only libraries can still need porting through HIP.
  • Memory capacity is AMD's main lever: more HBM per GPU means fewer GPUs to hold a large model and its KV cache, lowering inference cost.
  • Infinity Fabric links up to eight Instinct GPUs per server today; Helios moves AMD to a 72-GPU rack-scale domain, with open standards such as UALink and Ultra Ethernet on its roadmap.
  • Radeon and Instinct share chiplet and packaging know-how but differ in focus: RDNA keeps display, ray-tracing and media engines, while CDNA drops them for matrix cores and FP64.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming CUDA code runs on AMD unchanged: it must be ported to HIP or run through frameworks with ROCm support.
  • Assuming every Radeon card is officially supported by ROCm: check AMD's compatibility list for your GPU and operating system.
  • Comparing AMD and NVIDIA on peak FLOPS alone: memory capacity, software maturity and networking often decide real cost.

docs.title: 4.5 Intel GPUs and Gaudi AI Accelerators
docs.text:
Intel, famous for CPUs, also makes graphics chips and AI accelerators, but its data-centre efforts have been bumpy. Its Gaudi chips are cost-focused AI accelerators, its big Ponte Vecchio GPU powered a supercomputer before being discontinued, and its Arc cards compete in budget gaming. New inference GPUs and a rack-scale system are on Intel's roadmap.

Intel's accelerator journey. A mix of shipped products, a cancelled GPU and an inference-first restart.

Think of it like…

Intel's accelerator story is like a famous restaurant opening a new cuisine: some dishes did well, some were taken off the menu, and the next menu is still being written.

Real-world example

A fictional college, Harbourside Tech, builds a teaching cluster on a tight budget. It buys Arc Pro B60 cards with 24 GB each to teach PyTorch through Intel's XPU backend, and rents Gaudi 3 time for a research project because the quoted price per job is lower than the GPUs it compared. Students also use OpenVINO to run the trained model on laptop NPUs.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Intel's Xe GPU architecture spans integrated graphics, Arc gaming cards and data-centre parts.
  2. Data Center GPU Max (Ponte Vecchio) powered the Aurora supercomputer but was discontinued.
  3. Gaudi (from the Habana Labs acquisition, 2019) offers AI accelerators with built-in Ethernet; Gaudi 3 launched in 2024.
  4. Falcon Shores was cut back to an internal test chip; Crescent Island (inference GPU) and Jaguar Shores (rack-scale) are next.
  5. Software uses oneAPI, SYCL, the PyTorch XPU backend and OpenVINO.

Who uses it

Budget-conscious AI teams, HPC centres with Intel systems, PC gamers and developers targeting Intel laptops.

Key takeaway

Know the code names: Ponte Vecchio (discontinued), Gaudi 3 (shipping), Crescent Island and Jaguar Shores (upcoming) — interviewers like candidates who track roadmaps.

Going deeper

  • Gaudi differs from GPUs: matrix engines plus programmable tensor processor cores, with RoCE Ethernet ports on the chip itself, so clusters scale out without separate network cards.
  • Intel's pitch is cost and openness: standard Ethernet, oneAPI and SYCL and OpenVINO rather than proprietary interconnects, aimed at enterprises not training frontier models.
  • Aurora at Argonne combines 63,744 Ponte Vecchio GPUs with 21,248 Xeon Max CPUs and passed one exaFLOPS on HPL in 2024.
  • Integrated Xe graphics ship in most Intel laptops, so Intel GPUs reach far more users than its discrete cards; XMX engines in Arc and Xe3 accelerate AI locally.
  • Arc Pro B-series cards and Crescent Island use cheaper GDDR6 or LPDDR5X instead of HBM, trading bandwidth for capacity and cost, a strategy aimed at inference rather than training.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming roadmap chips will ship as announced: Falcon Shores shows plans can be cancelled or turned into test vehicles.
  • Confusing Intel's NPU, integrated GPU and Gaudi: they target laptop AI features, client graphics and data-centre AI respectively.
  • Expecting CUDA-specific code to run on Intel hardware: use SYCL, oneAPI or framework backends such as PyTorch XPU.
