docs.title: 4.6 Programming GPUs: CUDA, ROCm, SYCL, Triton and Friends
docs.text:
To use a GPU you write small functions called kernels that run on thousands of threads at once, or, more often, you call libraries and frameworks that already contain fast kernels. NVIDIA's CUDA is the most widely used platform; AMD's ROCm, Khronos standards like OpenCL, SYCL and Vulkan, and newer tools like Triton offer alternatives. Most AI developers work in PyTorch or JAX and only drop down to kernels for the last bit of speed.

The GPU software stack. Most developers stay near the top; performance engineers work down into kernels and libraries.

Think of it like…

Frameworks like PyTorch are a microwave meal (quick and good enough), libraries like cuBLAS are a professional kitchen's ready-made sauces, and hand-written CUDA kernels are cooking from scratch for the very best result.

Real-world example

Tom fine-tunes a model in PyTorch; one line, model.to('cuda'), moves it to the GPU and PyTorch calls cuBLAS and cuDNN underneath. Profiling with Nsight Systems shows a custom activation function wasting time, so he writes a 30-line Triton kernel that fuses three operations into one and saves 12% per step. His colleague runs the same PyTorch code unchanged on an AMD MI300X, because PyTorch's ROCm build maps the same calls to HIP and rocBLAS.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Start in a framework (PyTorch, JAX) that already uses GPU libraries.
  2. Libraries like cuBLAS, cuDNN, rocBLAS and oneDNN provide tuned kernels for maths and neural-network layers.
  3. For custom operations, write kernels in Triton (Python-like) or CUDA/HIP (C++-like).
  4. Multi-GPU jobs use NCCL (NVIDIA) or RCCL (AMD) for collective communication.
  5. Profile with Nsight Systems/Compute or ROCm tools, then optimise memory access first.

Who uses it

ML engineers, HPC developers, graphics programmers and compiler engineers; CUDA skills appear in many AI-infrastructure job adverts.

Key takeaway

In interviews, explain why CUDA is a moat: nearly two decades of libraries, tools and community code — and know that HIP is designed to look almost identical to CUDA for easy porting.

Going deeper

  • CUDA code compiles to PTX, a virtual instruction set, and to SASS machine code for specific GPUs; shipping PTX lets the driver JIT-compile it for newer GPUs.
  • A sensible optimisation order: use libraries first, fuse operations to cut memory traffic, tile data into shared memory, then tune occupancy and instruction mix with Nsight Compute.
  • Streams and CUDA Graphs overlap independent kernels and copies and cut launch overhead, which matters when a model runs thousands of small kernels per step.
  • Portability layers include HIP (runs on AMD and NVIDIA), SYCL, Kokkos, OpenMP offload and Vulkan compute; AI frameworks hide most of this from everyday developers.
  • torch.compile captures Python models as graphs and generates fused Triton kernels, often giving speed-ups without any hand-written CUDA.
  • NCCL and RCCL pick ring or tree algorithms based on topology and message size, so correct detection of NVLink, PCIe and network layout is vital for multi-GPU speed.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Timing kernels without synchronising: launches are asynchronous, so measure with CUDA events or cudaDeviceSynchronize, not just CPU timers.
  • Copying data between CPU and GPU every step: keep tensors resident on the GPU and transfer only what you need.
  • Hand-writing kernels before profiling: time often goes to data loading or a few library calls, not the code you suspect.

docs.title: Try it: A minimal CUDA kernel that adds two vectors (save as add.cu, build with nvcc add.cu -o add)
docs.text:
#include <cstdio>
__global__ void add(const float* a, const float* b, float* c, int n) {
  int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;   // global thread id
  if (i < n) c[i] = a[i] + b[i];
}
int main() {
  int n = 1 << 20; size_t sz = n * sizeof(float);
  float *a, *b, *c;
  cudaMallocManaged(&a, sz); cudaMallocManaged(&b, sz); cudaMallocManaged(&c, sz);
  for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { a[i] = 1.0f; b[i] = 2.0f; }
  add<<<(n + 255) / 256, 256>>>(a, b, c, n);   // grid of 256-thread blocks
  cudaDeviceSynchronize();
  printf("c[0] = %f\n", c[0]);                  // prints 3.000000
  cudaFree(a); cudaFree(b); cudaFree(c);
}

docs.title: 4.7 Graphics: The Rendering Pipeline, Ray Tracing and Displays
docs.text:
GPUs were invented to draw pictures: they turn 3D scenes made of triangles into millions of coloured pixels, many times every second. The steps — moving triangles into place, working out which pixels they cover, colouring each pixel and sending the finished frame to the screen — form the graphics pipeline. Modern GPUs add ray tracing for realistic light and AI upscaling to keep frame rates high.

The real-time rendering pipeline. Ray tracing plugs into this pipeline for selected effects; rasterisation still draws most of a game's image.

Think of it like…

Rendering is like a stage crew rebuilding every frame of a film live: one team positions the scenery (vertices), another works out what each seat can see (rasterisation), and painters colour every visible spot (pixel shading) — over a hundred times a second.

Real-world example

Aisha's racing game targets 120 frames per second, so each frame must be finished in about 8.3 ms. The CPU sends draw calls for the cars, track and crowd; the GPU transforms millions of triangles, rasterises them and shades about 8.3 million pixels for a 4K screen. Ray-traced reflections are too slow at full resolution, so she renders at 1440p and lets AI upscaling rebuild a 4K image, while variable refresh rate keeps the monitor in step with each frame.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The game engine on the CPU decides what might be visible and issues draw calls through an API such as DirectX 12, Vulkan or Metal.
  2. Vertex shaders transform each triangle's corners from 3D world positions into screen positions.
  3. The rasteriser works out which pixels each triangle covers and creates fragments for them.
  4. Pixel (fragment) shaders compute colours from textures, lights and materials, and the depth buffer keeps only the nearest surface.
  5. Ray-tracing units trace rays for reflections, shadows and lighting, and AI upscalers and denoisers fill in detail.
  6. The finished frame waits in a frame buffer until the display engine sends it over DisplayPort or HDMI at the next refresh.

Who uses it

Game and graphics programmers, technical artists, GPU driver and architecture engineers, visual-effects and visualisation studios, and simulation and digital-twin developers work with the graphics pipeline.

Key takeaway

Think in frame time, not just frames per second: 60 fps means 16.7 ms per frame and 120 fps means 8.3 ms, and the slowest stage — CPU, GPU or memory — sets the limit.

Going deeper

  • Shaders are small programs running on the same GPU cores used for compute; one 4K frame launches millions of pixel-shader threads, which is why GPUs were massively parallel long before AI arrived.
  • Ray-tracing hardware speeds up two jobs: walking a bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) of nested boxes around the scene, and testing rays against triangles; denoisers then clean up the few rays per pixel affordable in real time.
  • Path tracing follows light bouncing many times for film-quality lighting; offline renderers spend minutes to hours per frame, while games use it only with heavy upscaling and denoising.
  • AI upscalers such as NVIDIA DLSS 4, AMD FSR 4 and Intel XeSS 2 render fewer pixels and reconstruct the rest with neural networks on tensor or matrix units; frame generation inserts AI-predicted frames between rendered ones.
  • Generated frames improve smoothness but not responsiveness, because input is only sampled on rendered frames; latency reducers such as NVIDIA Reflex and AMD Anti-Lag shorten the render queue to compensate.
  • Mobile GPUs use tile-based rendering, shading the screen in small tiles held in on-chip memory to save DRAM bandwidth and power, an approach desktop GPUs have adopted only partly.
  • Fixed-function media engines encode and decode H.264, HEVC and AV1 video, so streaming a game or joining a video call barely loads the shader cores.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Judging smoothness by average fps alone: stutter comes from occasional long frames, so check 1% lows or a frame-time graph.
  • Believing frame generation reduces input lag: it adds visual smoothness but slightly increases latency, so competitive players often turn it off.
  • Assuming ray tracing has replaced rasterisation: games are hybrids that rasterise the scene and ray-trace selected effects such as reflections, shadows and global lighting.

docs.title: Try it: A minimal vertex and fragment shader pair (GLSL)
docs.text:
// vertex shader: place each corner on screen
#version 330 core
layout(location = 0) in vec3 pos;
uniform mat4 mvp;
void main() { gl_Position = mvp * vec4(pos, 1.0); }

// fragment shader: colour every covered pixel orange
#version 330 core
out vec4 colour;
void main() { colour = vec4(1.0, 0.5, 0.0, 1.0); }

docs.title: Key chips, architectures, standards, tools & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example Graphics pipelineGraphics APIs (Direct3D, Vulkan, OpenGL, Metal) · Concept · Current · Beginner The fixed order of stages that turns 3D geometry into a 2D image: vertex processing, rasterisation, pixel shading and output. Every frame of a game flows through the pipeline, from a car's 3D model to coloured pixels on the screen. Draw callGraphics APIs · Concept · Current · Intermediate A command from the CPU asking the GPU to render a batch of geometry with given shaders, textures and settings. A city scene issuing 20,000 draw calls may be CPU-bound; instancing draws a thousand identical trees in one call. Vertex and pixel (fragment) shadersGraphics APIs; HLSL, GLSL and Metal Shading Language · Concept · Current · Intermediate Programmable GPU stages: vertex shaders position geometry, and pixel shaders compute the colour of every covered pixel. A water shader moves vertices up and down to make waves, then adds reflections and foam per pixel. RasterisationGeneral graphics technique · Concept · Current · Beginner Converting triangles into the set of screen pixels they cover, producing fragments that are then shaded. A triangle covering a quarter of a 1080p screen produces about 500,000 fragments to shade. Texture mapping and texture unitsGPU hardware · Concept · Current · Intermediate Wrapping images onto surfaces; texture units fetch and filter texels quickly, and mipmaps reduce shimmering on distant surfaces. A brick wall is a flat rectangle plus a brick texture and a normal map that fakes the depth of the mortar. Depth buffer (Z-buffer)General graphics technique · Concept · Current · Intermediate A per-pixel record of the distance to the nearest surface drawn so far, so hidden surfaces are discarded whatever the drawing order. A car drawn after the building behind it still correctly hides that building's pixels. Frame buffer and double bufferingGeneral graphics technique · Concept · Current · Beginner Memory holding the finished image; drawing into a hidden back buffer while showing the front buffer prevents half-drawn frames. Swapping buffers only at the display's refresh (V-Sync) prevents tearing, at the cost of some extra latency. Ray tracing and BVHNVIDIA RT cores, AMD and Intel ray accelerators; DXR and Vulkan ray tracing · Technology · Current · Intermediate Simulating light rays to find what they hit, using a bounding volume hierarchy to skip most of the scene quickly. Ray-traced reflections in a puddle can show objects behind the camera, which screen-space tricks cannot. Path tracingFilm renderers; some real-time games · Technology · Current · Advanced A physically based method that follows many random light bounces per pixel to produce realistic global illumination. Animated films render each frame with path tracers on render farms, often taking hours per frame. AI upscaling and frame generation (DLSS, FSR, XeSS)NVIDIA; AMD; Intel · Technology · Current · Intermediate Neural networks rebuild high-resolution frames from lower-resolution renders and can insert generated frames between real ones. DLSS 4 multi-frame generation on GeForce RTX 50 cards can show up to three generated frames for each rendered frame. Frame rate, frame time and refresh rateGeneral · Metric · Current · Beginner Frame rate counts frames rendered per second, frame time is each frame's duration, and refresh rate is how often the display updates. A 144 Hz monitor refreshes every 6.9 ms; a game averaging 100 fps with occasional 30 ms frames still feels jerky. Variable refresh rate (G-SYNC, FreeSync)NVIDIA; AMD; VESA Adaptive-Sync; HDMI VRR · Technology · Current · Beginner The display waits for each new frame instead of refreshing on a fixed clock, removing tearing without V-Sync's extra lag. With FreeSync, a game dipping from 120 to 90 fps stays smooth because the monitor follows the GPU's pace. Display panels (LCD, OLED, mini-LED)Display industry · Technology · Current · Beginner LCDs filter a backlight, mini-LED backlights add thousands of dimming zones, and OLED pixels emit their own light for true blacks. A designer picks an OLED monitor for its contrast but hides static toolbars to reduce burn-in risk. Video encode and decode engines (H.264, HEVC, AV1)NVIDIA NVENC/NVDEC; AMD VCN; Intel Quick Sync; Apple media engine · Component · Current · Intermediate Fixed-function blocks that compress and decompress video far more efficiently than shader cores or the CPU. A streamer encodes 1440p AV1 on the GPU's encoder while the game keeps almost all of its frame rate. Game engines (Unreal Engine, Unity, Godot)Epic Games; Unity Technologies; Godot Foundation · Software · Current · Beginner Toolkits that handle rendering, physics, audio and scripting, so developers build games and simulations without writing a renderer. A car maker builds an interactive digital twin of its showroom in Unreal Engine 5.

docs.title: 4.8 Cloud Giants' Own AI Chips: TPU, Trainium, Maia and MTIA
docs.text:
The biggest cloud and internet companies now design their own AI chips instead of relying only on GPUs. Google's TPUs, Amazon's Trainium and Inferentia, Microsoft's Maia and Meta's MTIA are tuned for each company's own workloads and data centres. Outside customers can usually only rent them through that company's cloud, not buy them.

Hyperscalers' own AI chips. Each cloud builds chips for its own workloads, mostly with design partners and TSMC manufacturing.

Think of it like…

It is like a large supermarket chain launching its own-brand products: they are made for its own shelves, often cheaper per unit, and you can only get them in that shop.

Real-world example

A fictional video platform, StreamNest, compares costs for serving a recommendation model. Its own benchmark shows that serving on AWS Inferentia2 instances would cost about 35% less per million predictions than its rented GPUs, and a Google Cloud TPU v5e test gives a similar saving. The catch is porting: the team must compile its PyTorch model through the AWS Neuron SDK or use JAX/PyTorch-XLA for TPUs, which costs two engineer-weeks. They decide the saving pays back within a few months.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A cloud company spots a huge, predictable workload (search, ads ranking, chat assistants).
  2. It designs a custom chip (often with a partner such as Broadcom or Marvell) and has it made by TSMC.
  3. Chips are linked into pods or UltraServers using custom high-speed interconnects.
  4. A software layer (XLA, Neuron SDK, Maia SDK) lets PyTorch or JAX code run on the chip.
  5. The company uses the chip internally and rents it to customers as cloud instances.

Who uses it

Cloud architects, ML platform engineers and finance teams comparing cost per token or per training run.

Key takeaway

Remember which cloud owns which chip: Google = TPU, AWS = Trainium/Inferentia, Microsoft = Maia, Meta = MTIA (internal only).

Going deeper

  • Custom chips cut cost per token on a company's own predictable workloads by dropping features hyperscalers do not need, such as graphics, strong FP64 and general programmability.
  • TPU pods connect chips with inter-chip interconnect links in a 3D torus, and Google uses optical circuit switches to reconfigure slices and route around failed hardware.
  • Software is the real barrier: AWS Neuron, Google's XLA and JAX stack and Microsoft's Maia SDK must cover every operator a model uses, so porting effort often decides adoption.
  • Most custom accelerators use HBM from the same three suppliers and TSMC advanced packaging, so they compete with GPUs for the same scarce supply.
  • The 2025-26 trend is splitting chips by phase: inference-focused parts such as Ironwood, Maia 200 and TPU 8i emphasise memory capacity and bandwidth over raw training FLOPS.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming you can buy TPUs or Trainium for your own data centre: they are generally available only as cloud services.
  • Choosing a chip from datasheets alone: hourly price, availability, software support and porting time dominate total cost.
  • Expecting every PyTorch model to run unchanged: unsupported operators may need rewrites or fall back to slower paths.

docs.title: 4.9 AI Chip Start-ups and Wafer-Scale Engines
docs.text:
Dozens of newer companies build AI chips with radically different designs from GPUs, hoping to be faster or cheaper for specific jobs such as answering chatbot questions. Some make one giant chip from a whole silicon wafer, some keep the entire model in ultra-fast on-chip memory, and some build chips that only run transformer models. The market moves fast: start-ups get funded, listed on stock markets, licensed or bought every year.

Start-up bets against the GPU

Big idea Memory strategy Sold as Cerebras Whole-wafer chip 44 GB on-chip SRAM Systems and inference cloud Groq Deterministic LPU Weights in on-chip SRAM GroqCloud API SambaNova Reconfigurable dataflow SRAM + HBM + DDR tiers Racks and cloud Tenstorrent Tensix + RISC-V cores GDDR6, open software Cards, servers, IP licences Etched Transformer-only ASIC HBM Inference servers d-Matrix Digital in-memory compute Compute inside SRAM PCIe inference cards

Most designs attack the memory-bandwidth limit of token-by-token generation.

Think of it like…

If GPUs are excellent all-purpose delivery vans, these start-ups build racing motorbikes, giant lorries or single-route trams: brilliant on their chosen route, less flexible elsewhere.

Real-world example

Priya builds a voice assistant for a fictional bank, Ledgerly, and needs answers to start within 300 milliseconds. Her GPU setup produces about 60 tokens per second per user. She tests an SRAM-heavy inference cloud that streams several hundred tokens per second per user, so replies feel instant. She keeps GPUs for fine-tuning, because the specialised service only runs a fixed menu of popular open models.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Find a weakness of GPUs, such as slow off-chip memory during token-by-token generation.
  2. Design an architecture around it: wafer-scale chips, huge on-chip SRAM, dataflow layouts or transformer-only logic.
  3. Build a compiler that maps PyTorch or popular open models onto the new hardware.
  4. Sell systems or, increasingly, a cloud API that charges per token.
  5. Survive by winning a niche, being acquired or licensing the technology to a larger company.

Who uses it

AI infrastructure buyers, investors, hardware engineers and anyone comparing inference providers by speed and cost per token.

Key takeaway

Learn each start-up's one big idea: Cerebras = whole-wafer chip, Groq = deterministic SRAM LPU, SambaNova = reconfigurable dataflow, Tenstorrent = open RISC-V AI chips, Etched = transformer-only ASIC.

Going deeper

  • At batch size 1, generating each token reads every weight once, so speed ≈ memory bandwidth ÷ model bytes; SRAM-based designs exploit this with tens of TB/s of on-chip bandwidth.
  • The catch with SRAM-only designs is capacity: a large model must be split across many chips or wafers, so serving big models can need hundreds of chips.
  • Wafer-scale chips route around manufacturing defects with spare cores and need custom packaging, power delivery and water cooling for a single die of about 46,000 mm².
  • Business models are shifting from selling hardware to selling tokens: Cerebras, Groq and SambaNova all run inference APIs that compete on speed and price per million tokens.
  • Consolidation is common: SoftBank bought Graphcore, NVIDIA licensed Groq's technology and hired key staff, and others have pivoted or closed; software ecosystems remain the hardest barrier.
  • Edge AI start-ups such as Hailo, Axelera AI and DEEPX target cameras, robots and PCs at a few watts, where cost and power matter more than peak performance.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Judging chips on single-user tokens per second only: throughput per dollar with many concurrent users may still favour GPUs.
  • Assuming any model runs on any start-up's cloud: most support a curated list of models and features.
  • Treating vendor benchmarks as neutral: check MLPerf results or independent tests with your own workload.

docs.title: Try it: Why on-chip SRAM helps generation speed: a memory-bound tokens-per-second estimate
docs.text:
# Decode speed ~ memory bandwidth / bytes of weights read per token
params = 8e9            # 8B-parameter model
bytes_per_param = 1     # FP8
for name, bw in [('HBM3e GPU', 4.8e12), ('Hypothetical SRAM chip', 80e12)]:
    tps = bw / (params * bytes_per_param)
    print(f'{name}: ~{tps:,.0f} tokens/s upper bound (batch size 1)')

docs.title: 4.10 NPUs in PCs and Phones
docs.text:
An NPU (Neural Processing Unit) is a small, power-saving AI engine built into the main chip of modern laptops and phones. It runs features like background blur, live captions, photo enhancement and on-device assistants without draining the battery or sending data to the cloud. Its speed is usually quoted in TOPS, trillions of simple operations per second.

Laptop NPU ratings (vendor INT8 peak). Microsoft's Copilot+ PC threshold is 40 TOPS; real app speed also depends on memory and software.

Think of it like…

An NPU is like a calculator built into a cash register: it does one kind of sum very efficiently so the shop assistant (the CPU) can get on with everything else.

Real-world example

Jonah joins a video call on a Copilot+ laptop with a 45 TOPS NPU. Background blur, eye-contact correction and live captions run on the NPU using about 1-2 watts, so his CPU stays mostly idle and the fan stays quiet. When he ran the same effects on the CPU of his old laptop, the fans roared and the battery fell noticeably faster.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. An app asks the OS AI runtime (Windows ML, Core ML, Android NNAPI or LiteRT) to run a model.
  2. The runtime checks which engines exist and picks the NPU for supported operations.
  3. The model is usually quantised to INT8 or INT4 so it fits the NPU's strengths.
  4. The NPU's matrix arrays process each layer at low power; unsupported layers fall back to GPU or CPU.
  5. Results return to the app, and no data needs to leave the device.

Who uses it

Laptop and phone buyers, app developers adding on-device AI, and embedded engineers working with battery-powered devices.

Key takeaway

Know the Copilot+ PC bar — an NPU of at least 40 TOPS — and remember TOPS figures depend on precision, so compare like with like.

Going deeper

  • NPUs are built from multiply-accumulate arrays with local SRAM and DMA engines that run a pre-compiled graph of layers, very efficient at a few watts but less flexible than GPUs.
  • Models must be converted and quantised for each NPU with vendor tools (Qualcomm AI Hub and QNN, Intel OpenVINO, AMD Ryzen AI Software, Apple coremltools); unsupported operators fall back.
  • For on-device language models, memory bandwidth limits speed more than TOPS: a 3-billion-parameter 4-bit model must stream about 1.5 GB of weights for every generated token.
  • Phones spread AI across CPU, GPU, NPU, DSP and the image signal processor; camera pipelines run continuous AI on the ISP and NPU to save battery.
  • Windows ML, generally available since 2025, is built into Windows 11 and fetches vendor execution providers, so one app can target Qualcomm, Intel and AMD NPUs.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Believing a higher TOPS number means faster apps: software support, precision and memory bandwidth often matter more.
  • Assuming every AI feature uses the NPU: many apps still run AI on the GPU or in the cloud.
  • Comparing INT8 TOPS with FP16 TFLOPS directly: they measure different precisions and are not equivalent.

docs.title: 4.11 FPGAs and Custom ASICs
docs.text:
An FPGA is a chip full of blank logic blocks and wires that you can rewire with a configuration file, so it can become almost any digital circuit. An ASIC is a chip designed for one job and fixed for ever at the factory, so it is the fastest and most efficient option but very expensive to create. Engineers describe both using hardware description languages such as Verilog and VHDL.

CPU/GPU vs FPGA vs ASIC

CPU / GPU FPGA ASIC Flexibility Change software any time Rewire hardware in the field Fixed at manufacture Up-front cost None beyond buying chips Low to moderate Tens of millions at leading nodes Unit cost at volume Moderate High Lowest Performance per watt Lowest Good Best Time to deploy Days Weeks to months One to two years or more Typical use General software, AI Telecom, trading, prototypes Phones, TPUs, crypto mining

The more fixed the hardware, the better its efficiency and unit cost, and the higher the up-front risk.

Think of it like…

An FPGA is a giant LEGO board you can rebuild into a new model whenever you like; an ASIC is a moulded plastic toy, perfect and cheap in volume, but you cannot change it.

Real-world example

Sanjay works at a fictional trading firm, Quickfill. Its software trading engine reacts in about 5 microseconds, so he implements the market-data parser on an FPGA network card and reaction time falls to under 1 microsecond. Later the firm considers turning the design into an ASIC but rejects it: a modern ASIC tape-out can cost tens of millions, and the strategy changes every few months, which only an FPGA can follow.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Describe the circuit in Verilog, VHDL or SystemVerilog, or in C++ using high-level synthesis (HLS).
  2. Simulate it with test benches to check behaviour cycle by cycle.
  3. Synthesis turns the code into logic gates; place-and-route maps them onto the FPGA's blocks.
  4. The tool produces a bitstream that is loaded onto the FPGA, which can be reprogrammed later.
  5. For an ASIC, the verified design is turned into masks and manufactured (tape-out), with no changes afterwards.

Who uses it

FPGA and digital design engineers, chip verification engineers, telecom, defence, finance and embedded-systems companies.

Key takeaway

Remember the trade-off triangle: CPU = most flexible, FPGA = reconfigurable hardware, ASIC = fastest and most efficient but fixed and costly to design.

Going deeper

  • FPGA designs are limited by timing closure: every path between flip-flops must settle within one clock period, so typical FPGA designs run at a few hundred MHz, not multiple GHz.
  • Modern FPGAs add hard blocks such as DSP slices, block RAM, high-speed transceivers, PCIe and Ethernet controllers, Arm cores and even HBM, mixing fixed and programmable logic.
  • The ASIC flow runs RTL design, verification (often the biggest effort, with SystemVerilog and UVM), synthesis, physical design, sign-off and tape-out; leading-edge mask sets alone cost millions.
  • Prototyping ASICs on FPGAs is standard: large multi-FPGA emulation systems let software teams start work long before first silicon returns.
  • Microsoft's Project Catapult deployed FPGAs across its data-centre servers to accelerate Bing search and Azure networking, a well-known large-scale FPGA deployment.
  • Open-source silicon is growing: the SkyWater 130 nm open PDK, OpenROAD and community shuttle programmes let students tape out small chips cheaply.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Writing HDL like software: Verilog describes parallel hardware, so every statement becomes circuitry operating at the same time.
  • Skipping simulation and testing on the board: bugs are far harder to find in hardware than in a test bench.
  • Choosing an ASIC too early: if requirements change, a fixed chip becomes an expensive mistake.

docs.title: Try it: A tiny Verilog module: an 8-bit counter (simulate with Icarus Verilog or any online simulator)
docs.text:
module counter (
  input  wire       clk,
  input  wire       reset,
  output reg  [7:0] count
);
  always @(posedge clk) begin
    if (reset) count <= 8'd0;
    else       count <= count + 8'd1;   // wraps after 255
  end
endmodule

docs.title: 4.12 How a Chip Is Designed: From RTL to Tape-Out
docs.text:
Before a chip is manufactured, engineers describe its logic in a hardware description language, prove it works with simulations and other checks, and turn it into a physical layout of billions of transistors and wires. Specialised software called EDA (electronic design automation) does much of the heavy lifting. The finished layout goes to a foundry at 'tape-out', and the first chips that come back are tested in the lab.

The digital chip design flow. The later a bug is found, the more it costs — after tape-out it can mean new masks and months of delay.

Think of it like…

Designing a chip is like building a new city: architects write the zoning plan (RTL), inspectors check every rule (verification), planners place buildings and roads (place and route), and only when every permit passes do the bulldozers start (tape-out).

Real-world example

Kestrel Silicon, a fictional start-up, is building a small AI inference chip on a 5 nm process. Its RTL engineers write SystemVerilog for a matrix engine, while a larger verification team tests it with UVM simulations and formal tools, and an FPGA prototype runs real models months before silicon exists. Physical designers synthesise, place and route the design until timing closes at 1.5 GHz. After tape-out, the first wafers return a few months later for bring-up in the lab.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Architects write a specification and a performance model, often in C++ or Python, to choose features, sizes and power targets.
  2. RTL designers describe the logic in SystemVerilog or VHDL as registers and the logic between them.
  3. Verification engineers simulate the RTL with randomised tests, coverage tracking and formal proofs, and run real software on emulators or FPGA prototypes.
  4. Synthesis maps the RTL to a netlist of standard cells from the foundry's library; place and route positions those cells, builds the clock tree and wires everything up.
  5. Sign-off checks timing, power, signal integrity and manufacturing rules (DRC, LVS) before the layout files go to the foundry at tape-out.
  6. Returned chips go through bring-up, post-silicon validation and production testing; serious bugs may need a respin.

Who uses it

RTL design, design verification, physical design, DFT and post-silicon validation engineers, EDA tool developers and chip architects at chip companies, hyperscalers and start-ups follow this flow.

Key takeaway

Know the proportions: verification usually takes more engineering effort than writing the design, and a mask set at a leading-edge node can cost tens of millions of dollars, so first-time-right silicon matters.

Going deeper

  • Three companies dominate commercial EDA — Synopsys (which completed its acquisition of simulation firm Ansys in 2025), Cadence and Siemens EDA — covering simulation, synthesis, place and route and sign-off, plus licensable IP blocks.
  • A PDK (process design kit) from the foundry contains design rules, transistor models and libraries of standard cells, memories and I/O; designers cannot target a process without one.
  • Timing closure means every path between flip-flops meets setup and hold times at every process, voltage and temperature corner; static timing analysis checks billions of paths without simulation.
  • Verification combines SystemVerilog UVM testbenches, coverage metrics that expose untested behaviour, formal property checking, and hardware emulators such as Palladium, ZeBu and Veloce that boot operating systems before silicon exists.
  • Design for test inserts scan chains and built-in self-test so automatic test equipment can screen every die for manufacturing defects in seconds.
  • Open-source flows such as OpenROAD and OpenLane, open PDKs such as SkyWater SKY130, and shared-wafer programmes such as Tiny Tapeout let students take real designs to silicon cheaply.
  • Large chips are now assembled from chiplets, adding package design, die-to-die links such as UCIe, and multi-die timing, power and thermal analysis to the flow.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating RTL like software: it describes parallel hardware, so every always block runs at the same time and a loop becomes physical copies of logic.
  • Leaving verification until the end: it runs alongside design from day one, because a bug found after tape-out can force a costly respin.
  • Assuming a design that simulates correctly will run at the target clock: only static timing analysis on the placed-and-routed layout proves timing.

docs.title: Try it: Simulate a tiny counter with open-source Icarus Verilog
docs.text:
// counter.v - a 4-bit counter with synchronous reset
module counter(input clk, input rst, output reg [3:0] q);
  always @(posedge clk) q <= rst ? 4'd0 : q + 4'd1;
endmodule

# shell: compile with a testbench you write, then run the simulation
# iverilog -o sim counter.v counter_tb.v && vvp sim

docs.title: 4.13 Number Formats for AI: FP64 to FP4 and Quantisation
docs.text:
Computers store numbers in fixed-size formats; fewer bits means less memory and faster maths, but less precision. Scientific simulation needs 64-bit numbers, but AI models work well with 16, 8 or even 4 bits per number. Each new AI chip generation adds smaller formats, and quantisation is the art of shrinking a model's numbers without making it noticeably worse.

Weight memory for a 70B model by format. Each halving of bits halves the memory; block-scaled formats add a few percent for their scales.

Think of it like…

Choosing a number format is like choosing how precisely to measure ingredients: a pharmacist needs milligram scales (FP64), but a pizza chef is fine with 'a handful' (FP4) and works far faster.

Real-world example

Elena has a 70-billion-parameter model. In BF16 (2 bytes per number) the weights take about 140 GB, needing two 80 GB GPUs. Quantised to FP8 they need about 70 GB and fit on one H200, and in 4-bit about 35 GB, small enough for a single 48 GB workstation card. Her evaluation shows the 4-bit version loses about one point of accuracy on her test set, which she accepts for her customer-support bot.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A floating-point number has a sign bit, exponent bits (range) and mantissa bits (precision).
  2. Training usually uses BF16 or FP8 maths while keeping a master copy of weights in FP32 (mixed precision).
  3. Block-scaled formats (MXFP8, MXFP4, NVFP4) share one scale factor across small groups of values to keep accuracy.
  4. After training, quantisation converts weights, and sometimes activations, to INT8, FP8, INT4 or FP4.
  5. Always re-test model quality after changing precision.

Who uses it

ML engineers, inference-optimisation specialists, HPC scientists and chip architects choose formats daily.

Key takeaway

Memorise the bit layouts: FP32 = 1/8/23, FP16 = 1/5/10, BF16 = 1/8/7, FP8 E4M3 and E5M2, FP4 E2M1 — and remember BF16 keeps FP32's range.

Going deeper

  • Bit layouts (sign/exponent/mantissa): FP32 1/8/23, FP16 1/5/10, BF16 1/8/7, TF32 1/8/10, FP8 E4M3 and E5M2, FP6 E2M3 and E3M2, FP4 E2M1. Exponent bits set range; mantissa bits set precision.
  • Each halving of bit width roughly doubles tensor-core throughput and halves memory traffic, which is why inference moved from FP16 to FP8 and now FP4 on Blackwell-class chips.
  • Block scaling shares one scale per small block: MX formats use an 8-bit power-of-two scale per 32 values, while NVFP4 uses an FP8 E4M3 scale per 16 values plus a per-tensor FP32 scale.
  • Activations and the KV cache can be quantised too, for example an FP8 KV cache, which often saves more memory than weight quantisation in long-context serving.
  • Outliers are the enemy of low precision: a few huge activation values stretch the scale, so methods such as SmoothQuant and AWQ rebalance them before quantising.
  • Scientific HPC still needs FP64; some AI-focused GPUs cut FP64 throughput, so supercomputing centres check FP64 figures or use FP64 emulation on tensor cores.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Training in FP16 without loss scaling: small gradients underflow to zero and the model silently stops learning.
  • Assuming 4-bit is always good enough: reasoning, maths and coding tasks can degrade noticeably, so evaluate on your own tasks.
  • Comparing TFLOPS at different precisions: an FP4 figure is not comparable with a BF16 or FP64 figure.
  • Confusing FP16 with BF16: both use 16 bits, but BF16 keeps FP32's range while FP16 overflows above 65,504.

docs.title: Try it: Compare the range and precision of formats in PyTorch
docs.text:
import torch
for dt in [torch.float64, torch.float32, torch.bfloat16, torch.float16,
           torch.float8_e4m3fn, torch.float8_e5m2]:
    f = torch.finfo(dt)
    print(f'{str(dt):22} bits={f.bits:2}  max={f.max:.3g}  eps={f.eps:.3g}')

x = torch.tensor(0.1)
print(x.to(torch.bfloat16).item(), x.to(torch.float16).item())

docs.title: 4.14 AI Training vs Inference: Compute and Memory Maths
docs.text:
Training teaches a model by showing it huge amounts of text or images and adjusting its numbers; inference is using the finished model to answer questions. Training is a giant one-off job measured in total FLOPs and GPU-hours, while inference runs all day for every user and is measured in tokens per second, response time and cost per token. Simple rules of thumb let you estimate both before spending any money.

Training vs inference at a glance

Training Inference Goal Learn weights from data Answer users with fixed weights Compute ≈ 6 × N × D FLOPs in total ≈ 2 × N FLOPs per token Memory per parameter ~16 bytes (Adam, mixed precision) 1-2 bytes plus KV cache Main bottleneck Compute and interconnect Memory bandwidth (decode) Key metrics GPU-hours, MFU TTFT, tokens/s, cost per token Duration Weeks, one-off Continuous, every request

Training is a huge one-off compute job; inference is a never-ending memory-bandwidth job.

Think of it like…

Training is writing and printing an encyclopedia once (enormous effort); inference is people looking things up in it millions of times a day (each lookup is cheap, but they never stop).

Real-world example

Ravi plans to train a 7-billion-parameter model on 1 trillion tokens. Using 6 × N × D, that needs about 4.2 × 10²² FLOPs. An H100 offers about 989 teraFLOPS of dense BF16; at a realistic 40% utilisation that is about 4 × 10¹⁴ useful FLOPs per second, so the job needs roughly 29,500 GPU-hours — about 15 days on 80 GPUs. For serving, he budgets 14 GB for BF16 weights plus memory for each user's KV cache.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Training compute ≈ 6 × parameters × training tokens (forward plus backward pass).
  2. Inference compute ≈ 2 × parameters FLOPs per generated token.
  3. Memory for weights = parameters × bytes per parameter; training with Adam needs roughly 16 bytes per parameter plus activations.
  4. Inference adds a KV cache per user that grows with context length.
  5. Prefill (reading the prompt) is compute-bound; decode (writing tokens one by one) is memory-bandwidth-bound, so batching users together raises throughput.

Who uses it

ML engineers, AI infrastructure planners, cloud cost analysts and researchers sizing GPU clusters use these estimates daily.

Key takeaway

Memorise 6ND for training, 2N per token for inference, and '2 bytes per parameter in BF16' — together they answer most interview sizing questions.

Going deeper

  • Worked sizing: a 70B model in BF16 needs 140 GB of weights; with grouped-query attention its KV cache is about 2.5 GB per user at 8k context, so 32 users add roughly 80 GB.
  • Decode ceiling at batch size 1 ≈ memory bandwidth ÷ weight bytes: an H200 (about 4.8 TB/s) serving a 70 GB FP8 model tops out near 68 tokens per second per sequence.
  • Reasoning models shift spending toward inference: 'test-time compute' generates many hidden tokens per answer, so serving now dominates many AI compute budgets.
  • PagedAttention in vLLM stores the KV cache in fixed-size blocks, like virtual-memory pages, cutting fragmentation so many more concurrent requests fit on each GPU.
  • Large training runs are limited by failures as well as FLOPs: with tens of thousands of GPUs, hardware faults happen frequently, so jobs checkpoint often and restart automatically.
  • MFU counts only the model's useful FLOPs, while hardware FLOPs utilisation (HFU) also counts recomputation, so check which one a paper or vendor reports.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Sizing inference by weights alone: the KV cache for many users and long contexts can exceed the model's own memory.
  • Using peak FLOPS in training estimates: real MFU of 30-50% can double or triple the time and cost.
  • Maximising tokens per second per GPU while ignoring latency: users notice slow time-to-first-token even when throughput looks great.

docs.title: Try it: Estimate training GPU-hours and KV-cache size in Python
docs.text:
N, D = 7e9, 1e12                  # parameters, training tokens
flops = 6 * N * D
gpu_flops = 989e12 * 0.40          # H100 dense BF16 at 40% MFU
print(f'Training: {flops:.2e} FLOPs = {flops/gpu_flops/3600:,.0f} GPU-hours')

# KV cache per token = 2 (K and V) x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x bytes
layers, kv_heads, head_dim, bytes_ = 32, 8, 128, 2
per_tok = 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * bytes_
print(f'KV cache: {per_tok/1024:.0f} KiB/token, {per_tok*8192/2**30:.1f} GiB for 8k context')

A chat service targets TTFT under 500 ms and at least 50 tokens per second per user. A provider uses compute-heavy GPUs for prefill and memory-rich GPUs for decode, cutting cost per token. MoE: active vs total parametersMixture-of-experts models such as Mixtral and DeepSeek-V3 · Concept · Current · Intermediate Mixture-of-experts models route each token through a few experts, so compute follows active parameters while memory must hold all of them. DeepSeek-V3 has 671 billion parameters but activates about 37 billion per token, so its compute per token resembles a 37B dense model. Speculative decodingLeviathan et al. (Google) and Chen et al. (DeepMind), 2023 · Technology · Current · Advanced A small draft model proposes several tokens that the large model verifies in one pass, speeding generation without changing outputs. A service drafts with a 1B model and verifies with its 70B model, generating tokens two to three times faster.

docs.title: 4.15 Connecting Accelerators: Scale-Up and Scale-Out
docs.text:
Big AI models need hundreds or thousands of accelerators working as one, so the links between chips matter as much as the chips themselves. Scale-up links join a few dozen GPUs so closely that they can share memory like one giant GPU; scale-out networks join many such groups across a data centre. Standards such as NVLink, UALink, InfiniBand and Ultra Ethernet compete to provide these links.

Scale-up inside racks, scale-out between them. NVLink joins the GPUs inside each rack; every GPU's NIC also joins a rail of the InfiniBand or Ethernet fabric.

Think of it like…

Scale-up is like colleagues sitting around one table passing papers instantly; scale-out is like many offices connected by a fast courier service — still quick, but each trip takes longer.

Real-world example

Hannah's fictional lab, Orbitar AI, trains a large model across 1,152 GPUs in 16 NVL72 racks. Inside each rack, NVLink lets 72 GPUs exchange tensor-parallel data at about 1.8 TB/s per GPU. Between racks, each GPU has an 800 Gb/s network port on an InfiniBand fabric for data-parallel gradient averaging. When one optical cable fails, NCCL logs a slowdown and the job manager restarts from the latest checkpoint.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Inside a server or rack, GPUs connect through scale-up links (NVLink, Infinity Fabric, UALink) and switches.
  2. Each GPU also gets a high-speed network card (often 400-800 Gb/s) for scale-out.
  3. Scale-out fabrics (InfiniBand or RDMA Ethernet) link thousands of GPUs, usually in a rail-optimised fat-tree topology.
  4. GPUDirect RDMA lets network cards read and write GPU memory directly, skipping the CPU.
  5. Libraries like NCCL run collectives such as all-reduce, matching parallelism (tensor, pipeline, data) to the fastest links.

Who uses it

AI infrastructure engineers, network engineers in AI data centres, HPC architects and distributed-training specialists.

Key takeaway

Remember: tensor parallelism stays inside the scale-up domain (fastest links), while data parallelism can cross the scale-out network.

Going deeper

  • The bandwidth gap shapes parallelism: NVLink 5 gives each GPU about 900 GB/s per direction, while an 800 Gb/s NIC gives 100 GB/s, roughly nine times less.
  • Ring all-reduce sends about 2 × (n−1)/n times the data size per GPU, so gradient sync time depends on message size ÷ link bandwidth plus latency terms for small messages.
  • AI fabrics are usually non-blocking fat trees with rail optimisation; large clusters need three switch tiers, and topology-aware schedulers keep jobs within as few hops as possible.
  • Ethernet for AI needs congestion control: RoCE v2 relies on PFC and ECN-based schemes such as DCQCN, while Ultra Ethernet adds packet spraying and new transport to avoid hot spots.
  • Scale-up domains keep growing: 8 GPUs per HGX server, 72 in NVL72 racks and several hundred GPU dies in planned Rubin Ultra racks, while UALink targets up to 1,024 accelerators.
  • Co-packaged optics place lasers beside the switch chip to save power compared with pluggable transceivers; NVIDIA and Broadcom have announced CPO switches for AI networks.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Running tensor parallelism across racks: it needs the fastest links, so keep it inside one NVLink or scale-up domain.
  • Treating RoCE Ethernet and InfiniBand as drop-in equals: RoCE needs careful tuning of PFC, ECN and buffers to avoid stalls.
  • Ignoring one slow link or GPU: collective operations run at the speed of the slowest participant in the job.

docs.title: Try it: Show how GPUs and network cards are connected in your server
docs.text:
nvidia-smi topo -m        # matrix: NV# = NVLink, PIX/PXB = PCIe, SYS = across CPUs
nvidia-smi nvlink -s      # NVLink link status and speed
ibstat                    # InfiniBand ports (if present)

docs.title: Chapter 3: Memory & Storage
docs.text: A processor is only as fast as the data it can reach, so this chapter follows data from the tiny caches inside a CPU, through DRAM and new memory links like CXL, down to SSDs, hard drives, tape and networked storage. You will learn how each layer works, the standards and numbers that matter in 2026, and how file systems, RAID and backups keep data safe. By the end you will be able to choose the right memory and storage for a laptop, a server or an AI cluster and explain why.

docs.title: 3.1 The Memory Hierarchy
docs.text:
A computer stores data in several layers, from tiny, ultra-fast storage inside the processor to huge, slow storage such as hard drives, tape and the cloud. Faster layers are smaller and cost more per byte, so the computer keeps what it needs right now close to the processor and everything else further away. This stack of layers is called the memory hierarchy.

The memory and storage hierarchy. Each step down is bigger, cheaper per byte and roughly ten to a thousand times slower.

Think of it like…

A chef keeps the ingredient being chopped in hand, a few on the worktop, more in the fridge, bulk stock in the pantry and rarely used items at a warehouse across town.

Real-world example

Sam, a student game developer, rewrites his particle simulation to keep all positions in one continuous array instead of scattered objects. Each 64-byte cache line now carries 16 floats he is about to use, so most reads hit the L1 cache in about 1 ns rather than DRAM at around 100 ns. His frame time drops from 28 ms to 9 ms without changing the maths at all. A single read from his NVMe SSD would have cost roughly 100 µs, a thousand times worse again.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The CPU works on values held in registers, which it can use within a single clock cycle.
  2. If the data is not in a register, the CPU checks the L1, then L2, then L3 cache, each bigger but slower.
  3. A miss in every cache goes out to main memory (DRAM), roughly 100 times slower than L1.
  4. Data not in RAM must be fetched from an SSD or hard drive, thousands to millions of times slower.
  5. Hardware and the operating system keep recently used and nearby data in the fast layers, betting on locality.

Who uses it

Programmers, game and database developers, performance engineers and HPC specialists all design their code and systems around the hierarchy.

Key takeaway

Memorise the rough ladder: register under 1 ns, L1 about 1 ns, DRAM about 100 ns, NVMe SSD about 100 µs, hard drive about 10 ms.

Going deeper

  • At 4 GHz an L1 hit costs about 4-5 cycles, a DRAM access a few hundred cycles and an NVMe read hundreds of thousands of cycles, so one miss can outweigh thousands of instructions.
  • Average memory access time combines tiers: AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty. Small changes in miss rate matter because each lower level's penalty is so large.
  • Data moves between tiers in fixed units: 64-byte cache lines between caches and DRAM, 4 KiB pages between DRAM and storage, and large blocks or objects to archives.
  • Who manages each layer tells you what you can tune: hardware runs the caches, the OS runs the page cache and swap, and software or administrators place data on storage tiers.
  • Bandwidth shrinks down the hierarchy too: L1 can feed one core hundreds of GB/s, a 12-channel DDR5 socket about 600 GB/s, an NVMe SSD 7-14 GB/s and a hard drive about 0.3 GB/s.
  • AI systems add extra tiers: on-chip SRAM, stacked HBM beside the accelerator, CPU DDR, CXL memory and NVMe flash, with serving software offloading KV cache between them.
  • Energy follows the same ladder: fetching a value from off-chip DRAM costs hundreds of times more energy than a floating-point add on it, so keeping data close also saves power.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming more RAM always speeds things up: once the working set fits, extra RAM only helps as page cache, and the bottleneck may be elsewhere.
  • Treating storage as memory: swap on even a fast SSD is roughly a thousand times slower than DRAM, so heavy swapping cripples performance.
  • Believing data is saved once write() returns: it may still sit in the OS page cache or the drive's cache until flushed with fsync.
  • Mixing up GB and GiB, or bits and bytes per second, when comparing tiers; always check units before calculating a speed-up.

docs.text:
lscpu | grep -i cache                      # Linux: L1d, L1i, L2, L3 sizes

Get-CimInstance Win32_Processor | Select-Object Name,L2CacheSize,L3CacheSize   # Windows PowerShell (KB)

docs.title: Key chips, architectures, standards, tools & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example BandwidthGeneral performance concept · Metric · Current · Beginner How much data a memory or storage layer can deliver per second, usually measured in GB/s. One DDR5-6400 channel moves about 51 GB/s, while a PCIe 5.0 x4 SSD manages roughly 14 GB/s. Volatile vs non-volatile memoryGeneral hardware concept · Concept · Current · Beginner Volatile memory (SRAM, DRAM) loses its contents without power; non-volatile storage (flash, disks, tape) keeps data when switched off. Unsaved work in RAM vanishes in a power cut, but the document saved to the SSD is still there. Main memory (RAM)DRAM chips from SK hynix, Samsung, Micron and others · Component · Current · Beginner The computer's working memory, made of DRAM, that holds running programs and their data while the CPU uses them. Opening 40 browser tabs can use 8 GB of RAM; when it fills up, the OS starts swapping to disk. Storage tiering (hot, warm, cold)Storage industry practice · Concept · Current · Intermediate Placing frequently used data on fast, costly media and rarely used data on cheap, slow media such as HDD, tape or archive cloud. A video site keeps this week's uploads on NVMe SSDs, last year's on hard drives and old raw footage on tape. Memory wallTerm from Wulf and McKee, 1995 · Concept · Current · Advanced The growing gap between how fast processors compute and how fast memory can feed them data. AI accelerators add stacked HBM memory because their maths units would otherwise sit idle waiting for data. Primary, secondary and tertiary storageClassic computer-science classification · Concept · Current · Beginner Primary storage is memory the CPU addresses directly (registers, cache, RAM); secondary is drives; tertiary is removable or robotic archive media. Your laptop's RAM is primary storage, its SSD secondary, and the company's robotic tape library tertiary storage. Byte-addressable vs block-addressableGeneral hardware and OS concept · Concept · Current · Beginner RAM is read by CPU load and store instructions down to single bytes; drives are read through the OS in whole blocks, usually 4 KiB. Changing one byte of a file on an SSD still means reading and rewriting at least one whole 4 KiB block. Cost per gigabyteMarket prices (vary strongly over time) · Metric · Current · Beginner Price per stored gigabyte falls sharply down the hierarchy: DRAM costs tens of times more than SSD, which costs several times more than HDD. Upgrading a server from 256 GB to 512 GB of RAM can cost as much as tens of terabytes of hard-disk capacity. Working setPeter Denning (1968) · Concept · Current · Intermediate The code and data a program actively uses over a short period; speed drops sharply once it no longer fits in a faster tier. A database whose 40 GB hot working set fits in 64 GB of RAM is fast; when it grows to 80 GB, queries keep hitting the SSD. Page cache (buffer cache)Linux, Windows and macOS kernels · Technology · Current · Intermediate Spare RAM the operating system fills with recently read or written file data, so repeat reads skip the drive entirely. Searching a 2 GB log twice, the second run is far faster; Linux's free -h shows that memory as buff/cache. Durability and fsyncPOSIX fsync(); Windows FlushFileBuffers · Concept · Current · Intermediate Writes usually land in volatile caches first; data is only safe once flushed to non-volatile storage, for example by calling fsync. A payments database calls fsync before confirming a transfer, so a power cut a millisecond later cannot lose it. Scratchpad memoryUsed in GPUs (shared memory), DSPs, AI accelerators and microcontrollers · Component · Current · Intermediate Small, fast on-chip SRAM that software manages explicitly, unlike an automatic cache, giving predictable timing and no wasted fetches. A GPU kernel copies a tile into shared memory, and an AI chip's compiler decides exactly which weights sit in on-chip SRAM.

docs.title: 3.2 SRAM, DRAM and Memory Modules
docs.text:
SRAM and DRAM are the two main kinds of electronic working memory. SRAM is fast and needs no refreshing but takes up a lot of chip space, so it is used for caches; DRAM stores each bit as a tiny electric charge that slowly leaks away, so it must be refreshed constantly, but it is cheap and dense enough for gigabytes of main memory. DRAM chips are mounted on modules (sticks) that plug into the motherboard, and servers add error-correcting memory to catch mistakes.

SRAM vs DRAM

SRAM DRAM Cell 6 transistors (latch) 1 transistor + 1 capacitor Refresh None while powered Every row within 32-64 ms Access time About 1-10 ns on-chip About 80-120 ns from the CPU Density / cost Low density, high cost High density, low cost Typical size KB to hundreds of MB GB to TB Built on Same logic process as CPU Specialised DRAM process Used for Caches, registers, scratchpads Main memory, GDDR, HBM

SRAM buys speed with area; DRAM buys density with refresh and slower access.

Think of it like…

SRAM is like a light switch that stays where you put it; DRAM is like a bucket with a tiny hole that someone must top up every few milliseconds.

Real-world example

Tomás builds a small server for Brightwater Analytics, a fictional market-research firm. He picks a server board with 8 memory channels and fills each with one 64 GB DDR5 RDIMM, giving 512 GB with ECC protection. A month later the system log reports two corrected single-bit errors on one DIMM, so he swaps it during planned maintenance before it can cause a crash. On a desktop with consumer UDIMMs without ECC, those errors could have silently corrupted data.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. An SRAM cell uses about six transistors wired as a latch that holds a 0 or 1 while powered.
  2. A DRAM cell uses one transistor and one capacitor; a charged capacitor means 1, an empty one means 0.
  3. DRAM cells are arranged in rows and columns inside banks; reading opens a whole row into a row buffer.
  4. Because charge leaks, the memory controller refreshes every row, typically within a 32-64 ms window.
  5. Chips are grouped into ranks on a module (DIMM), and modules sit on channels wired to the CPU's memory controller.
  6. ECC adds extra bits so the controller can correct single-bit errors and detect worse ones.

Who uses it

Hardware engineers, server and data-centre technicians, PC builders and system administrators choose and troubleshoot memory every day.

Key takeaway

Populate every memory channel evenly; a server with half its channels empty can lose close to half its memory bandwidth.

Going deeper

  • Reading DRAM activates a whole row of thousands of bits into sense amplifiers (the row buffer); further reads from that open row are much faster than closing it and opening another.
  • DDR5 splits each DIMM into two independent 32-bit subchannels, or 40-bit with ECC, so a server ECC RDIMM carries 80 data bits and keeps more requests in flight.
  • Peak bandwidth per socket = channels × transfer rate × 8 bytes: twelve channels of DDR5-6400 give about 614 GB/s, which is why server platforms keep adding channels.
  • Server ECC goes beyond single-bit correction: Chipkill or SDDC-style schemes survive a whole failed DRAM chip, and patrol scrubbing fixes errors in the background before they accumulate.
  • Two DIMMs per channel usually lowers the supported memory speed, so architects trade capacity against bandwidth when specifying servers.
  • Rowhammer defences evolved from Target Row Refresh in DDR4 to Refresh Management and Per-Row Activation Counting (PRAC) in DDR5, which counts activations and refreshes victim rows.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking DDR5's on-die ECC makes consumer memory 'ECC memory': it only fixes errors inside the chip, not on the bus, and reports nothing to the OS.
  • Mixing RDIMMs with UDIMMs, or DDR4 with DDR5: they are electrically incompatible, and the slots are keyed differently.
  • Judging memory by MT/s alone: real latency in nanoseconds depends on both the transfer rate and the CAS latency.
  • Leaving server memory channels empty: bandwidth scales with populated channels, so spread DIMMs evenly across all of them.

docs.text:
Get-CimInstance Win32_PhysicalMemory | Select-Object BankLabel,Capacity,Speed,Manufacturer,PartNumber   # Windows PowerShell (wmic is deprecated)
sudo dmidecode --type memory | grep -E 'Size|Type:|Speed|Locator'   # Linux
free -h                                                              # Linux: total/used RAM

docs.title: Key chips, architectures, standards, tools & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example SRAM (static RAM)Built into CPUs, GPUs and SoCs by all chipmakers · Technology · Current · Beginner Fast memory made from about six transistors per bit that holds data without refresh; large per bit, so used for caches. A big server CPU's L3 cache, which can reach hundreds of megabytes across chiplets, is built from SRAM. DRAM (dynamic RAM)SK hynix, Samsung, Micron, CXMT and others; standards by JEDEC · Technology · Current · Beginner Dense, low-cost memory storing each bit as charge in a tiny capacitor, needing regular refresh; used for main memory. A 16 GB laptop stick contains billions of DRAM capacitors, each holding one bit of your open files. DRAM refreshJEDEC DRAM standards · Concept · Current · Intermediate Periodically reading and rewriting every DRAM row before its charge leaks away, typically every 32-64 ms, briefly blocking access. Server DRAM running very hot may refresh twice as often, slightly reducing available bandwidth. ECC memoryMemory controllers in Intel Xeon, AMD EPYC and other server CPUs · Technology · Current · Beginner Memory with extra check bits that lets the controller fix single-bit errors and detect multi-bit ones, preventing silent corruption. A bank's database servers use ECC RDIMMs so a cosmic-ray bit flip never alters an account balance. On-die ECC (DDR5)JEDEC JESD79-5 (DDR5) · Technology · Current · Intermediate Error correction inside each DDR5 chip that fixes internal bit errors; it does not replace full system-level ECC on servers. A gamer's non-ECC DDR5 kit still has on-die ECC, but errors on the bus to the CPU go unchecked. Channel, rank and bankJEDEC DRAM organisation · Concept · Current · Intermediate A channel is an independent path to memory; a rank is a set of chips answering together; banks are independent arrays inside each chip. A 12-channel server CPU with one 2-rank RDIMM per channel can keep many banks busy in parallel. UDIMMJEDEC module standard · Component · Current · Beginner Unbuffered DIMM: the standard desktop memory stick where the CPU talks to the DRAM chips directly; ECC versions exist. A home PC uses two 16 GB DDR5 UDIMMs in dual-channel mode. SO-DIMMJEDEC module standard · Component · Current · Beginner Small Outline DIMM, a shorter memory module used in laptops, mini PCs and some embedded boards. Upgrading a mini PC from 8 GB to 32 GB means swapping its DDR5 SO-DIMM sticks. RDIMMJEDEC module standard · Component · Current · Intermediate Registered DIMM, with a register clock driver chip that buffers commands so servers can use more and larger modules reliably. Most rack servers use ECC DDR5 RDIMMs of 32-128 GB each. LRDIMMJEDEC module standard · Component · Legacy · Advanced Load-Reduced DIMM, which also buffers data lines to support very high capacities; common with DDR4, rarer with DDR5. An older DDR4 database server reached 3 TB of RAM using 128 GB LRDIMMs. MRDIMMJEDEC DDR5 MRDIMM standard; supported by Intel Xeon 6 · Component · Emerging · Advanced Multiplexed-Rank DIMM that reads two ranks at once through data buffers, roughly doubling module bandwidth; 8800 MT/s now, Gen 2 targets 12800. An HPC centre picks MRDIMM-8800 for its Xeon 6 nodes to speed up memory-bound weather simulations. CAMM2 and LPCAMM2JEDEC JESD318 (CAMM2) · Component · Emerging · Intermediate Compression-Attached Memory Modules: thin, flat modules screwed onto the board, for DDR5 or LPDDR5X, replacing soldered laptop memory. A workstation laptop with an LPCAMM2 module can be upgraded from 32 GB to 64 GB instead of being stuck. RowhammerResearch by Kim et al., 2014; JEDEC mitigations such as PRAC in DDR5 · Concept · Current · Advanced A flaw where repeatedly activating one DRAM row can flip bits in neighbouring rows, a reliability and security risk. Security researchers showed Rowhammer could escalate privileges, prompting refresh-based defences in newer DRAM. PMIC and SPD hubJEDEC JESD79-5 (DDR5) module standards · Component · Current · Advanced DDR5 moves power regulation (PMIC) onto each module, and an SPD chip stores the module's size, speed and timing profile. The BIOS reads each stick's SPD at boot to set speed; a faulty PMIC can stop one DIMM powering up. DRAM timings (CL-tRCD-tRP-tRAS)JEDEC speed bins; module SPD, XMP and EXPO profiles · Metric · Current · Intermediate Delays, in clock cycles, between DRAM commands; CL (CAS latency) is the wait from a column read command to the first data. DDR5-6000 CL30 gives 30 ÷ 3000 MHz = 10 ns true latency, the same as DDR4-3200 CL16. Integrated memory controller (IMC)Inside Intel, AMD, Arm-based and Apple processors · Component · Current · Intermediate Logic on the processor that schedules DRAM commands, refresh, ECC and channel interleaving; it decides which speeds and capacities work. A desktop CPU's IMC may run four DDR5 sticks at a lower speed than two, because extra modules load each channel.

docs.title: 3.3 DRAM Generations and Standards (DDR, LPDDR, GDDR, HBM)
docs.text:
DRAM comes in families tuned for different jobs: DDR for PCs and servers, LPDDR for low-power phones and laptops, GDDR for graphics cards and HBM, tall stacks of chips placed beside AI accelerators. Each new generation moves more data per second while using less energy per bit. The rules for each family are published by an industry body called JEDEC so chips from different makers work together.

Peak bandwidth by memory family. Width matters as much as speed: HBM's very wide stacks beat faster but narrower buses.

Think of it like…

The families are like vehicles for different roads: DDR is a family car, LPDDR an efficient scooter, GDDR a sports car, and HBM a multi-lane motorway built right next to the factory.

Real-world example

Aisha compares three chips for a university project. A desktop with two DDR5-6400 channels gets about 2 × 6400 MT/s × 8 bytes ≈ 102 GB/s. A graphics card with a 256-bit GDDR7 bus at 28 Gbps gets 256 × 28 ÷ 8 = 896 GB/s. An AI accelerator with eight HBM3E stacks at about 1.2 TB/s each approaches 10 TB/s, which explains why AI chips use HBM despite its high cost.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. JEDEC committees, made of memory, CPU and GPU makers, agree a standard for each new generation.
  2. Memory makers (mainly SK hynix, Samsung and Micron) design chips that meet or exceed it.
  3. Speed is quoted in MT/s (megatransfers per second) or Gbps per pin; bandwidth = transfer rate × bus width in bytes.
  4. DDR and LPDDR use narrow fast buses, GDDR uses wider faster ones, and HBM uses very wide (1024- to 2048-bit) buses at moderate speed.
  5. HBM stacks DRAM dies vertically using through-silicon vias and sits on an interposer beside the processor.
  6. Newer generations add features such as on-die ECC, PAM signalling and lower voltages.

Who uses it

PC builders, hardware and GPU engineers, AI infrastructure teams and memory industry analysts track these standards closely.

Key takeaway

Bandwidth = transfer rate × bus width ÷ 8; practise this sum, because interviewers love asking why HBM beats DDR for AI.

Going deeper

  • Peak bandwidth = data rate per pin × bus width ÷ 8. DDR uses 64-bit channels, GDDR uses 32-bit chips ganged into 128-512-bit buses, and HBM uses 1024-bit (HBM3E) or 2048-bit (HBM4) stacks.
  • Signalling changed to reach higher speeds: DDR5 and LPDDR5 use two-level NRZ, GDDR6X uses four-level PAM4, and GDDR7 uses three-level PAM3, sending three bits every two cycles.
  • HBM stacks 8, 12 or 16 DRAM dies on a base die using through-silicon vias, and needs 2.5D packaging such as TSMC CoWoS, a long-running supply bottleneck for AI chips.
  • Capacity per HBM stack grew from 16-24 GB (HBM3) to 36 GB (12-high HBM3E) and up to 64 GB for 16-high HBM4, which is why accelerator memory rose from 80 GB to 288 GB.
  • LPDDR saves power with low voltages, deep sleep states and short traces, but is normally soldered; CAMM2, LPCAMM2 and SOCAMM modules bring replaceability back.
  • Memory is a cyclical commodity: in 2025-26 strong AI demand for HBM and server DRAM tightened supply and raised prices for PC and phone memory as well.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Comparing MT/s across families: LPDDR, DDR, GDDR and HBM use different bus widths, so compare bandwidth in GB/s instead.
  • Assuming a DDR5 motherboard accepts DDR4 sticks, or the reverse: the slots are keyed differently and the controllers are incompatible.
  • Treating XMP or EXPO speeds as guaranteed: they are overclocks, and stability depends on the CPU's memory controller and the board.
  • Believing HBM uses a special kind of memory cell: it is ordinary DRAM, stacked and connected through an extremely wide interface.

docs.title: Try it: Work out peak memory bandwidth in Python
docs.text:
def bw_gbs(mts, bus_bits):
    return mts * 1e6 * bus_bits / 8 / 1e9
print('DDR5-6400, 1 channel :', bw_gbs(6400, 64), 'GB/s')       # ~51.2
print('GDDR7 28 Gbps, 256-bit:', bw_gbs(28000, 256), 'GB/s')     # ~896
print('HBM4 8 Gbps, 2048-bit :', bw_gbs(8000, 2048), 'GB/s')      # ~2048 per stack
