docs.title: 3.4 Virtual Memory, Paging and the TLB
docs.text:
Virtual memory gives every program its own private, tidy address space, as if it had the whole memory to itself. The operating system and a hardware unit in the CPU translate these pretend (virtual) addresses into real (physical) ones, page by page. This keeps programs from reading each other's data, lets memory be shared safely and lets the system borrow disk space when RAM runs short.

Translating one virtual address. Most accesses stop at a TLB hit; only misses walk the page table, and only absent pages reach the OS.

Think of it like…

Each program has its own flat numbers 1, 2, 3, while the building manager keeps a directory saying which real room in which building each flat number maps to.

Real-world example

Lena runs a Python script that allocates a 10 GB array on a laptop with 16 GB of RAM. Linux hands out virtual pages instantly but only finds real memory when each 4 KiB page is first touched, triggering a minor page fault. When she also opens a video editor, RAM fills, so the kernel swaps idle pages to the SSD and everything slows down sharply. Running `free -h` and `vmstat 1` shows swap rising, so she processes the data in chunks instead.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Each process uses virtual addresses; the CPU's MMU splits them into a page number and an offset.
  2. The MMU first checks the TLB, a small cache of recent translations; a hit takes about a cycle.
  3. On a TLB miss, hardware walks the multi-level page table in memory to find the physical frame.
  4. If the page is not in RAM, a page fault hands control to the OS, which loads it (from disk or as a fresh zeroed page).
  5. When RAM is short, the OS evicts rarely used pages to swap and updates the page tables.
  6. Permissions bits in each entry (read, write, execute, user/kernel) enforce isolation and security.

Who uses it

Operating-system and kernel developers, system administrators, database tuners and security engineers work with virtual memory daily.

Key takeaway

Know the default page size (4 KiB on x86-64), what a TLB miss and a page fault are, and why huge pages help large-memory workloads.

Going deeper

  • x86-64 four-level paging translates 48-bit virtual addresses (256 TiB); five-level paging (LA57) extends this to 57 bits (128 PiB). Each level uses 9 address bits to index 512 entries.
  • One 2 MiB huge-page TLB entry covers 512 times the memory of a 4 KiB entry, and a 1 GiB entry covers 262,144 times, which is why huge pages help big in-memory workloads.
  • Minor faults, such as first touch of a fresh zero page, cost around a microsecond; major faults needing SSD reads cost tens to hundreds of microseconds, and milliseconds on hard disks.
  • Virtual machines add a second translation: guest virtual to guest physical to host physical, done in hardware by Intel EPT or AMD NPT, which makes each TLB miss more expensive.
  • Arm64 supports 4 KiB, 16 KiB and 64 KiB base pages; macOS on Apple silicon uses 16 KiB pages, a common surprise when porting low-level software.
  • Security features build on page tables: NX/XD stops code running from data pages, and SMEP/SMAP stop the kernel executing or touching user pages unexpectedly.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking virtual memory just means 'using disk as RAM': its main job is isolation and address translation; swapping is only one optional use.
  • Confusing a TLB miss with a page fault: a TLB miss is resolved by hardware walking tables, while a page fault traps into the OS.
  • Reading a large VIRT or VSZ value in top as real memory use: reserved address space is not RAM; check RSS or PSS instead.
  • Enabling Transparent Huge Pages everywhere: some databases advise disabling THP because background compaction can cause latency spikes.

docs.title: Try it: Inspect page size, memory, swap and huge pages on Linux
docs.text:
getconf PAGESIZE                       # usually 4096 bytes
free -h                                # RAM and swap usage
grep -i huge /proc/meminfo             # huge page settings
cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled
vmstat 1 5                             # 'si'/'so' columns = swap in/out
Get-CimInstance Win32_PageFileUsage    # Windows PowerShell: page file size

docs.title: Key chips, architectures, standards, tools & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example Virtual memoryOperating systems (Linux, Windows, macOS) with CPU hardware support · Concept · Current · Beginner Giving each process a private address space that the OS and hardware map onto real RAM or disk, page by page. Two programs can both use address 0x400000 without clashing because each maps to different physical memory. Physical vs virtual addressComputer architecture concept · Concept · Current · Beginner A virtual address is what the program sees; a physical address is the real location in RAM chips after translation. A debugger shows a pointer of 0x7ffd1234abcd, but the data actually sits in a frame near the 3 GB mark of RAM. MMU (Memory Management Unit)Built into CPUs (x86-64, Arm, RISC-V) · Component · Current · Intermediate The hardware in the CPU that translates virtual addresses to physical ones and checks access permissions on every memory access. When a buggy C program writes to a read-only page, the MMU raises a fault and Linux reports 'Segmentation fault'. Page and page frameOS and ISA convention; 4 KiB default on x86-64 · Concept · Current · Beginner Memory is managed in fixed-size blocks: a page in virtual memory maps to a same-sized frame in physical RAM. A 1 MiB buffer occupies 256 pages of 4 KiB, which may be scattered anywhere in physical RAM. Page tableDefined by each ISA (x86-64 4- or 5-level, Arm, RISC-V Sv39/Sv48) · Concept · Current · Intermediate The hardware-defined tree of tables, filled in by the OS, that the MMU walks to find each virtual page's physical frame and permissions. x86-64 uses four levels to translate 48-bit addresses, or five levels for 57-bit addresses on big servers. TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer)Built into CPU cores · Component · Current · Intermediate A small cache of recent virtual-to-physical translations so the CPU rarely has to walk the page table. A TLB with 2048 entries of 4 KiB pages covers 8 MiB; random access over 50 GB causes many TLB misses. Page faultOperating system mechanism · Concept · Current · Intermediate The exception the MMU raises when a page is unmapped, absent or forbidden; minor faults are cheap, major faults need disk I/O. Starting a large app causes thousands of major faults as code is read from SSD the first time. Huge pagesLinux HugeTLB and Transparent Huge Pages; Windows large pages · Technology · Current · Advanced Larger pages such as 2 MiB or 1 GiB that cut TLB misses for programs using lots of memory. A database team enables 2 MiB huge pages for a 256 GB buffer pool and measures several percent more throughput. Copy-on-write (fork)Unix/Linux kernels · Technology · Current · Advanced Parent and child processes share the same pages after fork until one writes, only then copying that page. A web server forks 20 workers instantly because the 500 MB code and data are shared, not duplicated. Memory-mapped files (mmap)POSIX mmap; Windows CreateFileMapping · Technology · Current · Advanced Mapping a file directly into a process's address space so file reads and writes become ordinary memory accesses. A search engine maps a 40 GB index file and lets the OS page in only the parts queries touch. ASLRAddress Space Layout Randomisation in Linux, Windows, macOS, Android, iOS · Technology · Current · Intermediate Placing a program's code, stack and libraries at random addresses each run, making memory-corruption attacks harder. An attacker's exploit that needs a fixed library address fails because the address changes on every launch. OOM killerLinux kernel · Software · Current · Intermediate The Linux mechanism that kills a process to free memory when RAM and swap are exhausted. A container hitting its 2 GB limit is killed and 'OOMKilled' appears in Kubernetes pod status. Page table entry (PTE) flagsx86-64, Arm and RISC-V page-table formats · Concept · Current · Advanced Bits in each entry marking a page present, writable, user-accessible, no-execute (NX), accessed or dirty, checked by the MMU on every access. The NX bit marks the stack non-executable, so injected shellcode placed there crashes the program instead of running. PCID and ASID (tagged TLB)x86-64 PCID; Arm and RISC-V address-space identifiers · Technology · Current · Advanced Tags on TLB entries naming their address space, so switching between processes need not flush every cached translation. Linux uses PCID to reduce the cost of the extra page-table switches added by the Meltdown fix (KPTI) on Intel CPUs. TLB shootdownOS kernels on multicore processors · Concept · Current · Advanced When the OS changes or removes a mapping, it interrupts other cores to invalidate their stale TLB entries, a cost that grows with core count. A 128-thread program that repeatedly unmaps memory spends noticeable time on inter-processor interrupts for shootdowns.

docs.title: 3.5 CXL: Compute Express Link and Memory Pooling
docs.text:
CXL is an open standard that lets processors, accelerators and extra memory share data quickly and safely over the same physical slots and wiring as PCIe. It lets a server add memory beyond its DIMM slots and, in newer versions, lets several servers draw from a shared pool of memory. This helps data centres stop wasting expensive RAM that sits idle in one server while another runs short.

CXL memory pooling through a switch. Each server sees its slice of the shared pool as an extra NUMA node without CPU cores.

Think of it like…

CXL is like a shared office supply room: instead of every desk hoarding its own paper, teams take what they need from a common store down the corridor.

Real-world example

Northfield Cloud, a fictional hosting company, finds its 1,000 servers use on average only 55% of their 768 GB of RAM, yet some jobs still run out. Engineers trial a CXL memory pool appliance shared by 16 servers, giving each 512 GB locally plus access to a shared pool. Memory-hungry jobs borrow extra capacity for a few hours, then release it. Because CXL memory is roughly as slow as a far-socket NUMA hop, they let the Linux kernel place cold pages there and keep hot pages in local DRAM.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A CXL device plugs into a PCIe-style slot or E3.S bay and negotiates CXL instead of plain PCIe at link-up.
  2. CXL.io handles discovery and configuration, just like PCIe.
  3. CXL.cache lets a device coherently cache host memory; CXL.mem lets the host read and write device memory with load/store instructions.
  4. The OS sees CXL memory as an extra NUMA node without CPU cores, usually a little slower than local DRAM.
  5. From CXL 2.0, switches allow one memory device to be split between hosts (pooling); CXL 3.x adds true sharing and fabrics.

Who uses it

Server architects, cloud and hyperscale infrastructure engineers, Linux kernel developers and AI platform teams work with CXL.

Key takeaway

Remember the three device types: Type 1 = accelerator with cache, Type 2 = accelerator with its own memory, Type 3 = memory expander.

Going deeper

  • CXL reuses the PCIe physical layer: CXL 1.1 and 2.0 run at 32 GT/s (PCIe 5.0), CXL 3.x at 64 GT/s (PCIe 6.0) and CXL 4.0 at 128 GT/s (PCIe 7.0).
  • A CXL.mem access typically adds very roughly 100 ns or more over local DRAM, similar to or worse than a remote-socket NUMA hop, so it suits capacity expansion and cooler data.
  • Pooling (CXL 2.0) assigns each slice of a device to one host at a time; sharing (CXL 3.x) lets several hosts access the same memory coherently, which needs careful software.
  • Cloud operators have reported that a meaningful share of server DRAM sits stranded, installed but unused; pooling aims to cut that cost because memory is a large part of server spend.
  • Management and security features include IDE link encryption (2.0), TEE Security Protocol support for confidential computing (3.1) and standard Fabric Manager interfaces for allocating pooled memory.
  • In 2026 Type 3 memory expanders are the mainstream deployment, supported by current Intel Xeon 6 and AMD EPYC server platforms and by Linux's NUMA and memory-tiering code.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating CXL memory as fast as local DRAM: its latency is higher, so keep hot data local and let tiering place the rest.
  • Thinking CXL is just PCIe: it shares slots and wiring, but adds cache-coherent load/store protocols that plain PCIe devices lack.
  • Assuming every platform supports pooling or sharing: check the CPU's CXL version, supported device types and OS support first.

docs.title: Try it: Look for CXL devices and NUMA nodes on a Linux server
docs.text:
ls /sys/bus/cxl/devices/ 2>/dev/null || echo 'no CXL devices'
cxl list -M          # from the ndctl/cxl-cli package, if installed
numactl --hardware   # CXL memory usually appears as a CPU-less NUMA node

docs.title: 3.6 NAND Flash and SSDs
docs.text:
An SSD (solid-state drive) stores data in NAND flash memory chips, which keep data without power and have no moving parts. Each flash cell traps electric charge to represent one or more bits, and modern chips stack hundreds of layers of cells vertically. A small computer inside the SSD, the controller, spreads writes evenly and hides flash's quirks so the drive looks like a simple disk.

How an SSD handles an overwrite. Flash cannot overwrite in place, so the controller writes elsewhere and cleans up later.

Think of it like…

Flash is like a notebook written in pencil where you can only erase whole pages at once, so a careful librarian (the controller) keeps rewriting pages elsewhere and tracks where everything really is.

Real-world example

Ravi buys a 2 TB TLC NVMe SSD rated for 1,200 TBW (terabytes written) with a 5-year warranty. His video editing writes about 100 GB per day, so 1,200,000 GB ÷ 100 GB ≈ 12,000 days, over 30 years of rated endurance. A friend's cheap DRAM-less QLC drive slows from 5 GB/s to under 200 MB/s after its SLC cache fills during a 300 GB copy. For a media server that mostly reads, the QLC drive would still be a good, cheap choice.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Each NAND cell stores charge in a charge-trap layer; the amount of charge encodes 1 to 4 (or 5) bits.
  2. Cells are written in pages (kilobytes) but can only be erased in much larger blocks (megabytes).
  3. The controller's flash translation layer (FTL) maps logical addresses from the OS to physical pages.
  4. Updated data is written to fresh pages; old pages are marked invalid and later reclaimed by garbage collection.
  5. Wear levelling spreads erase cycles evenly, because each block survives only a limited number of program/erase cycles.
  6. TRIM tells the drive which blocks the OS no longer needs, keeping write speeds high.

Who uses it

PC builders, storage engineers, data-centre operators, embedded and firmware developers, and anyone choosing laptops or servers.

Key takeaway

More bits per cell means cheaper and denser but slower and less durable: SLC > MLC > TLC > QLC > PLC in endurance.

Going deeper

  • Rated program/erase cycles fall as bits per cell rise: SLC tens of thousands, MLC several thousand, TLC roughly 1,000-3,000 and QLC several hundred to about 1,000, varying by vendor.
  • With 4 KiB mapping, the FTL table needs about 1 GB of DRAM per 1 TB of flash, which is why large enterprise drives use onboard DRAM or larger mapping units.
  • Controllers use strong LDPC error correction, read-retry and RAID-like parity across dies, because raw NAND error rates rise with wear, heat and time since writing.
  • NAND is organised as packages, dies, planes, blocks and pages; controllers keep many dies busy in parallel, so small drives with few dies are often slower.
  • Enterprise SSDs add power-loss protection capacitors to save data in flight and firmware tuned for consistent latency; consumer drives optimise for short bursts.
  • Unpowered flash slowly leaks charge: JEDEC client endurance ratings assume about a year of retention at 30 °C once rated wear is used up, so SSDs make poor long-term archives.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Judging an SSD by peak sequential speed alone: sustained writes after the SLC cache fills and random 4K performance matter more.
  • Assuming deleting files securely erases an SSD: copies can linger in remapped blocks; use the drive's secure-erase or sanitize command.
  • Worrying excessively about wear on a home PC: typical consumer drives exceed their TBW rating only under very heavy write workloads.

docs.title: Try it: Read SSD health and wear (read-only commands)
docs.text:
sudo smartctl -a /dev/nvme0             # Linux/macOS (smartmontools): 'Percentage Used', 'Data Units Written'
sudo nvme smart-log /dev/nvme0          # Linux nvme-cli
Get-PhysicalDisk | Get-StorageReliabilityCounter | Select-Object DeviceId,Wear,Temperature   # Windows PowerShell (admin)
fsutil behavior query DisableDeleteNotify   # Windows: 0 means TRIM is enabled

Wear levellingSSD firmware · Technology · Current · Intermediate Spreading writes and erases evenly over all blocks so no part of the flash wears out early. A log file rewritten every second is moved around the drive so one block is not erased millions of times. Garbage collection and write amplificationSSD firmware behaviour · Concept · Current · Advanced Reclaiming blocks by copying valid pages elsewhere before erasing; the extra internal writes are called write amplification. A write amplification factor of 3 means 100 GB from the OS causes 300 GB of flash writes. TRIM / DeallocateATA TRIM; NVMe Deallocate (Dataset Management) · Command · Current · Intermediate A command from the OS telling the SSD which blocks hold deleted data, so it can erase them in the background. Windows sends TRIM weekly via 'Optimise Drives'; Linux uses the fstrim.timer service. SLC cacheSSD firmware feature · Technology · Current · Intermediate Part of a TLC or QLC drive temporarily used in fast 1-bit mode to absorb bursts of writes. A large copy runs at full speed until the cache fills, then drops to the native QLC write speed. DRAM-less SSD and HMBNVMe Host Memory Buffer feature · Technology · Current · Intermediate Budget SSDs without onboard DRAM borrow a small slice of system RAM (HMB) to cache mapping tables. A budget laptop's DRAM-less NVMe drive uses 64 MB of host RAM via HMB and still feels quick. Endurance: TBW and DWPDSSD vendor datasheets · Metric · Current · Beginner TBW is total terabytes writable over the warranty; DWPD is full-drive writes per day the drive is rated for. A 3.84 TB enterprise SSD rated 1 DWPD for 5 years allows about 7,000 TB written. Over-provisioningSSD firmware and vendor configuration · Concept · Current · Intermediate Spare flash hidden from the user that gives garbage collection room to work, raising sustained write speed and endurance. A 3.2 TB enterprise SSD often uses the same raw flash as a 3.84 TB model, trading capacity for a higher DWPD rating.

docs.title: 3.7 Storage Interfaces and Form Factors (PCIe, NVMe, SATA, SAS)
docs.text:
A storage interface is the connection and language a drive uses to talk to the computer. Old drives used SATA or SAS cables designed for spinning disks, while modern SSDs plug straight into fast PCIe lanes and speak a protocol called NVMe built for flash. Drives also come in different physical shapes, called form factors, from the small M.2 stick in a laptop to hot-swappable server drives.

Interface ceiling for one SSD. Theoretical one-direction limits; each PCIe generation roughly doubles the x4 ceiling.

Think of it like…

SATA is a single-lane country road built for tractors; NVMe over PCIe is a multi-lane motorway with many toll booths open at once.

Real-world example

Hannah upgrades her 2019 desktop from a SATA SSD that tops out at about 550 MB/s to an M.2 NVMe drive on PCIe 4.0 x4. Copying a 50 GB game folder drops from about 95 seconds to under 15 seconds. Her new motherboard also has a PCIe 5.0 M.2 slot, where drives reach about 14 GB/s, but for gaming load times the difference is small. At work, her company's servers use hot-swappable EDSFF E3.S NVMe drives in the front panel instead.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The drive connects through a physical connector (SATA, SAS, M.2, U.2/U.3 or EDSFF) to the motherboard or a backplane.
  2. SATA and SAS drives speak AHCI or SCSI commands through a host controller; NVMe drives speak NVMe directly over PCIe lanes.
  3. NVMe supports up to 64K queues of 64K commands each, so many CPU cores can issue I/O in parallel.
  4. Each PCIe generation roughly doubles the speed per lane; drives typically use 4 lanes (x4).
  5. The OS driver turns file-system requests into commands, and the drive replies with data or completions.

Who uses it

PC builders, server and storage engineers, hardware designers and data-centre technicians choose interfaces and form factors.

Key takeaway

Approximate x4 SSD limits to remember: SATA III about 0.55 GB/s, PCIe 3.0 about 3.5 GB/s, 4.0 about 7 GB/s, 5.0 about 14 GB/s.

Going deeper

  • PCIe 3.0 to 5.0 use 128b/130b encoding, giving about 0.98, 1.97 and 3.94 GB/s per lane in each direction; PCIe 6.0 switches to PAM4 with FLIT mode and forward error correction.
  • NVMe was designed for parallelism: up to 65,535 I/O queues of up to 65,536 commands each, usually one queue pair per CPU core, against AHCI's single 32-command queue.
  • M.2 slots are keyed: M-key slots carry PCIe x4 and sometimes SATA, while B-key carries SATA or PCIe x2; an M.2 SATA SSD still runs at SATA speed.
  • Data centres favour hot-swappable EDSFF E1.S and E3.S drives over U.2 because they cool better, fit more drives per server and handle PCIe 5.0 and 6.0 signalling.
  • Benchmark storage with fio and report IOPS, bandwidth and latency percentiles (p99, p99.9) at a stated block size and queue depth, because averages hide stalls.
  • NVMe also defines namespaces, sanitize commands, self-encrypting drive support (TCG Opal) and NVMe-MI for out-of-band monitoring through a server's management controller.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming every M.2 drive is NVMe: some are SATA and limited to about 550 MB/s; check the key and the datasheet.
  • Expecting a PCIe 5.0 SSD to halve game load times: loading is often limited by CPU decompression and software, not drive bandwidth.
  • Forgetting lane sharing: on many motherboards, using certain M.2 slots disables SATA ports or reduces the graphics slot's lanes.

docs.title: Try it: See which interface and link speed your drives use
docs.text:
lsblk -d -o NAME,TRAN,MODEL,SIZE,ROTA      # Linux: TRAN = sata/nvme/usb, ROTA=1 means spinning disk
sudo lspci -vv | grep -E 'Non-Volatile|LnkSta:'   # Linux: PCIe link speed/width
Get-PhysicalDisk | Select-Object FriendlyName,BusType,MediaType,Size   # Windows PowerShell

docs.title: Key chips, architectures, standards, tools & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example PCIe (PCI Express)PCI-SIG · Interface · Current · Beginner The high-speed serial expansion bus made of lanes (x1, x4, x16) that links GPUs, SSDs and network cards to the CPU. An NVMe SSD uses four PCIe lanes; a graphics card uses sixteen. PCIe 4.0 and 5.0PCI-SIG (4.0 in 2017, 5.0 in 2019) · Standard · Current · Beginner Generations running 16 GT/s and 32 GT/s per lane, about 2 and 4 GB/s per lane each way; mainstream in 2026 PCs and servers. PCIe 6.0PCI-SIG (January 2022) · Standard · Emerging · Intermediate 64 GT/s per lane using PAM4 signalling and fixed-size FLIT packets with forward error correction; arriving in AI servers and SSDs. AI servers adopt PCIe 6.0 switches and network cards to feed GPUs faster. Most laptops and desktops in 2026 boot from an M.2 2280 NVMe SSD. A storage server takes 24 U.2 NVMe SSDs in front bays, swapped without powering down. EDSFF (E1.S, E1.L, E3.S, E3.L)SNIA SFF specifications (SFF-TA-1006, SFF-TA-1007, SFF-TA-1008) · Format · Current · Advanced Enterprise and Data Center SSD Form Factor family, designed for better cooling, density and PCIe 5.0/6.0 signal integrity. A video editor works directly off a 4 TB external SSD over Thunderbolt. An NVMe SSD may give 15,000 IOPS at queue depth 1 but over 1,000,000 at high depth. A cloud caching service tags short-lived and long-lived data with different FDP placement IDs, bringing write amplification close to 1.

docs.title: 3.8 Hard Disk Drives and Tape
docs.text:
A hard disk drive (HDD) stores data magnetically on spinning metal or glass platters, read and written by tiny heads on a moving arm. Hard drives are slower than SSDs but much cheaper per terabyte, so they still hold most of the world's cloud data. Magnetic tape is slower still to reach, but cheaper and very long-lasting, making it the classic choice for archives and offline backups.

SSD vs hard drive vs tape

NVMe SSD Hard drive LTO tape Access time ~0.05-0.1 ms ~5-10 ms Seconds to minutes Sequential speed 3-14 GB/s ~0.25-0.3 GB/s ~0.4 GB/s native Largest units (2026) ~245-256 TB QLC ~30-44 TB 30-40 TB (LTO-10) Power when idle Low Platters keep spinning Zero on the shelf Best for Hot, random I/O Warm bulk data Cold archive, air gap

Each medium wins a different job: speed, cheap online capacity, or cheap offline archive.

Think of it like…

A hard drive is like a record player whose needle can jump to any track; tape is like a cassette you must wind to the right spot.

Real-world example

Cobalt Archive, a fictional film-restoration studio, has 2 PB of footage. Fresh projects live on NVMe SSDs, last year's work sits on 20 servers full of 30 TB hard drives, and finished masters are written to LTO-10 tapes kept in a vault in another city. Each 30 TB tape costs a fraction of a hard drive per terabyte and uses no power on the shelf. Restoring a film takes a few hours instead of seconds, which is fine for archives.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Platters spin at a constant speed, typically 5,400-7,200 RPM for capacity drives or 10,000-15,000 RPM for older performance drives.
  2. An actuator arm moves the read/write heads to the right track (seek time).
  3. The drive waits for the right sector to rotate under the head (rotational latency).
  4. Heads write by flipping tiny magnetic regions and read by sensing them; recording tricks like SMR and HAMR squeeze in more bits.
  5. Tape drives stream data along long reels in a cartridge, which is great for big sequential writes and slow for random access.

Who uses it

Storage administrators, cloud and archive engineers, backup specialists, broadcasters and research data managers.

Key takeaway

HDD random access costs milliseconds (seek plus rotation), so HDDs suit big sequential files; SSDs win for small random I/O.

Going deeper

  • Access time = seek (about 4-9 ms on average) + rotational latency (half a turn, 4.17 ms at 7,200 RPM) + transfer, so random 4 KiB reads manage only about 100-200 IOPS.
  • Density gains now come from energy-assisted recording: Seagate ships HAMR, Western Digital uses ePMR and plans HAMR, and Toshiba uses MAMR, pushing 3.5-inch drives past 30 TB.
  • Cloud providers use host-managed SMR and zoned drives at scale, writing sequentially through software to gain capacity without the random-rewrite penalty.
  • Native LTO capacity rises each generation: LTO-8 12 TB, LTO-9 18 TB, LTO-10 30 TB. Quoted compressed figures assume 2.5:1 compression, rarely achieved by video or encrypted data.
  • Tape offers low cost per terabyte, near-zero idle power, very low error rates and a true air gap once cartridges leave the drive, so hyperscalers run huge libraries for archive tiers.
  • Dual-actuator drives such as Seagate MACH.2 split the heads into two independent groups, roughly doubling IOPS per drive to keep IOPS per terabyte acceptable as capacities grow.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Using SMR drives in RAID or ZFS NAS arrays: rebuilds and random rewrites can become extremely slow, so choose CMR models there.
  • Trusting the 'compressed' capacity printed on tape: video, photos and encrypted backups barely compress, so plan with the native figure.
  • Ignoring IOPS per terabyte: a 30 TB drive has about the same IOPS as a 4 TB one, so huge drives can starve busy workloads.

docs.title: Try it: Check a hard drive's health and see average rotational latency
docs.text:
sudo smartctl -H -A /dev/sda      # read-only: health, Reallocated_Sector_Ct, Power_On_Hours
# Average rotational latency = half a revolution:
python3 -c "rpm=7200; print(round(0.5*60/rpm*1000,2), 'ms')"   # ~4.17 ms

docs.title: Key chips, architectures, standards, tools & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example Hard disk drive (HDD)Seagate, Western Digital, Toshiba · Component · Current · Beginner A drive storing data magnetically on spinning platters; slower than SSDs but far cheaper per terabyte. A cloud provider fills racks with 3.5-inch HDDs for photo and video backups. Hard drive makersSeagate Technology, Western Digital, Toshiba · Organisation · Current · Beginner Only three companies still make hard disk drives, mainly selling high-capacity models to cloud providers. When a hyperscaler qualifies a new 3.5-inch drive model, it can mean orders of millions of units. Platters, heads and actuatorHDD internals · Component · Current · Beginner Magnetic disks, the tiny heads that fly nanometres above them and the arm that moves the heads across tracks. A 10-platter drive has 20 heads, one for each platter surface. RPMHDD specification · Metric · Current · Beginner Revolutions per minute of the platters; faster spinning lowers rotational latency. At 7,200 RPM one revolution takes 8.3 ms, so average rotational wait is about 4.2 ms. Seek timeHDD specification · Metric · Current · Intermediate Time for the arm to move the heads to the right track, typically several milliseconds. Random 4 KB reads on an HDD manage only about 100-200 IOPS because of seeks. CMR (conventional magnetic recording)HDD recording method · Technology · Current · Intermediate Tracks written side by side without overlap, so any sector can be rewritten freely; preferred for NAS and RAID. A NAS owner checks the datasheet to be sure the drives are CMR, not SMR. SMR (shingled magnetic recording)HDD recording method · Technology · Current · Intermediate Overlaps tracks like roof shingles to fit more data, but rewrites become slow; host-managed versions suit cloud archives. An SMR drive in a RAID rebuild slowed to a crawl, a lesson many home NAS users learnt. HAMRSeagate Mozaic platform (Mozaic 4+ up to 44 TB, 2026) · Technology · Emerging · Advanced Heat-Assisted Magnetic Recording: a tiny laser briefly heats the spot being written so much smaller bits stay stable. In 2026 Seagate shipped Mozaic 4+ HAMR drives of up to 44 TB to large cloud providers. ePMR and MAMRWestern Digital (ePMR), Toshiba (MAMR) · Technology · Current · Advanced Energy-assisted recording methods that use extra energy at the write head to raise density without full HAMR. Western Digital and Toshiba use energy-assisted recording in their 20-30+ TB drive families. Helium-filled drivesIntroduced by HGST (now Western Digital) in 2013 · Technology · Current · Intermediate Sealed drives filled with helium, which reduces drag and turbulence so more, thinner platters fit and use less power. Nearly all modern high-capacity enterprise HDDs are helium-sealed. S.M.A.R.T.Drive self-monitoring standard; smartmontools for reading it · Technology · Current · Beginner Self-Monitoring, Analysis and Reporting Technology: counters a drive keeps about errors, temperature and wear. A rising 'Reallocated Sector Count' warns an admin to replace a drive before it fails. LTO tapeLTO Program (HPE, IBM, Quantum) · Standard · Current · Intermediate Linear Tape-Open, the main data tape format: LTO-9 holds 18 TB native; LTO-10 holds 30 TB, or 40 TB on a newer cartridge. A university writes research data to LTO-10 tapes and stores a copy off-site for decades. LTFSLTO Program; SNIA LTFS standard · Format · Current · Advanced Linear Tape File System, which lets a tape appear like a disk with folders and files. A film studio drags video files onto an LTFS tape just like a USB drive. Tape libraryIBM, Quantum, HPE, Spectra Logic and others · System · Current · Intermediate A robotic cabinet with tape drives and thousands of cartridge slots, providing huge, air-gapped capacity. A cloud archive service retrieves a customer's tape-stored data within hours using robotic libraries. A data centre with 10,000 drives at 1.5% AFR should plan to replace about 150 drives a year, roughly three a week.

docs.title: 3.9 RAID, Erasure Coding and Backups
docs.text:
RAID combines several drives so they act as one, either to go faster, to survive a drive failure, or both. Some RAID levels copy data to two drives; others store extra 'parity' information so lost data can be rebuilt mathematically. Large cloud systems use a more flexible version called erasure coding, but neither replaces proper backups.

RAID levels and erasure coding at a glance

Min drives · usable Survives Typical use RAID 0 2 · 100% No failures Scratch space for speed RAID 1 2 · 50% 1 failure Boot drives RAID 5 3 · (n-1)/n 1 failure Small arrays of small drives RAID 6 4 · (n-2)/n 2 failures Large hard-drive arrays RAID 10 4 · 50% 1 per mirror pair Busy databases Erasure code 8+3 11 nodes · 73% Any 3 failures Object storage at scale

More redundancy costs capacity; erasure coding spreads protection across many servers.

Think of it like…

Parity is like a class register's total: if one pupil's mark goes missing, you can work it out from the total and everyone else's marks.

Real-world example

Kwame looks after a fictional design agency's file server with six 20 TB drives. In RAID 6 it gives 4 × 20 = 80 TB usable and survives two failed drives. When one drive dies, the rebuild must read all five surviving drives and write 20 TB, and at roughly 200 MB/s it takes more than a day, so the second parity drive is vital. When a ransomware attack later encrypts the shares, RAID copies the damage instantly, and only last night's immutable off-site backup saves the agency.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Choose a layout: striping (spread data for speed), mirroring (copies) or parity (computed recovery data).
  2. A hardware controller or software (mdadm, Storage Spaces, ZFS) splits each write across the drives.
  3. For parity, data blocks are XORed (RAID 5) or encoded with Reed-Solomon maths (RAID 6, erasure codes).
  4. When a drive fails, the array runs 'degraded' and rebuilds onto a replacement or hot spare.
  5. Backups with separate copies, versions and an off-site or offline copy protect against deletion, ransomware and disasters.

Who uses it

System and storage administrators, cloud engineers, NAS owners and backup and disaster-recovery specialists.

Key takeaway

RAID is about availability, not backup: it happily mirrors deletions and ransomware, so always follow the 3-2-1 rule.

Going deeper

  • RAID 5 parity is a simple XOR across the stripe; RAID 6 adds a second syndrome computed with Reed-Solomon (Galois-field) maths, so any two missing blocks can be solved.
  • Small random writes carry a penalty: about 4 disk I/Os in RAID 5 (read data and parity, write both) and 6 in RAID 6, against 2 in RAID 10.
  • Erasure codes are written k+m: data is split into k fragments plus m coded fragments on different drives, servers or zones; storage efficiency is k ÷ (k+m).
  • Large object stores combine erasure coding across zones with replication for small or hot objects, trading CPU and network traffic during rebuilds for lower raw-capacity cost.
  • Regular scrubbing reads every block and verifies parity or checksums, finding latent bad sectors before a drive failure turns them into data loss.
  • Modern backup practice extends 3-2-1 to 3-2-1-1-0: one copy immutable or offline, and zero errors after regularly tested restores that prove the RPO and RTO are met.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating RAID as backup: it faithfully copies deletions, corruption and ransomware encryption to every drive at once.
  • Using RAID 5 with very large hard drives: long rebuilds plus URE risk make RAID 6 or erasure coding the safer choice.
  • Never testing restores: a backup that has not been restored successfully is a hope, not a backup.
  • Building an array from drives of one batch without monitoring: correlated failures during a long rebuild become much more likely.

docs.title: Try it: Calculate usable capacity and minimum rebuild time
docs.text:
n, size_tb, mbps = 6, 20, 200
for level, usable in {'RAID 0': n, 'RAID 5': n-1, 'RAID 6': n-2, 'RAID 10': n/2}.items():
    print(level, usable*size_tb, 'TB usable')
hours = size_tb*1e12 / (mbps*1e6) / 3600
print(f'Rebuild of one {size_tb} TB drive >= {hours:.1f} h')   # ~27.8 h
# Linux software RAID status: cat /proc/mdstat

docs.title: Key chips, architectures, standards, tools & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example RAIDPatterson, Gibson and Katz, UC Berkeley (1988) · Technology · Current · Beginner Redundant Array of Independent Disks: combining drives for performance, capacity, fault tolerance or a mix. A small office NAS uses four drives in RAID 5 so one failure does not lose files. RAID 0 (striping)RAID level · Concept · Current · Beginner Spreads data across drives for speed and full capacity, with no redundancy; one failure loses everything. A video editor uses two SSDs in RAID 0 as a fast scratch disk, keeping originals elsewhere. RAID 1 (mirroring)RAID level · Concept · Current · Beginner Writes identical copies to two drives; survives one failure but gives half the raw capacity. A server's boot drives are two mirrored SSDs, so the OS keeps running if one dies. RAID 5RAID level · Concept · Current · Beginner Stripes data with one drive's worth of distributed parity; survives one failure, risky with very large drives. Four 8 TB drives in RAID 5 give 24 TB usable. RAID 6RAID level · Concept · Current · Intermediate Like RAID 5 but with two independent parity blocks, so it survives two simultaneous drive failures. Twelve 20 TB drives in RAID 6 give 200 TB usable and tolerate two failures. RAID 10 (1+0)RAID level · Concept · Current · Intermediate Stripes across mirrored pairs, giving high performance and fast rebuilds at the cost of half the capacity. A busy database uses eight SSDs in RAID 10 for fast random writes. Parity (XOR)Mathematics used in RAID · Concept · Current · Intermediate An extra block computed so any one missing block can be recalculated from the others using exclusive-OR. If data blocks are 1010 and 0110, parity is 1100; losing 0110 it is rebuilt as 1010 XOR 1100. Hot spare and rebuildStorage operations practice · Concept · Current · Intermediate A standby drive that automatically replaces a failed one; the rebuild recreates its data, often taking many hours. A 20 TB drive rebuild at 200 MB/s needs at least 28 hours, during which the array is vulnerable. Hardware vs software RAIDBroadcom MegaRAID; Linux mdadm; Windows Storage Spaces; ZFS RAID-Z · Concept · Current · Intermediate RAID can run on a dedicated controller card or in the operating system; software RAID is now common and flexible. A Linux admin builds RAID 6 with mdadm and monitors it with cat /proc/mdstat. Erasure codingUsed in Ceph, cloud object stores, HDFS and others · Technology · Current · Advanced Splitting data into k pieces plus m coded pieces spread across servers, so any m can be lost. An object store using 8+3 erasure coding survives three failed servers with only 37.5% overhead. Reed-Solomon codeIrving Reed and Gustave Solomon (1960) · Concept · Current · Advanced A classic error-correcting code that underpins RAID 6 and most erasure coding, as well as QR codes and CDs. A QR code can still scan with a corner torn off thanks to Reed-Solomon error correction. 3-2-1 backup ruleWidely used backup best practice · Concept · Current · Beginner Keep 3 copies of data on 2 different types of media, with 1 copy off-site; many now add an offline or immutable copy. A clinic keeps its live server, a local NAS backup and an encrypted cloud copy. Immutable backupObject lock (S3 Object Lock), WORM tape and backup software vendors · Technology · Current · Intermediate A backup copy that cannot be changed or deleted until a set date, protecting it from ransomware and mistakes. Backups stored with 30-day object lock survive even when attackers steal admin passwords. RPO and RTOBusiness continuity planning terms · Metric · Current · Intermediate Recovery Point Objective is how much data you can afford to lose; Recovery Time Objective is how fast you must recover. Nightly backups give an RPO of up to 24 hours; restoring within 4 hours meets an RTO of 4 hours. Unrecoverable read error (URE) rateDrive datasheets (e.g. 1 error per 10^15 bits read) · Metric · Current · Intermediate How often a drive fails to read a sector, typically quoted as 1 per 10^14 bits for consumer HDDs and 1 per 10^15 for enterprise. Rebuilding a large RAID 5 reads tens of terabytes; one URE during that rebuild can lose data, a key reason RAID 6 is preferred.

docs.title: 3.10 File Systems
docs.text:
A file system is the set of rules an operating system uses to organise data on a drive into files and folders. It keeps track of where each file's pieces live, their names, sizes, dates and permissions, and how to recover after a crash. Different systems use different file systems, and some add clever features like snapshots and built-in checksums.

Where the file system sits in the storage stack. Applications only see files; each layer below turns them into blocks and finally device commands.

Think of it like…

A file system is a library's catalogue and shelving plan: without it, the books (data) are still on the shelves but nobody can find anything.

Real-world example

Mei formats a 256 GB USB stick as FAT32 and cannot copy a 6 GB video because FAT32 files max out at 4 GiB, so she reformats it as exFAT, which both her Windows PC and Mac can read. On her Linux home server she uses ZFS, which checksums every block and takes an hourly snapshot. When she accidentally deletes a folder of photos, she restores it from the 2 pm snapshot in seconds. A scrub later finds and repairs one corrupted block using the mirror copy.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A drive is split into partitions using a partition table (GPT on modern systems).
  2. Formatting writes the file system's structures: superblock, allocation maps, directories and metadata such as inodes or the MFT.
  3. When you save a file, the file system chooses free blocks, writes the data and updates the metadata.
  4. Journaling file systems first log intended metadata changes, so a crash can be replayed or rolled back quickly.
  5. Copy-on-write file systems never overwrite in place; they write new blocks and switch pointers, making snapshots cheap.

Who uses it

System administrators, Linux and Windows engineers, storage engineers, forensic analysts and anyone formatting drives.

Key takeaway

Know the defaults: NTFS for Windows, APFS for Apple, ext4 or XFS for most Linux servers, exFAT for removable drives.

Going deeper

  • Allocation designs differ: FAT uses a linked table of clusters, ext4 uses extents and block groups, NTFS stores very small files inside their MFT record, and ZFS and Btrfs use checksummed trees.
  • ext4 offers three journaling modes: 'ordered' (default) journals metadata after writing data, 'journal' also logs file data, and 'writeback' is fastest but least safe after a crash.
  • Copy-on-write file systems (ZFS, Btrfs, APFS, ReFS) never overwrite live blocks; they write new blocks and switch pointers, so snapshots and clones are almost free and crashes leave consistent states.
  • End-to-end checksums catch silent corruption ('bit rot') from drives, cables or controllers; with mirrors or RAID-Z, ZFS and Btrfs repair bad blocks automatically during reads or scrubs.
  • Limits worth memorising: FAT32 files max 4 GiB, MBR disks max 2 TiB, while exFAT, NTFS, ext4, XFS and APFS all handle files of many terabytes.
  • The same file interface covers special file systems: NFS and SMB mounts look local, tmpfs lives in RAM, and Linux's /proc and /sys expose kernel information as files.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating snapshots as backups: they live on the same disks, so a failed pool or an attacker with admin rights destroys them too.
  • Formatting a drive shared between Windows and Mac as NTFS or APFS: exFAT is the safest cross-platform choice.
  • Running fsck on a mounted file system: it can cause corruption; unmount the volume or check it at boot instead.
  • Filling a copy-on-write file system almost completely: performance collapses, and even deleting files needs some free space.

docs.title: Key chips, architectures, standards, tools & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example File systemOperating system component · Concept · Current · Beginner The structure and rules an OS uses to store, name, find and protect files and folders on a drive. Formatting a new drive in Windows asks you to choose NTFS or exFAT. GPT and MBRGPT: UEFI specification; MBR: IBM PC legacy · Standard · Current · Beginner Partition table formats; GPT supports huge disks and many partitions, while old MBR is limited to 2 TiB disks. A 4 TB data disk must use GPT, or only 2 TiB of it is usable. JournalingUsed by NTFS, ext4, XFS and others · Technology · Current · Intermediate Recording planned metadata changes in a log before applying them, so the file system recovers quickly after a crash. After a power cut, ext4 replays its journal in seconds instead of a long full disk check. SnapshotZFS, Btrfs, APFS, LVM, Windows VSS, storage arrays · Technology · Current · Beginner A frozen, read-only view of a file system at a moment in time; quick to create, but not a backup on its own. macOS Time Machine creates local APFS snapshots so you can roll back yesterday's edit. FAT32Microsoft (1996) · Standard · Legacy · Beginner An old, simple file system supported almost everywhere, but files are limited to 4 GiB. Some car stereos and game consoles still need USB sticks formatted as FAT32. exFATMicrosoft (2006); specification published 2019, in Linux since 5.4 · Standard · Current · Beginner A lightweight file system for flash drives and SD cards with no practical file-size limit and wide OS support. Cameras format 128 GB SDXC cards as exFAT so long 4K videos fit in one file. NTFSMicrosoft (1993, Windows NT) · Standard · Current · Beginner The default Windows file system, with journaling, permissions (ACLs), compression and encryption support. Windows 11 installs to an NTFS-formatted C: drive. ReFSMicrosoft (2012, Windows Server) · Standard · Current · Intermediate Resilient File System for Windows servers and Dev Drives, with checksums, integrity streams and block cloning. A Hyper-V host stores VM disks on ReFS, so checkpoints merge much faster. ext4Linux kernel community (2008) · Standard · Current · Beginner The long-standing default Linux file system: journaled, mature and reliable for most workloads. Ubuntu formats its root partition as ext4 by default. XFSOriginally SGI (1993); Linux kernel community · Standard · Current · Intermediate A high-performance journaling file system strong with large files and parallel I/O; default on Red Hat Enterprise Linux. A media company stores multi-terabyte video files on XFS volumes. BtrfsLinux kernel community (originally Oracle) · Standard · Current · Intermediate A copy-on-write Linux file system with snapshots, checksums, compression and subvolumes; default on Fedora Workstation and openSUSE. openSUSE takes a Btrfs snapshot before each update, so a bad update can be rolled back from the boot menu. ZFS / OpenZFSOriginally Sun Microsystems (2005); OpenZFS project · Software · Current · Intermediate A combined file system and volume manager with end-to-end checksums, RAID-Z, snapshots, compression and replication. A TrueNAS box uses ZFS RAID-Z2 and weekly scrubs to detect and heal silent corruption. APFSApple (2017) · Standard · Current · Beginner Apple File System for macOS, iOS and other Apple devices, built for flash, with copy-on-write, snapshots and native encryption. Duplicating a 5 GB file on a Mac is instant because APFS clones it rather than copying. Inode and MFTUnix and Linux file systems (inode); NTFS Master File Table · Concept · Current · Intermediate Per-file metadata records holding size, owner, permissions, timestamps and data-block locations; directory entries simply map names to them. A server holding millions of tiny files runs out of ext4 inodes while df still shows free space; df -i reveals the problem. fsck and chkdskLinux e2fsprogs and xfsprogs; Windows chkdsk · Tool · Current · Beginner Tools that check a file system's metadata for inconsistencies and repair it, normally on an unmounted volume. After a USB stick is pulled out mid-copy, Windows offers to scan and fix it, running chkdsk behind the scenes. Full-disk encryption (BitLocker, FileVault, LUKS)Microsoft BitLocker; Apple FileVault; Linux LUKS and dm-crypt · Technology · Current · Beginner Encrypting an entire volume so its data is unreadable without the key, protecting lost or stolen laptops and drives. A stolen company laptop with BitLocker enabled exposes no client files, because the disk cannot be read without the key.

docs.title: 3.11 Block, File and Object Storage on the Network
docs.text:
Storage can be attached directly to one computer or shared over a network. Data can be offered as raw blocks (like a blank disk), as files in folders, or as objects (whole files with labels, fetched by web requests). Big organisations, clouds and supercomputers combine these to give thousands of computers fast, shared, reliable storage.

Block vs file vs object storage

Block File Object Unit Numbered blocks (LUNs, volumes) Files in folders Objects with metadata Protocols iSCSI, Fibre Channel, NVMe-oF NFS, SMB HTTP S3 API Namespace None; host formats it Hierarchical directories Flat buckets and keys Latency Lowest (µs to ms) Low to moderate Higher (ms) Scale TB per volume PB per cluster Exabytes, billions of objects Typical use Databases, VM disks Shared folders, home dirs Backups, media, data lakes

Pick by workload: raw disks for databases, shared folders for people, buckets for huge unstructured data.

Think of it like…

Block storage is renting an empty warehouse unit, file storage is a shared office filing cabinet, and object storage is a cloakroom where you hand over a coat and get a ticket to claim it back.

Real-world example

Orbital Labs, a fictional biotech start-up, runs its database on block volumes from a SAN using NVMe over TCP, because databases want low-latency raw disks. Scientists share documents through an SMB file share on a NAS, and the Linux compute cluster mounts the same data over NFS. Billions of microscope images go to an S3-compatible object store built on Ceph. When they rent time on a national supercomputer, results stream into a Lustre parallel file system at hundreds of GB/s.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Decide the access type: block (a raw disk for databases and VMs), file (shared folders) or object (HTTP API for huge unstructured data).
  2. Block storage is reached locally (DAS) or over a SAN using iSCSI, Fibre Channel or NVMe-oF.
  3. File storage is served by a NAS using NFS (mostly Linux/Unix) or SMB (mostly Windows and macOS).
  4. Object storage stores data with metadata in flat buckets and is reached with HTTP calls, usually the S3 API.
  5. Distributed and parallel systems (Ceph, Lustre, IBM Storage Scale) spread data across many servers for scale and redundancy.

Who uses it

Storage, cloud and HPC engineers, system and database administrators, and data-platform and AI infrastructure teams.

Key takeaway

Remember the trio: block = disks (SAN, iSCSI), file = folders (NAS, NFS/SMB), object = buckets (S3), and match each to its workload.

Going deeper

  • Most enterprise Fibre Channel SANs run at 16, 32 or 64 Gb/s, while iSCSI and NVMe/TCP use ordinary 25-400 Gb/s Ethernet, which is why Ethernet-based block storage keeps gaining ground.
  • NVMe-oF runs over RDMA (RoCE, InfiniBand), TCP or Fibre Channel; NVMe/TCP needs no special network cards and adds only tens of microseconds, making it popular for shared flash.
  • NFSv4 added stateful sessions, Kerberos security and parallel NFS (pNFS); SMB 3 added multichannel, encryption and SMB Direct over RDMA for fast Windows file serving.
  • Amazon S3 has provided strong read-after-write consistency since December 2020; many S3-compatible stores now match it, simplifying applications built on object storage.
  • Ceph places data with its CRUSH algorithm, calculating where objects live instead of looking them up in a central table, so clusters scale to thousands of drives.
  • AI training clusters use parallel or high-performance all-flash platforms (Lustre, IBM Storage Scale, WEKA, VAST, DDN) and GPUDirect Storage to move data straight into GPU memory.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Running a busy database on object storage or an overloaded NAS: databases need low-latency block storage or carefully tuned file protocols.
  • Treating object storage as a file system: renaming a 'folder' copies every object, and small edits rewrite whole objects.
  • Exposing NFS or SMB shares to the Internet: keep them on private networks or VPNs, and disable the old SMB1 protocol.
  • Forgetting request and egress fees when estimating cloud object-storage costs: retrieval can cost more than storage.

findmnt -t nfs,nfs4,cifs          # Linux: mounted NFS/SMB shares
Get-SmbMapping                     # Windows PowerShell: mapped SMB shares
# Listing a bucket you own with the AWS CLI (needs your own configured account):

docs.title: 3.12 Emerging Memory and Processing-in-Memory
docs.text:
Engineers are searching for memories that combine DRAM's speed with flash's ability to keep data without power, and for ways to stop wasting energy moving data back and forth. New technologies store bits as magnetism, resistance or crystal state instead of electric charge. Others put simple computing right inside or beside memory chips, or stack flash next to AI chips.

Emerging memories vs today's DRAM and NAND

Stores a bit as Strength Where used today DRAM (reference) Charge in a capacitor Fast, cheap Main memory (volatile) NAND (reference) Trapped charge Very dense, cheap SSDs (wears out) MRAM Magnetic orientation Fast, high endurance Embedded MCUs, space ReRAM Filament resistance Simple, low power Embedded NVM PCM Glassy vs crystal phase Dense, multi-level Embedded automotive memory FeRAM Electric polarisation Ultra-low-power writes Meters, industrial logging

Each new memory stores a bit in a different physical way, and most win niches before mass markets.

Think of it like…

Instead of carrying every book from the library to your desk to count words, processing-in-memory sends a helper into the library to count them where they sit.

Real-world example

Zainab, a PhD student, reviews why Intel's Optane persistent memory, which sat between DRAM and SSD, was discontinued in 2022 despite its speed: it was costly and never reached high volume. She compares it with MRAM, now built into some microcontrollers as fast, durable on-chip storage, and with processing-in-memory prototypes that cut data movement for AI. Her conclusion is that DRAM and NAND will dominate for years, while new memories win specific niches first.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Identify the gap: DRAM is fast but volatile; flash is non-volatile but slower and wears out.
  2. Storage-class memories (MRAM, ReRAM, PCM, FeRAM) store bits as magnetism, resistance or polarisation.
  3. Most begin as embedded memory in microcontrollers and chips before (if ever) competing as standalone products.
  4. Processing-in-memory adds simple compute units inside memory to avoid moving data to the CPU.
  5. New tiers, such as high-bandwidth flash for AI inference, are being standardised to sit between HBM and SSD.

Who uses it

Semiconductor researchers, memory and chip designers, embedded engineers, computer-architecture students and AI hardware teams.

Key takeaway

Know that Intel Optane (3D XPoint) was discontinued in 2022: a favourite example of great technology that failed on cost and volume.

Going deeper

  • Moving data, not computing on it, dominates energy: an off-chip DRAM access costs hundreds of times a simple arithmetic operation, which is why PIM and near-memory compute attract investment.
  • Optane failed commercially because it sat between DRAM and NAND on price and speed without either's volume economics; much of its persistent-memory role is moving to CXL-attached memory.
  • Embedded MRAM and ReRAM are replacing embedded flash at advanced process nodes, roughly 28 nm and below, where adding flash's extra manufacturing steps becomes difficult and costly.
  • Samsung's HBM-PIM placed programmable units inside HBM banks, and SK hynix's AiM adds multiply-accumulate units to GDDR6; both target memory-bound AI steps such as matrix-vector products.
  • Computational storage is defined by SNIA's architecture work and the NVMe Computational Programs command set, letting hosts send functions to run inside the drive.
  • New tiers proposed for AI inference include High Bandwidth Flash for huge read-mostly weights and CXL memory pools for KV cache, filling the gap between HBM and SSD.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming a lab breakthrough means products soon: new memories often take a decade to reach volume, and many never do.
  • Thinking non-volatile memory removes the need for backups: persistent data still suffers bugs, corruption and hardware failures.
  • Treating PIM as a general CPU replacement: it speeds simple, data-parallel operations, not complex branch-heavy code.

docs.title: Try it: Estimate how much energy data movement costs (illustrative figures)
docs.text:
# Rough, order-of-magnitude energy per 64-bit operation (illustrative only)
add_pj, dram_read_pj = 1, 1000          # arithmetic vs fetching from off-chip DRAM
print('DRAM fetch costs about', dram_read_pj // add_pj, 'x an add')
# Moving data, not maths, dominates energy - the motivation for processing-in-memory

An accelerator designer orders HBM4 with a custom base die, moving some memory-control logic out of the main GPU die. 3D DRAMResearch and development at major DRAM makers · Technology · Emerging · Advanced Efforts to stack DRAM cells vertically, as 3D NAND did for flash, to keep density rising as flat cell shrinking slows. Industry roadmaps discuss vertical-channel and stacked DRAM cells as a possible path for main memory in the 2030s.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Operating Systems, Firmware & Virtualization
docs.text: Hardware does nothing useful until software organises it. This chapter explains how operating systems share processors and memory between programs, how a computer boots from firmware into a running OS, how drivers talk to devices, and how compilers, linkers and language runtimes turn code into running programs. It then shows how hypervisors, containers, Kubernetes and WebAssembly let one machine safely run many isolated workloads — the foundation of every cloud.

docs.title: 5.1 What an Operating System Does
docs.text:
An operating system (OS) is the master program that runs your computer: it shares out processor time and memory, talks to hardware such as disks and Wi-Fi chips, and gives apps simple services like 'open a file' or 'send this over the network'. Its innermost part, the kernel, has full control of the hardware, while everything else (apps, the desktop, background services) asks the kernel for help. Without an OS every app would have to know how to drive every possible device itself.

Layers of a running system. Everything above the system-call interface runs in user mode; only the kernel touches the hardware directly.

Think of it like…

An OS is like the management of a busy hotel: guests (apps) never wire their own rooms or cook in the kitchen; they ask reception (the kernel), which shares out rooms, staff and keys fairly and keeps guests out of each other's rooms.

Real-world example

Leo opens a photo editor, a music player and 40 browser tabs on his laptop with 8 cores and 16 GB of RAM. The Windows kernel gives each program its own private memory, switches the 8 cores between hundreds of threads many times a second, and passes the photo editor's 'save' request to the SSD driver. When the music player crashes, the kernel cleans up its memory and the other programs carry on untouched.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Firmware starts the machine and loads the kernel into memory.
  2. The kernel takes control of the CPU, memory and devices, then starts the first user-space program (init, e.g. systemd or Windows smss.exe).
  3. Services (background programs) and a shell or desktop start on top.
  4. Apps request work through system calls; the kernel checks permissions and does it on their behalf.
  5. The kernel keeps scheduling, protecting memory and handling hardware events until shutdown.

Who uses it

Every developer, system administrator, DevOps and cloud engineer works with an OS daily, and kernel and embedded engineers build them.

Key takeaway

Learn the three classic kernel designs — monolithic (Linux), microkernel (QNX, seL4) and hybrid (Windows NT, macOS XNU) — and one trade-off of each.

Going deeper

  • An OS has three classic jobs: abstraction (files, sockets and processes instead of raw hardware), resource management (sharing CPU, memory and I/O fairly) and protection (keeping programs and users apart).
  • The Linux kernel source runs to tens of millions of lines of C, Rust and assembly, and most of it is device drivers; the scheduler, memory manager and system-call core are comparatively small.
  • Windows NT layers user-mode subsystems over ntdll.dll, the executive and kernel in ntoskrnl.exe and a hardware abstraction layer (hal.dll); macOS's XNU combines Mach, BSD and the IOKit driver framework.
  • Kernel design is a trade-off: monolithic kernels are fast because components call each other directly, while microkernels pay for message passing but contain faults and shrink the trusted code base.
  • 'Everything is a file' is Unix's unifying idea: disks (/dev/sda), kernel data (/proc), pipes and terminals are all used through the same open, read, write and close calls.
  • POSIX (IEEE 1003.1) and the Single UNIX Specification keep code portable; macOS is certified UNIX 03, whereas Linux distributions are largely compatible but generally not formally certified.
  • Unikernels compile one application together with just the OS pieces it needs into a single image, trading generality for tiny size and very fast boot as cloud VMs.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Calling Linux a complete operating system when you mean a distribution: Linux is the kernel; Ubuntu or RHEL add the init system, libraries, shells and package manager.
  • Assuming microkernels are always too slow. Designs such as seL4 and QNX have fast message passing; the real cost depends on how often components talk.
  • Running everything as root or Administrator to dodge permission errors. It removes the OS's protection, so one bug or piece of malware gets full control.

docs.title: Try it: See which OS and kernel version you are running
docs.text:
uname -a                      # Linux / macOS
cat /etc/os-release           # Linux distribution details
Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem | Select-Object Caption, Version, OSArchitecture   # Windows PowerShell

docs.title: Key chips, architectures, standards, tools & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example KernelCore of every OS · Concept · Current · Beginner The privileged core of the OS that manages CPU time, memory, devices and security, running with full hardware access. The Linux kernel, the Windows NT kernel (ntoskrnl.exe) and Apple's XNU are the kernels behind most computers and phones. User spaceGeneral OS concept · Concept · Current · Beginner Everything that runs outside the kernel with restricted rights: apps, shells, desktops and services, which must ask the kernel for hardware access. Your web browser runs in user space, so a crash in it cannot directly corrupt the kernel's memory. ShellBash, Zsh (GNU / open source); PowerShell (Microsoft) · Software · Current · Beginner A program that reads your typed commands and asks the OS to run them; graphical desktops are a visual kind of shell. Typing 'ls -l' in Bash or 'Get-ChildItem' in PowerShell lists files in the current folder. Service / daemonsystemd units (Linux); Windows Services; launchd (macOS) · Concept · Current · Beginner A background program that starts automatically and keeps running without a window, providing a function such as printing, logging or a web server. The sshd daemon waits for remote logins; on Windows the Print Spooler service manages print jobs. Hardware abstractionGeneral OS concept · Concept · Current · Beginner The OS hides hardware differences behind standard interfaces, so programs use 'files' and 'sockets' instead of disk sectors and network chip registers. The same Python script can save a file on an NVMe SSD, a USB stick or a network share without code changes. Monolithic kernele.g. Linux, FreeBSD · Architecture · Current · Intermediate A design where the scheduler, memory manager, file systems and drivers all run together in kernel mode as one large program. Linux is monolithic but loads drivers as modules, so a Wi-Fi driver bug can still crash the whole system. Microkernele.g. QNX, seL4, MINIX 3 · Architecture · Current · Intermediate A minimal kernel that only handles scheduling, memory and messaging; drivers and file systems run as separate user-space servers. In QNX, a crashed audio driver can be restarted without rebooting the car's infotainment system. Hybrid kernele.g. Windows NT, Apple XNU · Architecture · Current · Intermediate A mix of both designs: microkernel-style structure, but most services kept in kernel mode for speed. Apple's XNU combines the Mach microkernel with BSD Unix code; Windows NT keeps its executive and many drivers in kernel mode. seL4seL4 Foundation (Linux Foundation) · Software · Current · Advanced A microkernel with a machine-checked mathematical proof that its code matches its specification, used where security is critical. Defence and aerospace projects use seL4 to isolate flight-control software from less-trusted components. POSIXIEEE Std 1003.1 / The Open Group · Standard · Current · Intermediate A standard set of OS interfaces (processes, files, threads, shell) that lets programs move between Unix-like systems with little change. A C program using fork(), open() and pthreads compiles on Linux, macOS and FreeBSD alike. Init system (PID 1)systemd, OpenRC, launchd; Windows smss/wininit · Concept · Current · Intermediate The first user-space process the kernel starts; it launches and supervises every other service. Running 'ps -p 1' on Ubuntu shows systemd as process number 1. UnixBell Labs (1969); now The Open Group trademark · Architecture · Legacy · Beginner The influential 1970s OS whose ideas — files, pipes, small tools, multi-user — shaped Linux, macOS and BSD. The pipe in 'cat log.txt | grep error' comes straight from Unix design in the early 1970s.

docs.title: 5.2 Processes, Threads & Concurrency
docs.text:
A process is a running program with its own private memory; a thread is one line of work inside a process, and a process can have many threads sharing the same memory. The OS keeps a record of each process, switches between them quickly to create the illusion that everything runs at once, and offers tools so they can talk and take turns safely. When threads share data carelessly you get race conditions and deadlocks, the classic bugs of concurrent programming.

Life cycle of a process or thread. Only one thread per core is Running at any instant; everything else waits in Ready or Waiting.

Think of it like…

A process is a restaurant kitchen with its own pantry; threads are the cooks inside it sharing that pantry, and a mutex is the single key to the spice cupboard so two cooks never grab the same jar at once.

Real-world example

Amara writes a ticket-booking server for a fictional theatre, Lantern Hall. Two threads both read 'seats left = 1', both sell the seat, and two customers hold the same ticket — a race condition. She wraps the check-and-sell code in a mutex so only one thread at a time can run it. Later two threads each hold one lock and wait forever for the other's lock; she fixes this deadlock by always taking locks in the same order.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Starting a program makes the OS create a process with an ID, address space and a control block (PCB).
  2. On Unix, fork() copies the current process and exec() replaces the copy with a new program; Windows uses CreateProcess.
  3. Each process starts with one thread and may create more; threads share memory but have their own stack and registers.
  4. The scheduler moves threads between states — new, ready, running, waiting, terminated — with a context switch each time.
  5. Processes exchange data through IPC: pipes, sockets, shared memory, message queues or signals.
  6. Locks such as mutexes and semaphores protect shared data so threads do not corrupt it.

Who uses it

Back-end, systems and game developers, SREs debugging hung services, and anyone preparing for OS exam questions on deadlock.

Key takeaway

Memorise the four Coffman conditions for deadlock — mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait — and that breaking any one prevents deadlock.

Going deeper

  • A thread's private state is small — registers, program counter, a stack (8 MiB by default on many Linux systems) and thread-local storage — while code, heap, open files and the address space are shared.
  • Linux barely distinguishes processes from threads: both are tasks created by clone(), whose flags choose what is shared, such as the address space (CLONE_VM) or the open-file table (CLONE_FILES).
  • A finished child whose parent has not called wait() lingers as a zombie holding its PID; children whose parent dies are re-parented to init or a designated subreaper.
  • Switching between threads of one process is cheaper than switching processes, because the address space and its TLB entries stay valid; a process switch must change page tables.
  • Beyond mutexes and semaphores, condition variables let a thread sleep until another signals a state change, and read-write locks allow many readers or one writer at a time.
  • Languages add lightweight concurrency on top of OS threads: Go goroutines, Java virtual threads (final in Java 21) and async/await in Python, JavaScript and Rust multiplex many tasks onto few threads.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming threads run in the order you start them. The scheduler decides; without synchronisation any interleaving can happen, and bugs often appear only under load.
  • Reaching for kill -9 first. SIGKILL gives no chance to flush files or release locks; send SIGTERM, wait, and only then escalate.
  • Using sleep() calls or 'it worked in testing' as protection for shared data. Timing is not synchronisation; use a mutex, an atomic or a channel.

docs.title: Try it: List running processes, biggest memory users first, and count a process's threads
docs.text:
ps aux --sort=-%mem | head -n 6     # Linux: top 5 memory users
ps -o pid,nlwp,cmd -p $$            # threads (NLWP) of your shell
Get-Process | Sort-Object WS -Descending | Select-Object -First 5 Name, Id, Threads   # Windows

Opening two Notepad windows creates two separate processes with different process IDs (PIDs). ThreadPOSIX threads (pthreads); Windows threads · Concept · Current · Beginner The smallest unit the OS schedules on a CPU core; threads in one process share memory but each has its own stack. A game runs rendering, audio and physics on separate threads so the sound never stutters while graphics load. Process Control Block (PCB)Linux task_struct; Windows EPROCESS/ETHREAD · Concept · Current · Intermediate The kernel's record for each process: PID, state, saved registers, memory maps, open files and scheduling data. When a thread is paused, its registers are saved in the kernel's task record so it can resume exactly where it stopped. Process statesGeneral OS concept · Concept · Current · Beginner The life cycle of a process or thread: new, ready, running, waiting (blocked) and terminated. A program waiting for a keyboard press sits in the waiting state, using no CPU until the key arrives.
