docs.text: Name What it does Example Clock synchronisation (NTP and PTP)IETF RFC 5905 (NTPv4); IEEE 1588 (PTP) · Standard · Current · Intermediate Physical clocks drift; NTP keeps servers within milliseconds, while PTP with hardware support reaches sub-microsecond accuracy on local networks. Two servers whose clocks differ by 50 ms may log a reply as happening before the request that caused it. Lamport clockLeslie Lamport (1978) · Concept · Current · Intermediate A counter each process increments and attaches to its messages, giving events an order consistent with cause and effect. If event a causes event b then L(a) < L(b), although a smaller timestamp alone doesn't prove causation. Vector clockColin Fidge and Friedemann Mattern (1988) · Concept · Current · Advanced Each process keeps one counter per process, so the system can tell whether two events are causally ordered or concurrent. Amazon's Dynamo design used vector clocks to detect conflicting concurrent updates to the same shopping cart. Hybrid logical clocks and TrueTimeKulkarni et al. (HLC, 2014); Google Spanner TrueTime (2012) · Technology · Current · Advanced Combine physical time with logical counters, or with bounded clock uncertainty, to give timestamps meaningful across the globe. Spanner waits out TrueTime's uncertainty before committing so timestamps respect real-time order; CockroachDB uses hybrid logical clocks. ConsensusDistributed systems theory · Concept · Current · Beginner Getting a group of nodes to agree on one value, or one sequence of values, despite crashes and message delays. Three replicas of a lock service agree that client 42 holds the lock, even though one replica has just rebooted. FLP impossibilityFischer, Lynch and Paterson (1985) · Concept · Current · Advanced No deterministic algorithm can guarantee consensus in a fully asynchronous system if even one process may crash. Real systems sidestep FLP with timeouts and randomised elections, accepting that progress may pause during instability. PaxosLeslie Lamport ('The Part-Time Parliament', 1998) · Concept · Current · Advanced The classic consensus protocol: proposers and acceptors use majority quorums to choose values safely; famously hard to understand. Google's Chubby lock service and Spanner database both build on Paxos variants. RaftDiego Ongaro and John Ousterhout (2014) · Concept · Current · Intermediate A consensus algorithm designed to be understandable: leader election, log replication and safety, using terms and heartbeats. etcd, Consul, CockroachDB, TiKV and Kafka's KRaft mode all rely on Raft or close variants. Byzantine fault tolerance (PBFT)Lamport, Shostak and Pease (1982); Castro and Liskov (PBFT, 1999) · Concept · Current · Advanced Consensus that tolerates nodes lying or behaving maliciously; it needs 3f + 1 nodes to survive f faulty ones. Blockchains and some safety-critical control systems use BFT-style protocols because a faulty node might send conflicting messages. etcdCloud Native Computing Foundation (originally CoreOS) · Software · Current · Intermediate A distributed key-value store using Raft; it holds all the cluster state for Kubernetes. kubectl apply stores your Deployment in etcd via the API server; losing etcd's quorum freezes all cluster changes. Apache ZooKeeperApache Software Foundation (originally Yahoo!) · Software · Current · Intermediate A coordination service using the ZAB protocol for configuration, naming, locks and leader election. HBase and older Kafka versions relied on ZooKeeper; Kafka 4.0 (2025) dropped it in favour of built-in KRaft mode. Leader election and leasesDistributed systems design pattern · Concept · Current · Intermediate Choosing one node to coordinate, with a time-limited lease so a stale leader stops acting once its lease expires. A scheduler cluster grants a 10-second lease; if the leader cannot renew it, another node safely takes over. Failure detection (heartbeats)Distributed systems design pattern; phi accrual detector (Hayashibara et al., 2004) · Concept · Current · Intermediate Nodes send regular heartbeats; missing ones suggest failure, though a very slow node can't be told apart from a dead one for sure. Cassandra's phi accrual detector raises suspicion gradually as heartbeats arrive late, rather than using one fixed timeout. Two-phase commit (2PC)Distributed database protocol · Concept · Current · Intermediate A coordinator asks all participants to prepare a transaction, then tells them all to commit or all to abort. Moving money between two database shards uses 2PC so the debit and the credit both happen, or neither does.

docs.title: 6.12 Big Data & Distributed Compute Frameworks
docs.text:
Big-data frameworks let you process datasets far too large for one computer — terabytes or petabytes — by spreading the work across a cluster. They hide the messy parts, like splitting files, moving data between machines and recovering from crashes. You write fairly ordinary code (SQL, Python, Java or Scala), and the framework turns it into thousands of parallel tasks.

Word count, the MapReduce way. The shuffle is the only step that moves data between machines — and usually the most expensive one.

Think of it like…

It's like a national census: instead of one clerk counting every form, each town counts its own forms (map) and regional offices add up the totals (reduce).

Real-world example

GreenCart, a fictional grocery delivery company, keeps 40 TB of order history as Parquet files in cloud object storage. An analyst writes a 10-line PySpark job to find the top products in each city; Spark splits it into 3,000 tasks on 50 machines and finishes in 8 minutes. Meanwhile Kafka streams live orders into a Flink job that updates delivery-time estimates every few seconds, and the data-science team uses Ray to train 200 forecasting models in parallel.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Store data in a distributed file system or object store (HDFS or S3-compatible), often as columnar Parquet files.
  2. Write the job as transformations — map, filter, group-by, aggregate, join — or as SQL.
  3. The framework builds a plan (a graph of stages) and splits the data into partitions processed in parallel.
  4. Between stages, data is shuffled across the network when grouping or joining by key.
  5. Failed tasks are re-run automatically, and results are written back to storage or streamed onwards.

Who uses it

Data engineers, analytics engineers, data scientists and ML engineers at retailers, banks, telecoms, media and tech companies.

Key takeaway

Shuffles — moving data between machines to group by key — are usually the most expensive part of a job, so filter early and avoid unnecessary wide transformations.

Going deeper

  • Spark evaluates lazily: transformations such as filter and groupBy only build a plan (a DAG), and an action such as count or write triggers execution, split into stages at shuffle boundaries.
  • Spark's driver plans the job while executors run one task per data partition; partitions of roughly 100-200 MB keep tasks neither tiny nor memory-hungry.
  • Adaptive Query Execution, on by default since Spark 3.2, re-optimises at run time — merging small shuffle partitions, switching to broadcast joins and splitting skewed partitions.
  • Kafka topics are split into partitions, each an ordered, replicated log; consumers in a group divide the partitions and track offsets, so ordering is guaranteed only within a partition.
  • Flink achieves exactly-once state with asynchronous distributed snapshots inspired by the Chandy-Lamport algorithm, and handles late events using event-time watermarks.
  • Columnar formats pay off through column pruning, compression and predicate pushdown: Parquet stores min/max statistics per row group so whole chunks can be skipped.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Calling collect() or toPandas() on a huge DataFrame. It pulls everything onto the driver and crashes it; aggregate or sample first.
  • Writing millions of tiny files. They overload metadata and slow queries; compact output into files of a few hundred megabytes.
  • Ignoring data skew. One hot key can keep a single task running for hours; salt the key or let AQE split skewed partitions.

docs.title: Try it: MapReduce-style word count with a Python multiprocessing Pool
docs.text:
from multiprocessing import Pool
from collections import Counter

def count_words(line):                  # the 'map' step
    return Counter(line.lower().split())

if __name__ == "__main__":
    lines = ["the cat sat", "the dog sat", "a cat and a dog"] * 1000
    with Pool() as pool:                # one worker per CPU core by default
        partials = pool.map(count_words, lines, chunksize=100)
    total = sum(partials, Counter())    # the 'reduce' step
    print(total.most_common(3))

docs.title: 6.13 Distributed AI Training: Data, Tensor, Pipeline & Expert Parallelism
docs.text:
Training a large AI model needs far more computation and memory than one GPU has, so the work is spread across many GPUs — sometimes tens or hundreds of thousands. You can split the data (each GPU sees different examples), split the model (each GPU holds part of each layer, or some of the layers), or combine both. The GPUs constantly swap results using collective operations such as all-reduce.

What each kind of parallelism splits

Splits Communication Usual scope Data parallel Batches; full model per GPU All-reduce gradients each step Whole cluster ZeRO / FSDP Optimiser state, grads, weights All-gather + reduce-scatter Data-parallel group Tensor Each layer's matrices Collectives every layer Inside an NVLink domain Pipeline Groups of layers Activations between stages Across servers Context / sequence Tokens of long inputs Ring-passing key/value blocks Inside or across servers Expert (MoE) Experts of MoE layers All-to-all token routing Across servers

Bandwidth-hungry splits (tensor, expert) stay inside fast NVLink domains; data parallelism stretches across the whole cluster.

Think of it like…

Data parallelism is like several teachers each marking a different pile of the same exam and then agreeing on the marking scheme; model parallelism is like an assembly line where each worker builds one part of the car.

Real-world example

Mei's team at the fictional start-up Lumio trains a 70-billion-parameter language model. In BF16 the weights alone take 140 GB — more than one 80 GB GPU — and with Adam optimiser states training needs about 16 bytes per parameter, over 1.1 TB. They use 8-way tensor parallelism inside each NVLink-connected server, 4-way pipeline parallelism across servers and 32-way sharded data parallelism: 8 × 4 × 32 = 1,024 GPUs. Hourly checkpoints mean a single GPU failure costs at most an hour of work.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Data parallel: every GPU holds a model copy, processes a different mini-batch, and gradients are averaged with all-reduce.
  2. Sharded data parallel (ZeRO/FSDP): split optimiser states, gradients and weights across GPUs to save memory.
  3. Tensor parallel: split each layer's weight matrices across GPUs inside a fast NVLink domain.
  4. Pipeline parallel: put groups of layers on different GPUs and stream micro-batches through them.
  5. Sequence/context and expert parallel: split very long inputs or mixture-of-experts layers across GPUs.
  6. Checkpoint regularly and restart automatically when hardware fails.

Who uses it

ML engineers, AI infrastructure engineers and research engineers at AI labs, cloud providers and companies training or fine-tuning large models.

Key takeaway

Rule of thumb: mixed-precision training with the Adam optimiser needs about 16 bytes per parameter before activations — which is why big models must be sharded.

Going deeper

  • Memory per parameter with mixed-precision Adam: 2 bytes of BF16 weights, 2 of gradients and 12 of FP32 master weights plus two Adam moments — 16 bytes before any activations.
  • ZeRO stage 1 shards optimiser states, stage 2 also gradients and stage 3 also parameters; PyTorch FSDP implements the stage-3 idea, gathering each layer's weights just in time.
  • Pipeline bubbles waste time while stages fill and drain: with p stages and m micro-batches a GPipe-style schedule idles about (p − 1)/(m + p − 1) of the time, so more micro-batches help.
  • Ring all-reduce is a reduce-scatter followed by an all-gather; each GPU sends about 2(N − 1)/N times the gradient size, so bandwidth cost stays nearly flat as GPUs are added.
  • Gradient accumulation sums gradients over several micro-batches before one optimiser step, reaching a large effective batch size without extra GPU memory.
  • Failures are routine at scale: Meta reported 419 unexpected interruptions in a 54-day period of Llama 3 405B pre-training on 16,384 GPUs, so fast checkpoint-restart is essential.
  • Collectives run through NCCL (NVIDIA) or RCCL (AMD), which pick ring or tree algorithms over NVLink, InfiniBand or RoCE; setting NCCL_DEBUG=INFO reveals their choices.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Raising the global batch size with GPU count without retuning learning rate and warm-up. Training can diverge or generalise worse.
  • Stretching tensor parallelism across servers. It communicates every layer and needs NVLink-class bandwidth, so keep it inside one node or rack domain.
  • Checkpointing too rarely to save time. One failure then wastes hours of thousands of GPUs; use asynchronous, sharded checkpoints.

docs.title: Try it: An all-reduce with PyTorch on your own CPU (no GPU needed)
docs.text:
# ddp_demo.py   run with:  torchrun --nproc_per_node=2 ddp_demo.py
import torch, torch.distributed as dist
dist.init_process_group("gloo")             # use "nccl" on NVIDIA GPUs
rank = dist.get_rank()
t = torch.tensor([float(rank + 1)])
dist.all_reduce(t, op=dist.ReduceOp.SUM)    # every rank ends with 1 + 2 = 3
print(f"rank {rank}: all-reduced value = {t.item()}")
dist.destroy_process_group()

Megatron-LM and Megatron CoreNVIDIA (open source) · Framework · Current · Advanced A library and reference code for training large transformers with tensor, pipeline, sequence, context and expert parallelism. Researchers combine Megatron Core's parallelism options to train models with hundreds of billions of parameters on thousands of GPUs. DeepSpeedMicrosoft; LF AI & Data Foundation project since 2025 · Framework · Current · Intermediate A training and inference optimisation library offering ZeRO, offloading to CPU or NVMe, and pipeline parallelism. A university lab fine-tunes a 13-billion-parameter model on four GPUs using ZeRO-3 with optimiser states offloaded to CPU memory. Distributed checkpointingPyTorch Distributed Checkpoint and similar tools · Technology · Current · Advanced Saving model and optimiser state regularly, sharded across GPUs, so training can resume after a failure. Each of 1,024 GPUs writes its own shard in parallel, and the checkpoint can later be reloaded onto a different GPU count. AI supercluster (AI factory)Built by AI labs and cloud providers · System · Current · Intermediate Data-centre-scale clusters of 100,000 or more accelerators, linked by NVLink domains and scale-out networks, for training frontier models. xAI's Colossus in Memphis began in 2024 with about 100,000 NVIDIA H100 GPUs and has since expanded far beyond that. 3D parallelism (combining DP, TP and PP)Megatron-LM, DeepSpeed and similar frameworks · Concept · Current · Advanced Layering tensor parallelism inside a server, pipeline parallelism across servers and data parallelism across replicas, so total GPUs = TP × PP × DP. Lumio's 1,024 GPUs are 8-way tensor × 4-way pipeline × 32-way data parallel; adding context or expert parallelism makes it 4D or 5D. Activation checkpointingPyTorch torch.utils.checkpoint; Megatron-LM; DeepSpeed · Technology · Current · Intermediate Keeping only some layer outputs in the forward pass and recomputing the rest during backward, trading roughly a third more compute for far less memory. Enabling activation checkpointing lets a team double its sequence length on the same 80 GB GPUs, at the cost of slower steps. Model FLOPs Utilisation (MFU)Defined in Google's PaLM paper (2022) · Metric · Current · Intermediate Useful model maths achieved per second as a share of the GPUs' peak FLOPS; roughly 30-50% is common for large dense-model training. A run reaching 400 TFLOP/s per GPU on hardware with a 1,000 TFLOP/s dense BF16 peak has 40% MFU.

docs.title: 6.14 Reliability at Scale: RAS, ECC, Silent Data Corruption and Failures
docs.text:
Hardware fails: memory bits flip, cores occasionally miscalculate, GPUs crash and links drop. In one laptop this is rare, but in a cluster of 100,000 GPUs something breaks every few hours. RAS — reliability, availability and serviceability — is the set of hardware and software features that detect, correct, contain and report these faults so systems keep running and data stays correct.

Downtime allowed per year. Each extra nine cuts allowed downtime tenfold — and usually needs much more redundancy.

Think of it like…

A large cluster is like an airline fleet: with thousands of aircraft, some part is always failing somewhere, so you plan for inspections, spares, redundancy and fast repairs instead of hoping nothing breaks.

Real-world example

Orbital AI, a fictional lab, trains a model on 16,000 GPUs for two months. It expects frequent interruptions, so it saves checkpoints every 30 minutes, runs health checks between jobs and keeps spare nodes ready. One week the training loss spikes; tests trace it to one GPU silently producing wrong results with no error logged. The node is drained, the job restarts from the last good checkpoint on a spare, and the faulty GPU goes back to the vendor.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Prevent: design margins, ECC on memories and caches, CRCs and retries on links, and burn-in screening of new hardware.
  2. Detect and correct: ECC fixes single-bit memory errors automatically, and background scrubbing finds latent errors before they combine.
  3. Contain and report: uncorrectable errors raise machine-check exceptions; the OS kills the affected process or retires the bad memory page and logs the event.
  4. Recover: redundancy (RAID, replicas, spare nodes) and checkpoint/restart let work continue after a failure.
  5. Service: telemetry and health checks flag failing parts so technicians replace them, ideally hot-swapping without downtime.

Who uses it

Site reliability engineers, HPC and ML infrastructure engineers, data-centre technicians, server and chip RAS architects, and anyone running large fleets of machines rely on RAS.

Key takeaway

Know the nines: 99.9% availability allows about 8.8 hours of downtime a year, 99.99% about 53 minutes and 99.999% about 5 minutes.

Going deeper

  • SECDED ECC adds 8 check bits to every 64 data bits to correct any single-bit error and detect double-bit errors; server Chipkill or SDDC schemes spread codes across chips so even a whole failed DRAM device is tolerated.
  • DDR5's on-die ECC only repairs errors inside each DRAM chip and reports nothing to the system, so servers still need ECC RDIMMs with extra chips for end-to-end protection.
  • Machine Check Architecture on x86, and the Arm RAS extension, record hardware errors in bank registers; Linux reports them through EDAC and rasdaemon, and Windows through WHEA events.
  • Silent data corruption — wrong results with no error raised — was traced by Google ('Cores that don't count', 2021) and Meta to a few defective CPU cores per several thousand servers, so fleets now run periodic known-answer tests.
  • Meta reported 419 unexpected interruptions in 54 days while training Llama 3 405B on 16,384 H100 GPUs — roughly one every three hours — with GPU and HBM memory faults the largest causes.
  • Memory self-repair features such as post-package repair (PPR) and page offlining remap or stop using failing DRAM rows before they cause crashes; NVIDIA data-centre GPUs similarly remap failing HBM rows.
  • End-to-end checksums in file systems such as ZFS and in storage protocols (T10 Protection Information) catch corruption anywhere between application and disk, which RAID parity alone cannot detect.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming DDR5 on-die ECC equals ECC memory: it is internal to each chip; only ECC modules with extra chips protect the full data path.
  • Ignoring corrected-error counts: a rising count on one DIMM or GPU often predicts an uncorrectable failure, so replace the part proactively.
  • Believing hardware is either working or broken: silent data corruption produces plausible wrong answers, so validate results and screen hardware regularly.
  • Checkpointing too rarely or too often: rare checkpoints lose hours of work per failure, while very frequent ones waste time writing state.

docs.title: Try it: Check memory error counters and hardware error logs (Linux)
docs.text:
ras-mc-ctl --summary            # corrected/uncorrected memory errors (rasdaemon package)
journalctl -k | grep -i -E 'mce|machine check|edac|AER'
nvidia-smi -q -d ECC            # GPU ECC counters, on NVIDIA GPUs
# Windows: Event Viewer > System, source 'WHEA-Logger'

docs.title: Key chips, architectures, standards, tools & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example RAS (reliability, availability, serviceability)Industry term, originally from IBM mainframes · Concept · Current · Intermediate Hardware and software features that keep systems running correctly: avoiding faults, tolerating them, and making repairs quick. Server CPUs advertise RAS features such as memory mirroring, error containment and hot-plug that desktop chips lack. MTBF, MTTR and availabilityReliability engineering · Metric · Current · Beginner Mean time between failures, mean time to repair, and availability = MTBF ÷ (MTBF + MTTR), often quoted in 'nines'. A switch with a 50,000-hour MTBF and 4-hour repair time is about 99.99% available. Soft errors (cosmic rays and alpha particles)Semiconductor physics · Concept · Current · Intermediate Temporary bit flips caused by particle strikes rather than permanent damage; more frequent at high altitude and in dense memory. Supercomputers at high-altitude sites see more memory bit flips than identical machines at sea level. SECDED ECC (Hamming code)Richard Hamming (1950); JEDEC ECC modules · Concept · Current · Intermediate An error-correcting code whose extra check bits correct any single-bit error and detect any double-bit error in a word. A DDR4 ECC module stores 72 bits for every 64 data bits; the extra 8 bits let the controller fix a flipped bit. Chipkill and SDDCIBM (Chipkill); Intel SDDC; AMD · Technology · Current · Advanced Advanced ECC spreading each word across many DRAM chips, so even a completely failed chip is corrected without data loss. When one DRAM chip on a server module dies, Chipkill keeps the machine running until a technician swaps the module. Memory scrubbing (patrol scrub)Server memory controllers · Technology · Current · Intermediate The memory controller reads and corrects all memory in the background, fixing single errors before a second one accumulates. Patrol scrub walks a 1 TB server's memory about once a day, quietly correcting stray bit flips. Machine Check Architecture (MCA) and MCEsIntel and AMD (x86); Arm RAS extension · Architecture · Current · Advanced A CPU mechanism that logs hardware errors in bank registers and raises machine-check exceptions for uncorrectable ones. The kernel message 'Machine check events logged' leads an administrator to a failing memory module. Silent data corruption (SDC)Fleet studies by Google, Meta and others (2021 onwards) · Concept · Current · Advanced Hardware producing wrong results without any error signal, often from a marginal or defective CPU core or GPU. A defective core occasionally miscalculates during decompression, so a database returns wrong values without crashing. Fleet hardware screeningHyperscaler practice; vendor tools such as NVIDIA DCGM diagnostics · Concept · Current · Advanced Running known-answer stress tests on production servers at intervals to catch defective cores, GPUs or memory before they corrupt data. Nodes run a short GPU diagnostic between jobs, and any mismatch removes the node from the scheduler. Page retirement and post-package repair (PPR)Operating-system kernels; JEDEC DDR4/DDR5 PPR · Technology · Current · Advanced Stopping use of memory pages with repeated errors, or permanently remapping a failing DRAM row to a spare row. After repeated errors, an NVIDIA data-centre GPU schedules a row remap in its HBM that takes effect at the next reset. PCIe AER and link errorsPCI-SIG Advanced Error Reporting · Standard · Current · Advanced Reporting of correctable and uncorrectable PCIe errors, such as corrupted packets or link retraining, so the OS can log or recover. dmesg shows repeated 'PCIe Bus Error: severity=Corrected' for a GPU, hinting at a loose riser or failing retimer. Lockstep and redundant executionSafety processors (e.g. Arm Cortex-R) and automotive microcontrollers · Technology · Current · Advanced Running the same instructions on two cores at once and comparing results every cycle to catch errors instantly. A car's braking controller uses a dual-core lockstep chip, so a miscalculation is detected and the system enters a safe state. Checkpoint/restartHPC and AI training practice · Concept · Current · Intermediate Saving a job's state regularly so that after a failure it resumes from the last checkpoint rather than from the beginning. A 30-day simulation checkpoints every two hours, so a node crash costs at most two hours of compute. GPU error reporting (XID errors, ECC counters)NVIDIA (XID, DCGM); AMD (amd-smi) · Tool · Current · Advanced Error codes and counters GPUs log for faults such as memory errors, hangs or dropping off the bus, used to triage failures. An XID 79 error, 'GPU has fallen off the bus', tells an admin to check power, PCIe seating or the GPU itself. rasdaemon, EDAC and WHEALinux kernel EDAC; rasdaemon project; Microsoft WHEA · Tool · Current · Intermediate Frameworks and tools that collect hardware error reports: EDAC and rasdaemon on Linux, Windows Hardware Error Architecture on Windows. 'ras-mc-ctl --summary' shows 300 corrected errors on one DIMM slot, so a technician schedules a replacement. End-to-end data integrity (checksums, T10 PI)ZFS and Btrfs; INCITS T10 Protection Information · Technology · Current · Advanced Checksums or protection tags carried with data from application to disk and back, catching corruption anywhere along the path. A ZFS scrub finds a block whose checksum fails, repairs it from the mirror copy and flags the faulty disk.

docs.title: 6.15 Scientific Workloads & Getting Started in HPC
docs.text:
Supercomputers exist to answer questions that experiments alone can't: tomorrow's weather, how air flows over a wing, how a drug molecule binds to a protein, or how a patient's genome differs from a reference. Most of this work runs on well-known open-source codes. You can learn to use them — and HPC in general — through free lessons, student competitions and practice clusters.

The simulation science loop. Each turn of the loop refines the model; supercomputers make each turn fast enough to matter.

Think of it like…

A simulation is a virtual laboratory: instead of building 50 prototype helmets for a wind tunnel, engineers test 50 digital helmets overnight.

Real-world example

Zara, a chemistry undergraduate, joins her university's team for a student cluster competition. Over three months she learns Linux, Slurm and Spack, builds GROMACS with GPU support, and tunes a protein simulation until it runs three times faster than her first attempt. At the competition her team also runs an unfamiliar CFD code under a strict power limit. That experience lands her an internship as a junior HPC support engineer.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Model the physical system as equations (fluid flow, Newton's laws for atoms, atmospheric physics).
  2. Discretise space and time into a mesh, grid or set of particles.
  3. Decompose the domain across MPI ranks and GPUs, exchanging boundary 'halo' data every time step.
  4. Run with regular checkpoints, then post-process the output with visualisation tools such as ParaView.
  5. Validate against experiments or observations, refine the model and repeat.

Who uses it

Meteorologists, aerospace and automotive engineers, computational chemists, bioinformaticians, and the HPC engineers and research software engineers who support them.

Key takeaway

For HPC interviews, be able to explain domain decomposition with halo exchange, write a Slurm script from memory, and describe how you built software with Spack or modules.

Going deeper

  • Explicit time-stepping codes obey the CFL condition: the time step must be small enough that information crosses no more than about one cell per step, so finer grids also need smaller steps.
  • Doubling a 3D grid's resolution multiplies the cells by 8 and, through the CFL limit, the time steps by about 2 — roughly 16 times the work, which is why resolution upgrades need bigger machines.
  • Molecular-dynamics speed is quoted as nanoseconds of simulated time per day (ns/day); small proteins on one modern GPU in GROMACS commonly reach hundreds of ns/day.
  • Reproducibility matters: record code version, compiler, MPI library, inputs and random seeds, and use workflow managers such as Nextflow or Snakemake to rerun pipelines exactly.
  • Job titles to search for: HPC systems engineer, research computing facilitator, HPC application or performance engineer, computational scientist, research software engineer and AI infrastructure engineer.
  • Free ways in: HPC Carpentry lessons, training from national centres such as NERSC or EuroHPC, US ACCESS allocations for students, and the Student Cluster Competitions at SC and ISC.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Trusting results because the code ran without errors. Validate with known test cases, convergence studies and experimental data.
  • Writing every time step at full resolution. Output can fill quotas and slow the shared file system; save selectively and compress.
  • Learning only graphical tools. HPC work needs the Linux shell, Git, a job scheduler and scripting, so practise them early.

docs.title: Try it: Domain decomposition: each MPI rank's share of a 3D grid and its halo overhead
docs.text:
nx = ny = nz = 2048          # global grid points per side
px, py, pz = 8, 8, 8         # 512 MPI ranks arranged as 8 x 8 x 8
lx, ly, lz = nx // px, ny // py, nz // pz
cells = lx * ly * lz
halo = 2 * (lx*ly + ly*lz + lx*lz)   # one layer of ghost cells on each face
print(f"local block {lx}x{ly}x{lz} = {cells:,} cells")
print(f"halo cells {halo:,} = {halo/cells:.1%} of the block")

docs.title: Chapter 8: Performance, Tools, Careers & Learning
docs.text: Knowing how computers work becomes truly useful when you can measure them, make them faster and turn that skill into a career. This chapter covers fair benchmarking, the main benchmark suites, profiling tools and analysis methods, optimisation, power and cooling, and how to choose a PC or server. It finishes with careers, certifications, books, hands-on projects and model interview answers to take you from student to job-ready.

docs.title: 8.1 Benchmarking Basics & Pitfalls
docs.text:
A benchmark is a repeatable test that measures how fast a computer or program does a fixed job, so you can compare machines or check whether a change helped. Good benchmarking is surprisingly hard: results wobble from run to run, and a test that does not resemble your real work can point you in the wrong direction. The golden rule is to measure carefully, several times, under controlled conditions.

The benchmarking loop. Every code or configuration change sends you round the loop again.

Think of it like…

Benchmarking is like timing runners: you need the same track, the same distance, a proper warm-up and several heats before you can say who is really faster.

Real-world example

Leon, an intern at a fictional video start-up called Clipwise, ran a compression test once on two laptops and declared laptop A 30% faster. His mentor made him repeat it ten times after a warm-up run, with both laptops plugged in and cooled. The median times were 41.2 s and 39.8 s, a gap of only about 3.5%, smaller than the run-to-run spread of 2-4%. The first result had been caused by laptop B indexing files in the background.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Define the question and pick a workload that resembles real use.
  2. Fix the conditions: same software versions, power plan, temperature and background load.
  3. Do warm-up runs, then repeat the measurement many times and record every result.
  4. Report the median (or mean) with the spread, such as standard deviation or min-max.
  5. Compare with ratios and summarise several tests with a geometric mean, never a single cherry-picked number.

Who uses it

Hardware reviewers, performance engineers, HPC and cloud teams, and anyone deciding which machine or setting is genuinely faster.

Key takeaway

In interviews, mention warm-up, repetition, variance and representative workloads; it shows you know that one run proves nothing.

Going deeper

  • Common noise sources: turbo and thermal state, background services, CPU frequency governors, memory-layout changes from ASLR, interrupts and busy SMT siblings. Experts pin threads, fix clock speeds and isolate cores for stable results.
  • Report distributions, not single numbers: median and interquartile range resist outliers, and latency results should show p50, p95, p99 and maximum, ideally as a histogram or CDF plot.
  • Optimising compilers can delete work whose result is never used or hoist it out of loops; harnesses provide helpers such as DoNotOptimize (Google Benchmark) and Blackhole (JMH) to prevent this.
  • Summarise ratios with the geometric mean, as SPEC does; an arithmetic mean of ratios gives different answers depending on which machine you choose as the baseline.
  • For load tests, constant-arrival-rate tools such as wrk2 and k6 avoid coordinated omission, whereas closed-loop tools that wait for each reply under-report latency during overload.
  • Continuous benchmarking in CI catches regressions early, but needs dedicated quiet machines — shared cloud CI runners are too noisy for small differences.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Running a test once and trusting it — repeat it and report the spread.
  • Benchmarking debug builds or with a profiler attached — measure optimised release builds under normal conditions.
  • Comparing a laptop on battery with one on mains power, or hot with cold — fix and record power and thermal state.
  • Averaging speed-up ratios arithmetically — use the geometric mean instead.

docs.title: Try it: Time a function properly in Python with repeats and report median and spread
docs.text:
import timeit, statistics
t = timeit.repeat('sum(range(1_000_000))', repeat=10, number=5)
print(f'median {statistics.median(t):.4f}s  stdev {statistics.stdev(t):.4f}s  min {min(t):.4f}s')

docs.title: Key chips, architectures, standards, tools & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example BenchmarkGeneral performance engineering · Concept · Current · Beginner A standard, repeatable workload run to measure and compare the performance of hardware, software or configurations. Running the same video export on three laptops and comparing the times is a simple benchmark. Microbenchmark vs macrobenchmarkGeneral performance engineering · Concept · Current · Intermediate A microbenchmark times one tiny operation; a macrobenchmark times a whole realistic application or workload. Timing one hash function is a microbenchmark; timing a full web request through the app stack is a macrobenchmark. Warm-up runGeneral performance engineering · Concept · Current · Beginner Discarded first runs that let caches fill, JIT compilers optimise and CPU clocks settle before real timing starts. A Java service is run for 60 seconds before measuring, so the JIT has compiled hot methods. Run-to-run varianceStatistics · Metric · Current · Beginner The natural spread of results between identical runs, caused by background tasks, temperature, turbo behaviour and memory layout. Ten runs of a render range from 52 to 55 seconds; any claimed gain under about 3 seconds is noise. Median and percentilesStatistics · Metric · Current · Intermediate The median is the middle result; percentiles like p99 show the worst typical cases, which matter for latency. An API averages 20 ms, but its p99 is 400 ms, so one request in a hundred feels slow. Geometric meanStatistics; used by SPEC · Metric · Current · Intermediate The nth root of the product of n ratios; the fair way to combine speed-up ratios from several tests. Speed-ups of 2x and 0.5x give a geometric mean of 1.0x, correctly showing no overall gain. Representative workloadGeneral performance engineering · Concept · Current · Beginner A test that uses data sizes, access patterns and operations similar to the real job you care about. A database team benchmarks with a copy of last month's real query log instead of a toy table. Confidence intervals and significanceStatistics · Metric · Current · Intermediate A range likely to contain the true result; if two configurations' intervals overlap heavily, the apparent difference may just be noise. Build A takes 41.2 ± 0.9 s and build B 40.8 ± 1.1 s at 95% confidence — there is no real winner. Throughput vs latencyGeneral performance engineering · Concept · Current · Beginner Report both: throughput (operations per second at full load) and latency at a stated load, because one number hides the trade-off. Batching AI requests raises tokens per second but makes each user wait slightly longer for the first word. Thermal and power state controlGeneral performance engineering · Concept · Current · Intermediate Laptop power plans, turbo boost and heat change clock speeds, so they must be fixed and recorded during tests. A laptop scores 15% lower on battery than on mains power, so reviewers test both and label them. BenchmarketingIndustry slang · Concept · Current · Beginner Vendor charts that pick flattering tests, settings or scales so a product looks better than real-world use would show. A slide shows a bar chart starting at 90 instead of 0, making a 4% lead look like double. Coordinated omissionTerm popularised by Gil Tene · Concept · Current · Advanced A load-testing mistake where slow responses delay new requests, so the tool silently under-reports bad latency. A tester switches to a constant-rate load generator and finds p99 latency is ten times worse than first reported. Reproducibility recordGeneral performance engineering · Concept · Current · Intermediate Writing down hardware, firmware, OS, compiler, flags, settings and raw results so anyone can repeat the test. Each result in a team spreadsheet lists BIOS version, kernel, gcc flags and the ten raw timings. hyperfine and benchmark harnesseshyperfine (David Peter); Google Benchmark; JMH (OpenJDK); Criterion.rs; pytest-benchmark · Tool · Current · Intermediate Tools that handle warm-up, repetition and statistics for you, from whole commands (hyperfine) to single functions in C++, Java, Rust or Python. 'hyperfine --warmup 3 ./old ./new' reports each command's mean and spread, and how many times faster the new build is.

docs.title: 8.2 Benchmark Suites You Will Meet
docs.text:
Instead of inventing your own tests, you can use well-known benchmark suites that everyone recognises, so results can be compared across the world. Some target desktop users (Geekbench, Cinebench, 3DMark), some target servers and supercomputers (SPEC, HPL, STREAM) and some target AI systems (MLPerf). Each one measures something specific, so you must know what a score really means before trusting it.

Which suite answers which question? Pick the suite that matches the question, then confirm with your own workload.

Think of it like…

Benchmark suites are like standardised school exams: everyone sits the same paper, so marks can be compared, but a maths exam says nothing about how well you sing.

Real-world example

Aisha is choosing between two cloud server types for a fictional engineering firm, Ridgeway Analytics. She checks published SPEC CPU rate results for raw compute, runs STREAM to compare memory bandwidth, and uses fio to test the attached storage. One server wins SPEC by 12% but loses STREAM by 25%; because Ridgeway's simulations are memory-bound, she picks the second server.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Decide what you care about: single-thread speed, multi-core throughput, graphics, memory, storage or AI.
  2. Pick the suite designed for that question and use its official rules and settings.
  3. Run it several times on an otherwise idle, well-cooled machine.
  4. Compare only scores from the same suite version, because new versions reset the scale.
  5. Cross-check with a test of your own real workload before spending money.

Who uses it

Reviewers, system buyers, cloud and HPC architects, chip vendors' marketing and engineering teams, and students comparing laptops.

Key takeaway

Never compare scores across versions: Geekbench 6 vs 7 or Cinebench 2024 vs 2026 numbers are on different scales.

Going deeper

  • SPEC CPU 2017 contains 43 benchmarks in four suites — SPECspeed and SPECrate, each integer and floating point. 'Base' results require consistent compiler flags; 'peak' allows per-benchmark tuning.
  • SPEC scores are ratios against a fixed reference machine, combined with a geometric mean; published results must follow the run rules and are reviewed before appearing on spec.org.
  • MLPerf Inference defines scenarios — SingleStream, MultiStream, Server (latency-bounded queries) and Offline (batch throughput) — and 'closed' (same model and accuracy) versus 'open' divisions.
  • STREAM's arrays must be much larger than all caches combined (the documented rule of thumb is at least four times), otherwise you measure cache rather than DRAM bandwidth; Triad is the figure usually quoted.
  • fio essentials: direct=1 bypasses the page cache, iodepth sets queue depth, and SSDs should be preconditioned before testing random 4 KiB and sequential large-block patterns separately.
  • Consumer suites use short runs that can miss throttling; Cinebench's 10-minute mode or looped 3DMark stress tests reveal sustained behaviour and cooling quality.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Comparing scores across versions or settings — Geekbench 6 vs 7, SPEC base vs peak and Cinebench 2024 vs 2026 are different scales.
  • Treating one suite as 'overall speed' — each measures one type of workload.
  • Trusting vendor-run results without reading the configuration — compiler flags, memory and power settings can swing scores widely.

docs.title: Try it: Run quick, harmless CPU and storage benchmarks on Linux
docs.text:
sudo apt install sysbench fio
sysbench cpu --threads=4 run

docs.title: 8.3 Profiling & Monitoring Tools
docs.text:
A profiler shows where a program spends its time, so you can fix the slow part instead of guessing. Monitoring tools show what the whole machine is doing right now: how busy the CPU, memory, disks, network and GPU are. Together they turn 'it feels slow' into a clear picture of the real bottleneck.

Where each tool looks. Start at the top with a broad view, then drill down only as far as needed.

Think of it like…

A profiler is like a fitness tracker for code that shows which exercise tires you most, while monitoring tools are the dashboard gauges of a car.

Real-world example

Tomás, a back-end developer at a fictional ticket site called Gatehouse, saw checkout requests take 900 ms. htop showed one CPU core pinned at 100%, so he ran 'perf record' and drew a flame graph. 70% of the time was spent re-parsing a config file on every request. Caching it once cut checkout time to 120 ms.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Start broad with a monitor (htop, Task Manager, nvidia-smi) to see which resource is busy.
  2. Use a sampling profiler (perf, VTune, uProf, Instruments) to find the hottest functions.
  3. Visualise the call stacks, for example as a flame graph, to see which path is expensive.
  4. Drill into hardware counters or a GPU profiler (Nsight Systems, then Nsight Compute) if the hot spot is still unclear.
  5. Fix one thing, then measure again with the same tools to confirm the gain.

Who uses it

Software, performance, SRE, HPC, game and GPU engineers, plus sysadmins who must explain why a server is slow.

Key takeaway

Learn 'perf stat', 'perf record' and 'perf report' plus flame graphs; they appear in almost every Linux performance interview.

Going deeper

  • Sampling profilers such as perf interrupt the program (for example 99 times per second per CPU) and record stacks with low overhead; instrumenting tools like gprof and Callgrind count every call but can slow programs dozens of times.
  • Useful stacks need symbols and frame pointers: build with -g and -fno-omit-frame-pointer, or use DWARF or LBR unwinding. Fedora and Ubuntu 24.04 re-enabled frame pointers by default to make profiling easier.
  • Hardware performance counters (cycles, instructions, cache and branch misses) come from the CPU's PMU; 'perf stat' reads them cheaply, and multiplexes when you request more events than there are counters.
  • CPU profilers cannot see time spent waiting on locks, disk or network; off-CPU tools such as BCC's offcputime or wall-clock profilers reveal it.
  • nvidia-smi 'utilisation' only means a kernel was running, not that the GPU's SMs were busy; DCGM and Nsight metrics such as SM occupancy and memory throughput show real efficiency.
  • Modern observability combines metrics (Prometheus), logs, traces and profiles; OpenTelemetry, a CNCF project, standardises how traces, metrics and logs are collected.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Profiling a debug build — optimisation changes hot spots; profile release builds compiled with symbols.
  • Reading 100% GPU utilisation as 'fully efficient' — it only means some kernel was running.
  • Profiling too short a run or an unrealistic input — collect enough samples on a representative workload.

docs.title: 8.4 Performance Analysis Methods
docs.text:
Performance analysis methods are step-by-step ways of thinking that stop you from wasting time on random fixes. They help you answer two questions: which resource is the bottleneck, and how much faster could things get if you fixed it. The first rule of all of them is simple: measure first, then optimise.

A methodical performance investigation. Change one thing at a time and always re-measure against the baseline.

Think of it like…

It is like a doctor's examination: check vital signs in a fixed order before deciding on treatment, rather than guessing from one symptom.

Real-world example

Mei, an HPC engineer at the fictional Northvale Weather Centre, was asked to speed up a forecast model. Applying the USE method, she found memory bandwidth near saturation while CPU cores sat 40% stalled. A roofline plot confirmed the main kernel's arithmetic intensity was only 0.3 FLOP per byte, so faster cores would not help. Restructuring loops to reuse cached data raised intensity and cut run time by 35%.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Measure first: profile to find the hot spot that dominates run time.
  2. Check each resource for utilisation, saturation and errors (the USE method).
  3. Use Amdahl's law to estimate the best possible gain before investing effort.
  4. Place the hot kernel on a roofline chart to see if it is compute-bound or memory-bound.
  5. For CPU code, use top-down analysis to see whether the front end, back end or bad speculation is to blame.

Who uses it

Performance engineers, HPC specialists, SREs, compiler and CPU architects, and any developer handed a 'make it faster' ticket.

Key takeaway

Learn the USE checklist and the queueing knee: a resource at 90% utilisation already makes requests wait about ten times their service time, which is why healthy systems keep headroom.

Going deeper

  • Gregg's 'Linux performance analysis in 60 seconds' uses commands such as uptime, dmesg, vmstat 1, mpstat -P ALL 1, pidstat 1, iostat -xz 1, free -m, sar -n DEV 1 and top for a fast first USE pass.
  • Top-down level 1 splits pipeline slots into Retiring, Bad Speculation, Front-End Bound and Back-End Bound, with Back-End split into Memory-Bound and Core-Bound; 'perf stat --topdown' and VTune report it.
  • Little's law (L = λW) holds for any stable system and drives capacity planning: 10,000 requests per second at 50 ms each means about 500 requests in flight at once.
  • Characterise the workload first — who causes the load, which operations, what sizes and mix; many 'performance bugs' turn out to be unexpected load such as a bot or a retry storm.
  • Tail at scale (Dean and Barroso, 2013): if a request fans out to 100 servers that are each slow 1% of the time, about 63% of requests hit at least one slow server.
  • Amdahl's and Gustafson's laws, covered in earlier chapters, set the ceiling for any fix: estimate the possible gain before investing days of effort.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Optimising without a target — define the metric and what 'good enough' means first.
  • Watching only averages — tail latency and saturation hide behind a healthy mean.
  • Changing several things at once — you cannot tell which change helped or hurt.
  • Assuming high CPU means the CPU is the problem — spinning locks and memory stalls also look like busy CPU.

docs.title: Try it: The queueing knee and a roofline check in Python
docs.text:
S = 0.010                       # service time: 10 ms
for U in (0.5, 0.8, 0.9, 0.95):  # utilisation
    print(f'{U:.0%} busy -> response ~ {S/(1-U)*1000:.0f} ms')

peak_gflops, bw_gbs, ai = 2000, 200, 0.5   # ai = FLOP per byte
print('Roofline limit:', min(peak_gflops, bw_gbs*ai), 'GFLOP/s')

docs.title: 8.5 Optimisation Basics
docs.text:
Optimisation means making a program use less time, memory or energy while giving the same answers. The biggest wins usually come from a better algorithm, then from arranging data so the CPU's caches and vector units are used well, and only then from compiler flags, parallel threads or a GPU. Always keep a correct, measured baseline so you know each change really helped.

Kofi's collision checker, step by step. The algorithm change alone gave a 35× win — bigger than all later steps combined.

Think of it like…

Optimising is like planning a supermarket trip: choosing the right shop (algorithm) matters most, then a sensible route down the aisles (memory layout), and only then walking faster (compiler tricks).

Real-world example

Kofi, a student at a fictional robotics club, had a collision checker that compared all 20,000 objects with each other: 200 million pairs, taking 14 s. Switching to a spatial grid cut checks to about 300,000 and time to 0.4 s. Storing positions as separate x, y and z arrays (SoA) and compiling with -O3 -march=native let the compiler vectorise the loop, dropping time to 0.15 s. Adding OpenMP across 8 cores brought it to 0.03 s.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Measure a correct baseline and find the hot spot.
  2. Improve the algorithm and data structures first (lower big-O complexity).
  3. Make memory access cache-friendly: contiguous arrays, sequential access, tiling, SoA layout.
  4. Let the compiler help: -O2/-O3, -march=native, then PGO and LTO, and check its vectorisation report.
  5. Parallelise with threads or OpenMP, avoiding false sharing, and offload suitable work to a GPU.
  6. Re-measure after every change and keep tests to prove results are still correct.

Who uses it

Software, game, HPC, embedded, quant-finance and ML engineers, and compiler developers.

Key takeaway

Say 'algorithm first, then memory, then parallelism' in interviews, and quote Knuth: premature optimisation wastes effort when you have not measured.

Going deeper

  • Typical order of wins: algorithms and data structures (often 10-1000×), memory layout and locality (2-10×), vectorisation (up to the SIMD width, e.g. 8 floats with AVX2) and threads (up to the core count).
  • -O2 is the usual release default; -O3 adds more aggressive inlining and vectorisation. -march=native, or a level such as x86-64-v3, enables AVX2 — ship builds targeting the oldest CPUs you support.
  • PGO plus LTO commonly gives several to around 15 per cent on large, branchy programs such as browsers, compilers and databases; post-link optimisers like LLVM BOLT can add more by reordering hot code.
  • Swapping the default malloc for jemalloc or mimalloc can speed up allocation-heavy multithreaded servers and reduce memory fragmentation.
  • Data-oriented design, popular in game engines, organises data by how it is processed, giving contiguous arrays that suit caches and SIMD.
  • Guard correctness: keep unit tests and golden outputs, allow tolerances when floating-point order changes, and run sanitizers (ASan, UBSan, TSan) after risky optimisations.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Micro-optimising before profiling — the slow code is rarely where you guess.
  • Using -ffast-math or -march=native blindly — results or portability can change silently.
  • Hand-writing what a library already does — tuned BLAS and FFT libraries are very hard to beat.
  • Testing only one input size — caches change the picture between small and large inputs.

docs.text:
gcc -O3 -march=native -fopt-info-vec-optimized -o saxpy saxpy.c
# saxpy.c: for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) y[i] = a * x[i] + y[i];
# output like: saxpy.c:5:21: optimized: loop vectorized using 32 byte vectors

docs.title: 8.6 Power, Thermals & TDP
docs.text:
Every chip turns the electricity it uses into heat, and if that heat is not removed the chip slows itself down to stay safe. TDP and related power limits tell you roughly how much heat a cooler must handle and how hard a processor is allowed to boost. Performance per watt, how much work you get for each unit of energy, now matters as much as raw speed, from phones to AI data centres.

Where a chip's heat goes. The weakest link — often the paste or the fan — sets the clock speed you can sustain.

Think of it like…

A processor is like a sprinter: it can run flat out for a short burst (turbo), but over a long race it must settle to a pace its body can cool (sustained power).

Real-world example

Ravi's fictional design studio, Lumen & Line, bought two identical workstations, but one rendered 18% slower. Monitoring showed its CPU hitting 100 °C and throttling because the cooler had been fitted without enough thermal paste. After re-seating the cooler, temperatures fell to 82 °C and clocks held steady. The studio then capped package power at 200 W instead of 250 W, losing only about 4% speed while cutting noise noticeably.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The chip draws power; almost all of it becomes heat in a very small area.
  2. The firmware allows short bursts above the sustained limit (turbo) while temperature and current permit.
  3. Heat moves through the heat spreader and thermal paste into a heatsink, liquid loop or cold plate.
  4. Fans or pumps carry heat away into the room air or, in data centres, into facility water.
  5. If temperature or power limits are reached, clocks drop (throttling) to protect the chip.

Who uses it

PC builders, laptop designers, data-centre and HPC engineers, chip power architects and anyone sizing cooling or power supplies.

Key takeaway

Remember that TDP is a cooling guideline, not the maximum power draw; modern CPUs and GPUs can exceed it briefly.

Going deeper

  • Dynamic power ≈ C × V² × f. Because voltage must rise with frequency, the last few hundred MHz cost disproportionate power — which is why modest undervolts or power caps lose little performance.
  • Intel lists Processor Base Power and Maximum Turbo Power (125 W and 250 W for the Core Ultra 9 285K); motherboard defaults sometimes exceed them, so reviews may not match stock behaviour.
  • On AMD's AM4/AM5 desktop chips, PPT is about 1.35 × TDP: 65 W → 88 W, 105 W → 142 W, 120 W → 162 W and 170 W → 230 W.
  • RAPL energy counters (Intel since Sandy Bridge, AMD on Zen) are readable through Linux powercap in /sys/class/powercap or with 'perf stat -e power/energy-pkg/', so you can report joules per job.
  • Thin laptops often sustain around 15-30 W while thick gaming laptops sustain 45 W or more; skin temperature and fan noise limits, not just Tjmax, decide the policy.
  • Turbo, DVFS and thermal throttling mechanics are explained in the processors chapter; this section focuses on measuring, sizing and cooling for real machines.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating TDP as maximum draw — CPUs and GPUs exceed it during boost; size power supplies and coolers on real peaks.
  • Panicking at 90-95 °C under load — many modern CPUs are designed to boost until they reach that limit.
  • Comparing laptops by processor name alone — sustained power settings matter more.
  • Leaving the protective film on a new cooler's base — a classic cause of instant overheating.

docs.title: Try it: Estimate a GPU server's yearly energy cost and perf per watt in Python
docs.text:
watts, hours, price = 10_000, 24*365, 0.20   # 10 kW server, $/kWh
kwh = watts/1000*hours
print(f'{kwh:,.0f} kWh/year = ${kwh*price:,.0f}')
print('Perf/W:', 5000/watts, 'TFLOPS per W at 5,000 TFLOPS')

A 65 W desktop CPU needs a cooler rated for at least 65 W of sustained heat. A Core Ultra 9 285K is rated 125 W base power and 250 W maximum turbo power. Motherboard makers sometimes set PL1 equal to PL2 out of the box, so the CPU boosts indefinitely. A Ryzen chip with a 105 W TDP has a PPT of 142 W. Junction temperature (Tjmax)Intel, AMD and NVIDIA datasheets · Metric · Current · Intermediate The maximum safe silicon temperature, typically about 95-105 °C for desktop CPUs, at which clocks drop to protect the chip. A Ryzen 9000 chip sitting at 95 °C under full load is behaving as designed, not failing. Power telemetry (RAPL, turbostat, HWiNFO)Intel and AMD RAPL counters; Linux turbostat; HWiNFO (Windows) · Tool · Current · Intermediate On-chip energy counters and tools reporting package power, clocks, temperatures and throttling reasons, so you measure instead of guess. Switching a laptop to 'performance' with powerprofilesctl raises its compile speed noticeably but shortens battery life. Undervolting and power cappingVendor tools, BIOS, nvidia-smi -pl · Concept · Current · Intermediate Lowering voltage or power limits to reduce heat and noise, often with only a small speed loss. An admin sets GPU power limits 15% lower and loses only about 5% throughput. Thermal interface materialPaste, pads, liquid metal · Component · Current · Beginner Material filling microscopic gaps between chip and cooler so heat flows efficiently. Old dried paste on a five-year-old PC is replaced, dropping load temperature by 15 °C. Air cooler, AIO and custom loopCooling vendors · Component · Current · Beginner Heatsink-and-fan coolers, sealed all-in-one liquid coolers, and hand-built water loops with separate pumps and radiators. A gamer picks a large tower air cooler for a 120 W CPU; an enthusiast uses a 360 mm AIO. GPU power ratings (TGP / TBP)NVIDIA (Total Graphics Power); AMD (Total Board Power) · Metric · Current · Intermediate The sustained power a graphics card is designed to draw, used to size power supplies, connectors and case cooling. An RTX 5090 is rated at 575 W, so builders pair it with a 1,000 W-class ATX 3.1 power supply. Energy to solution (race to idle)HPC and mobile power engineering · Metric · Current · Intermediate Total joules to finish a job (power × time); finishing fast and then sleeping can use less energy than running slowly. A job at 200 W for 60 s uses 12 kJ, beating a 'greener' 120 W setting that takes 120 s and 14.4 kJ. cTDP and laptop power modesIntel configurable TDP; laptop makers' performance modes · Concept · Current · Intermediate Laptop makers and users run the same chip at different sustained power levels, so identical processors can perform very differently. Two laptops with the same CPU differ by 30% in rendering because one sustains 28 W and the other 45 W.

docs.title: 8.7 Building or Choosing a PC
docs.text:
A PC is a set of parts that must fit together: processor, motherboard, memory, graphics card, storage, power supply, case and cooling. Choosing well means matching parts to what you actually do (gaming, coding, video, AI) and making sure nothing holds the rest back. You also decide between a laptop's portability and a desktop's power, upgradability and cooling.

How the main PC parts connect. The fastest links go straight to the CPU; the chipset adds extra, slower I/O.

Think of it like…

Building a PC is like assembling a team: a star striker (GPU) is wasted if the midfield (CPU) and defence (power supply and cooling) cannot keep up.

Real-world example

Zara, a computing student, has a budget of about 1,200 pounds for coding and 1440p gaming. She chooses a mid-range 6- to 8-core CPU on a current socket, a B-series motherboard, 32 GB of DDR5 in two sticks, a 1 TB NVMe SSD, a mid-range current-generation GPU and a quality 750 W ATX 3.1 power supply. Benchmarks show her games are GPU-bound, so the money saved on the CPU went where it mattered. Two sticks of RAM keep dual-channel bandwidth.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. List your workloads and budget, and decide laptop or desktop.
  2. Pick the CPU and a compatible motherboard (same socket, suitable chipset).
  3. Add RAM in matched pairs, NVMe storage and a GPU sized for your games or AI work.
  4. Size a quality power supply with headroom and the right GPU connectors.
  5. Choose a case and cooler that fit the parts and keep temperatures sensible.
  6. After building, update BIOS, enable XMP/EXPO memory profiles and stress-test temperatures.

Who uses it

Students, gamers, creators, IT technicians and anyone advising friends, family or a small office on hardware.

Key takeaway

Check socket, chipset, RAM type, case clearance and power connectors before buying; compatibility mistakes cause most failed builds.

Going deeper

  • On AMD's AM5 the CPU provides 24 usable PCIe 5.0-capable lanes (x16 for graphics plus two x4 NVMe links), while the chipset adds more lanes, USB and SATA over a narrower uplink.
  • Two DDR5 sticks (one per channel) usually run fastest; four sticks often force lower speeds. DDR5-6000 means 6,000 MT/s, with an actual clock of 3,000 MHz.
  • Size a power supply by adding CPU and GPU peak power plus about 100 W for everything else, then 20-30% headroom; ATX 3.x units are designed to ride through short GPU power spikes.
  • After building, stress-test: MemTest86+ for memory, Cinebench or Prime95 for the CPU and looped 3DMark for the GPU, while watching temperatures in HWiNFO.
  • Prebuilt PCs include a warranty and support but may cut corners on RAM speed, power supply quality or airflow; self-builds give control but you do your own troubleshooting.
  • Upgrade paths depend on platform longevity (AMD has supported AM5 across several CPU generations), spare RAM and M.2 slots, and power-supply headroom.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Pairing a high-end GPU with a cheap, unrated power supply — buy a quality ATX 3.x unit with native connectors.
  • Forgetting to enable XMP or EXPO — memory then runs at slower default speeds.
  • Not pushing the 12V-2x6 plug fully home, or bending it sharply — it can overheat.
  • Ignoring case clearance — check GPU length and cooler height before buying.

docs.title: Try it: See what hardware your own computer has
docs.text:
lscpu; free -h; lsblk; lspci | grep -i -E 'vga|nvme'      # Linux
system_profiler SPHardwareDataType                           # macOS
Get-CimInstance Win32_Processor | Select Name,NumberOfCores  # Windows PowerShell

docs.title: 8.8 Choosing a Server or Workstation
docs.text:
Servers and workstations are built for reliability and heavy, continuous work rather than looks or gaming. They add features such as error-correcting memory, more processor sockets, remote management and spare power supplies. Choosing one means balancing performance, reliability, space, power and total cost, including whether renting in the cloud is cheaper.

Desktop vs workstation vs rack server

Desktop PC Workstation Rack server Memory Non-ECC, 2 channels ECC, 4-8 channels ECC RDIMM, 8-12 channels/socket CPUs 1 consumer chip 1 Xeon W or Threadripper PRO 1-2 Xeon 6 or EPYC Management None Sometimes BMC (iDRAC, iLO, Redfish) Redundancy Single PSU Sometimes dual PSU Hot-swap PSUs, fans, drives Form factor Tower Tower or rack 1U/2U, blade, multi-node Noise Quiet Moderate Loud — machine rooms only

ECC memory, remote management and redundancy are what you pay extra for.

Think of it like…

A desktop PC is a family car; a server is a delivery lorry built to run all day, every day, with spare tyres and a tracker so the depot can check it remotely.

Real-world example

Orchid Bio, a fictional genomics lab, needed to analyse 40 TB of sequencing data each month. They compared a 2U dual-socket server with 1 TB of ECC RDIMM memory and two GPUs against renting similar cloud instances. The cloud cost about 9,000 dollars a month at their usage, while the server, power and support worked out near 3,500 a month over four years. Because the workload ran around the clock, they bought the server and used cloud only for peaks.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Profile the workload: cores, memory size, bandwidth, GPUs, storage and network.
  2. Choose form factor: tower workstation, or rack server sized in rack units.
  3. Pick CPUs (single or dual socket), ECC memory, GPUs and storage with growth room.
  4. Add reliability: redundant power supplies and fans, RAID or replicated storage, and a BMC.
  5. Compare total cost of ownership with cloud over three to five years, including power and staff.

Who uses it

Sysadmins, HPC and infrastructure engineers, IT managers, researchers and procurement teams.

Key takeaway

Always mention ECC memory, redundancy and out-of-band management (BMC) as the key differences between servers and desktops.

Going deeper

  • AMD EPYC 9005 offers up to 192 cores and 12 DDR5 channels per socket; Intel Xeon 6 offers up to 128 performance cores (6900P) or 288 efficient cores (6900E), also with 12 channels on top models.
  • Server reliability goes beyond ECC: patrol scrubbing, chipkill-style multi-bit correction, PCIe error containment and predictive-failure alerts recorded in the BMC's event log.
  • Enterprises usually refresh servers every three to six years; newer, denser machines can replace several old ones and cut power and licence bills, while refurbished servers suit labs and homelabs.
  • Workstation platforms (Threadripper PRO, Xeon W) provide many cores, eight memory channels and plenty of PCIe lanes for multi-GPU rigs, plus ISV-certified drivers for CAD and simulation.
  • 8-GPU HGX servers for AI training can draw over 10 kW each, needing high-power racks, often liquid cooling and several 400 Gb/s network links per node.
  • Security baseline: Secure Boot, TPM 2.0, signed firmware, a silicon root of trust in the BMC, and an isolated management network that never faces the Internet.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Exposing BMC web interfaces to the Internet — keep them on a separate management network and patch their firmware.
  • Leaving memory channels empty to save money — bandwidth drops sharply for memory-bound workloads.
  • Ignoring software licensing when choosing core counts — licences can cost more than the hardware.
  • Running critical systems without a support contract — waiting days for parts means days of downtime.

docs.title: Try it: Query a server's BMC and hardware from the OS (on your own server)
docs.text:
sudo ipmitool sensor list | head      # temperatures, fans, voltages via BMC
sudo ipmitool sel list | tail         # hardware event log
sudo dmidecode -t memory | grep -E 'Type:|Speed|Error'

docs.title: 8.9 Careers in Computing Systems
docs.text:
Knowing how computers really work opens many careers, from designing chips to keeping huge cloud and AI systems running. Some jobs are close to the hardware (chip design, firmware, data-centre work), while others are about software that squeezes the best out of hardware (kernels, GPU programming, performance and reliability). Most share the same core skills: computer architecture, operating systems, Linux, programming and careful measurement.

Career map from silicon to service. Most people move between neighbouring tiers as their skills grow.

Think of it like…

The computing industry is like a city: some people design the buildings (architects), some build and wire them (hardware and firmware engineers), and some keep the lights on and traffic flowing (sysadmins, SREs and data-centre technicians).

Real-world example

Jamal studied computer science and enjoyed his architecture module most. In his final year he built a RISC-V core on a cheap FPGA and profiled CUDA code on a free cloud notebook, putting both on GitHub. He landed a graduate role as a performance engineer at a fictional cloud firm, Stratacloud, tuning servers. Two years later he moved into ML infrastructure, managing GPU clusters for model training.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Learn the core: programming (C/C++ and Python), computer architecture, operating systems and Linux.
  2. Pick a direction: hardware design, low-level software, HPC/AI infrastructure or operations.
  3. Build visible projects and contribute to open source in that direction.
  4. Add a relevant certification or course if targeting IT and cloud roles.
  5. Apply for internships and graduate roles, and practise explaining your projects clearly.

Who uses it

Students choosing a specialism, career changers and early-career engineers planning their next move.

Key takeaway

Employers value a working project you can explain in depth more than a long list of buzzwords on a CV.

Going deeper

  • Chip-design roles usually expect an electrical or computer engineering degree, often a master's; software-side roles (kernel, performance, cloud) welcome computer science graduates and strong self-taught portfolios.
  • IT support and data-centre technician jobs are common entry routes; many cloud engineers and SREs started there and moved up after a few years of hands-on experience.
  • Demand in 2025-26 is driven by AI data-centre build-outs (GPU cluster engineers, technicians, power and cooling specialists), custom silicon at hyperscalers and the growing RISC-V ecosystem.
  • Interviews across these roles probe architecture (caches, pipelines), operating systems (processes, virtual memory), C/C++ or Python, Linux skills and a debugging story from your own project.
  • Strong portfolio signals include measured GitHub projects, open-source contributions (Linux kernel, LLVM, OpenBMC, Zephyr), Student Cluster Competition entries and clear technical write-ups.
  • Titles vary: 'performance engineer' may mean load testing at one company and CPU microarchitecture analysis at another — read the responsibilities, not just the title.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Collecting certificates without projects — employers want evidence you can build and debug real systems.
  • Assuming hardware careers need a PhD — many RTL, verification and firmware roles hire bachelor's graduates.
  • Neglecting communication — explaining trade-offs clearly is assessed in nearly every interview.

docs.title: 8.10 Certifications & Courses
docs.text:
Certifications are exams that prove you know a defined set of skills, and many employers use them to filter CVs, especially for IT, Linux and cloud roles. University courses, many free online, teach the deeper theory of how computers work. A sensible plan mixes one or two certifications with solid courses and hands-on projects.

A typical certification path. Back each step with a hands-on project that uses the same skills.

Think of it like…

A certification is like a driving licence that proves you passed a standard test, while courses and projects are the hours of real driving that make you good.

Real-world example

Hannah worked in retail and wanted an IT career. She passed CompTIA A+ in four months, then took Linux+ while building a home lab. Her first job was desktop support at a fictional council, Westbrook District. A year later she earned AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner and then Solutions Architect - Associate, moving into a junior cloud engineer role.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Choose a target role, then list the certifications that job adverts for it mention.
  2. Start with a foundation (A+, a cloud fundamentals exam or an NVIDIA associate exam).
  3. Study with official objectives, a course and plenty of hands-on labs.
  4. Book the exam once practice tests are consistently comfortable, and note renewal rules.
  5. Back the certificate with a portfolio project that uses the same skills.

Who uses it

Students, career changers, IT staff seeking promotion and employers checking baseline skills.

Key takeaway

Exam codes change every few years, so always check the vendor's site for the current version before buying study materials.

Going deeper

  • Formats differ: CompTIA and most cloud exams use multiple choice plus some performance-based tasks, while Red Hat and Linux Foundation exams are entirely hands-on in live systems — harder but highly respected.
  • Renewal rules: CompTIA certifications last three years (renewable through continuing education), AWS certifications three years, and Microsoft role-based certifications need a free online renewal assessment every year.
  • Exam fees range from roughly US$100 for fundamentals exams to about US$500 for hands-on professional exams; student discounts, training-programme vouchers and employer funding are common.
  • University courses such as MIT 6.1910, CMU 15-213 and Berkeley CS61C give no certificate but build the architecture and systems depth that hardware and performance interviews test.
  • Linux and Kubernetes certifications (RHCSA, LFCS, Linux+, CKA, CKAD) are described in the operating-systems chapter; they pair naturally with the cloud certifications listed here.
  • NVIDIA's programme spans associate exams (AI infrastructure and operations, generative AI) and professional ones (AI infrastructure, AI networking), useful for GPU-cluster jobs.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Using exam 'dumps' — they break exam agreements, can get certifications revoked and leave you unable to do the job.
  • Buying study material for a retired exam version — check the current exam code on the vendor's site first.
  • Stacking many fundamentals badges — one foundation, one hands-on associate certification and real projects impress more.

docs.title: 8.11 Books & Learning Resources
docs.text:
A handful of classic books and websites explain computers from the transistor up, and most professionals have read at least one of them. Some are gentle introductions, others are university textbooks, and some are practical references used daily at work. Pick one at your level, work through it with exercises, and use online resources to see real hardware details.

A reading ladder from beginner to expert. Climb one rung at a time and do the exercises on each.

Think of it like…

These resources are like a ladder: friendly popular-science books are the first rungs, textbooks the middle, and vendor manuals and expert blogs the top.

Real-world example

Nadia set herself a one-year plan. She read Petzold's 'Code' for the big picture, worked through nand2tetris to build a computer in software, then studied CS:APP chapters on memory and linking alongside OSTEP for operating systems. In her final term she read parts of Hennessy and Patterson's quantitative book and followed Chips and Cheese articles to see real CPUs analysed. She now explains caches confidently in interviews.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Start with a gentle overview (Code, or Ben Eater's videos).
  2. Build something from the ground up (nand2tetris).
  3. Study a core textbook with exercises (Patterson and Hennessy, CS:APP, OSTEP).
  4. Go deeper with advanced books on architecture, GPUs or performance.
  5. Keep up with expert blogs, vendor manuals and Compiler Explorer experiments.

Who uses it

Students, self-taught programmers, interview candidates and working engineers refreshing fundamentals.

Key takeaway

Check the edition: newer editions add RISC-V, AI accelerators and modern GPUs, which interviewers increasingly ask about.

Going deeper

  • Free and legal: OSTEP, Agner Fog's manuals, nand2tetris course materials, MIT OpenCourseWare and the Intel, AMD, Arm and RISC-V architecture manuals cost nothing.
  • Pick the right edition: Computer Organization and Design exists in MIPS, Arm and RISC-V editions — choose RISC-V for current courses; CS:APP's 3rd edition (x86-64) remains the standard.
  • Read actively: do the exercises, reproduce experiments such as cache-stride and branch-prediction tests on your own machine, and write notes or a blog — that is what makes knowledge stick for interviews.
  • Stay current with expert sources: Chips and Cheese, Brendan Gregg's blog, LWN.net for Linux kernel news, and talks from Hot Chips, ISCA, SC and USENIX conferences.
  • Primary references behind most blog posts are the Intel 64 and IA-32 Software Developer's Manuals, the Arm Architecture Reference Manual, the RISC-V ISA specifications and NVIDIA's CUDA C++ Programming Guide.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Starting with the hardest textbook — CA:AQA without COD basics overwhelms most beginners.
  • Reading without doing — skipping exercises and labs leaves knowledge shallow.
  • Relying on outdated or pirated PDFs — use current editions and legitimate free resources.
