docs.title: 8.12 Hands-On Projects & Lab Ideas
docs.text:
The fastest way to really understand computers is to build and measure things yourself. Many great projects are free or cheap: simulate a CPU, program a small FPGA, cluster a few single-board computers or run GPU code in a free online notebook. Finished projects also make an excellent portfolio for interviews.

Projects by level. Start at the top and finish one project before starting the next.

Think of it like…

Reading about computers without building anything is like learning to swim from a book; projects are getting into the pool.

Real-world example

Ethan, a first-year student, spent one term on three projects. He built an 8-bit CPU in the free Digital simulator, benchmarked his laptop's memory bandwidth with a short NumPy script (about 18 GB/s on a single thread), and ran a CUDA matrix multiply on a free cloud GPU notebook that was 40 times faster than his plain Python loop. He wrote up each one on GitHub with graphs, and an interviewer spent most of his interview asking about them.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Pick a project that matches the career direction you are curious about.
  2. Start small and get a minimal version working end to end.
  3. Measure results (speed, resource use) and record them in a table or graph.
  4. Write a short README explaining what you built, what you measured and what you learned.
  5. Publish it (for example on GitHub) and be ready to discuss it in interviews.

Who uses it

Students, self-learners and job-seekers building a portfolio for hardware, systems, HPC or cloud roles.

Key takeaway

Always include numbers and graphs in your write-up; 'it got 3.2x faster because of X' is far more impressive than 'I optimised it'.

Going deeper

  • A strong write-up states the question, method, hardware and software versions, results with graphs and error bars, and an explanation linking the results to theory such as caches or Amdahl's law.
  • Cheap hardware goes far: iCE40 FPGA boards cost tens of dollars with fully open toolchains (Yosys, nextpnr), Pico boards cost a few dollars, and used office mini-PCs make excellent homelab nodes.
  • Free compute: Google Colab and Kaggle notebooks give limited free GPU time, while cloud free tiers and student credits cover small experiments — set budget alerts first.
  • Simulators avoid buying hardware: Verilator for Verilog, QEMU for whole systems including RISC-V, gem5 for architecture research and Wokwi for online microcontroller projects.
  • When contributing upstream, start with small fixes, follow the project's contribution guide, include benchmark evidence with performance patches and expect several review rounds.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Starting too big, such as an out-of-order CPU first — finish a small working version, then extend it.
  • Publishing results without method or raw data — readers and interviewers cannot trust them.
  • Leaving cloud resources running after an experiment — set budget alerts and delete everything afterwards.

docs.title: Try it: A STREAM-like memory bandwidth test with NumPy
docs.text:
import numpy as np, time
n = 50_000_000                      # ~400 MB per array
a = np.ones(n); b = np.ones(n); c = np.empty(n)
for _ in range(3):
    t = time.perf_counter(); np.add(a, b, out=c); dt = time.perf_counter() - t
    print(f'Add bandwidth: {3*8*n/dt/1e9:.1f} GB/s')   # 2 reads + 1 write

docs.title: 8.13 Interview Questions & Model Answers
docs.text:
Technical interviews for systems, hardware, HPC and cloud jobs repeat a core set of questions about how computers work. Short, clear answers with an example show real understanding. Each item below is a common question, a short model answer and a hint on how to say it well.

Structuring a strong technical answer. About a minute, then let the interviewer steer the follow-up.

Think of it like…

Preparing these is like learning the key moves before a match: you will not know every play, but the basics come up every time.

Real-world example

In her interview at a fictional chip start-up, Ola was asked what happens on a cache miss. She explained the lookup, the request to the next level, the line fill and the restart, then added that out-of-order cores keep working on other instructions meanwhile. She finished with a real example from her cache-stride experiment. The interviewer moved straight on to harder questions, a good sign.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Listen for what the question is really testing (concept, trade-off or debugging approach).
  2. Give a one-sentence definition first.
  3. Explain how it works in two or three steps.
  4. Add a trade-off, number or real example from your own projects.
  5. If unsure, reason aloud from first principles rather than guessing silently.

Who uses it

Anyone interviewing for software, systems, hardware, HPC, cloud or ML infrastructure roles.

Key takeaway

Practise answering aloud in under one minute, then be ready for the follow-up 'why?' or 'what would you measure?'.

Going deeper

  • Use STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) for behavioural and project questions, and keep technical answers to about a minute before inviting follow-ups.
  • Numbers worth knowing: L1 hit about 1 ns, DRAM about 100 ns, NVMe read tens of microseconds, same-data-centre round trip about 0.5 ms, intercontinental 100 ms or more; cache line 64 bytes; page 4 KiB.
  • Debugging questions reward method: state a hypothesis, the tool you would use (top, vmstat, iostat, perf, strace), the evidence you expect and how you would confirm the fix.
  • Hardware interviews often include whiteboard design — a FIFO, a cache lookup, a pipeline hazard diagram or a finite-state machine in Verilog — so practise drawing them.
  • Prepare questions for the interviewer about the team's hardware, tools, on-call duties and how performance or reliability is measured; it signals genuine interest.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Bluffing when unsure — say what you know and reason aloud; honest reasoning scores better.
  • Reciting definitions without examples — tie answers to numbers or your own projects.
  • Jumping straight to a fix in debugging questions — gather data and narrow the cause first.

docs.title: Key chips, architectures, standards, tools & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example What happens when a cache miss occurs?Computer architecture · Concept · Current · Intermediate The CPU fetches the missing line from the next cache level or memory, stores it, possibly evicting another, then completes the access. Mention the 64-byte line, latency rising from about a nanosecond to around 100 ns, and that out-of-order cores keep working meanwhile. Process vs thread?Operating systems · Concept · Current · Beginner A process has its own address space; threads within a process share memory but have separate stacks and registers. Say: processes isolate, threads share. Browsers use separate processes per site for safety and threads inside each for speed. Explain virtual memory.Operating systems · Concept · Current · Intermediate Each process sees its own private address space; page tables and the TLB map virtual pages to physical memory or disk. Add that it gives isolation and lets programs use more memory than RAM, at the cost of page faults. Why are GPUs fast for AI?GPU architecture · Concept · Current · Beginner AI is mostly huge matrix multiplications; GPUs run thousands of parallel lanes with tensor cores and very high-bandwidth memory. Contrast with CPUs: few powerful cores for branchy code versus many simple lanes for identical maths on lots of data. Latency vs bandwidth?Performance fundamentals · Concept · Current · Beginner Latency is how long one item takes to arrive; bandwidth is how much data arrives per second. Use a motorway analogy: speed limit is latency, number of lanes is bandwidth; HBM has huge bandwidth, not lower latency. What is Amdahl's law?Gene Amdahl · Concept · Current · Intermediate Speed-up from parallelising is limited by the serial fraction: with 10% serial, maximum speed-up is 10x. Write the formula and work an example; then mention Gustafson's law for growing problem sizes. What does a branch misprediction cost?CPU microarchitecture · Concept · Current · Intermediate The pipeline must discard speculative work and restart from the correct path, wasting roughly 10-20 cycles on modern cores. Mention sorted data making branches predictable, and branchless code or lookup tables as fixes. What happens when you type a command and press Enter?Operating systems · Concept · Current · Intermediate The shell parses it, forks a child process, execs the program, the kernel loads it and schedules it, and output returns through system calls. Name fork, exec, wait and system calls; interviewers love candidates who mention the dynamic loader. What is false sharing?Multicore programming · Concept · Current · Advanced Threads updating different variables on the same cache line make cores repeatedly invalidate each other's caches. Give the fix: pad or align per-thread data to separate cache lines, then show the before and after timing. How would you find why a server is slow?Performance methodology · Concept · Current · Intermediate Check CPU, memory, disk and network for utilisation, saturation and errors, then profile the busiest process. Name tools in order: uptime, top or htop, vmstat, iostat, then perf and a flame graph. What is the difference between RISC and CISC?Computer architecture · Concept · Current · Beginner RISC uses simple, fixed-length instructions; CISC has complex, variable-length ones. Modern x86 decodes into simpler internal micro-operations. Mention Arm and RISC-V as RISC, x86-64 as CISC, and that the line has blurred in practice. What is a deadlock and how do you prevent it?Operating systems and concurrency · Concept · Current · Intermediate Threads wait forever for locks held by each other; prevent it by always acquiring locks in a fixed order or using timeouts. Name the four Coffman conditions and say which one your fix breaks. Why can memory be the bottleneck, not the CPU?Memory hierarchy; roofline model · Concept · Current · Advanced Cores compute far faster than DRAM can supply data, so low-reuse code waits on memory. Mention the roofline model, arithmetic intensity and fixes such as tiling and better data layout. How does a computer boot?Firmware and operating systems · Concept · Current · Beginner Firmware (UEFI) initialises hardware, finds a boot loader, which loads the kernel; the kernel then starts the first user process. Mention Secure Boot checking signatures, and systemd as PID 1 on most Linux systems. TLB miss vs page fault?Memory management · Concept · Current · Intermediate TLB miss: the translation isn't cached, so hardware walks the page table. Page fault: the page isn't mapped or present, so the OS steps in. Add scale: a TLB miss costs tens to hundreds of cycles, while a major page fault that reads from disk can cost milliseconds. How would you debug a slow GPU training job?ML infrastructure · Concept · Current · Advanced Check GPU utilisation and memory, then profile to see whether the GPU waits on data loading, CPU work, communication or slow kernels. Name nvidia-smi, Nsight Systems and PyTorch Profiler; fixes include more loader workers, mixed precision and overlapping communication with compute.

docs.title: Chapter 2: Processors & CPU Architecture
docs.text: The CPU is the general-purpose brain of every computer, from a smartwatch to a 256-core cloud server. This chapter opens up the processor: the parts inside a core, the instruction sets it speaks and the assembly code they run, and the tricks — pipelining, out-of-order execution, branch prediction, caches and SIMD — that make modern chips fast. It then covers how chips are packaged, the real 2026 processor families from Intel, AMD, Apple, Arm, cloud providers and RISC-V vendors, and finishes with interrupts and privilege levels, the buses and I/O links that connect devices, and the security features and hardware attacks that matter in modern CPUs.

docs.title: 2.1 Inside a CPU: The Parts That Do the Work
docs.text:
A CPU (central processing unit) is the chip that follows a program's instructions one small step at a time. Inside it, a control unit reads each instruction and decides what to do, an arithmetic unit does the maths, and a handful of tiny super-fast storage slots called registers hold the numbers being worked on. A clock ticks billions of times a second, and every tick moves the work forward.

Inside a modern CPU core. The front end supplies instructions, the back end executes them, and registers and caches keep both fed.

Think of it like…

A CPU is like a chef working from a recipe card: the control unit reads the next line, the chopping board and knives are the arithmetic unit, the few bowls on the counter are registers, and a kitchen timer beats out the rhythm.

Real-world example

Leo, a first-year student, writes total = price + tax in C. The compiler turns it into roughly three machine instructions: load price into a register, add tax, store the result. His 4 GHz laptop CPU ticks 4 billion times a second, so even if each instruction needed a full tick, those three would finish in under a nanosecond. The program counter then simply moves on to the next instruction.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Fetch: the program counter holds the address of the next instruction, which is read from memory (usually from a cache).
  2. Decode: the control unit works out what the instruction means and which registers and units it needs.
  3. Execute: the ALU, floating-point unit or load/store unit carries out the operation.
  4. Write back: the result goes into a register (or memory) and status flags such as 'result was zero' are updated.
  5. The program counter advances (or jumps, for a branch) and the cycle repeats billions of times per second.

Who uses it

Computer-architecture and embedded students, compiler writers, performance engineers and anyone reading assembly or debugging low-level code meets these parts.

Key takeaway

Be able to recite fetch-decode-execute-write back and name what the program counter, registers, ALU and flags each do — it is a classic exam and interview opener.

Going deeper

  • Engineers describe a core as a front end (branch prediction, fetch, decode, micro-op cache) that supplies work and a back end (rename, schedulers, execution units, load/store queues) that does it; profilers label stalls as front-end or back-end bound.
  • Top-down microarchitecture analysis, popularised by Intel and supported in AMD and Arm tools, divides every pipeline slot into retiring, bad speculation, front-end bound or back-end bound, showing where optimisation will pay off.
  • High-end 2025-26 cores have six or more integer ALUs, several 256- or 512-bit vector pipes and three or more load ports, yet typical code averages only about 1-3 instructions per cycle because of cache misses and mispredictions.
  • Architectural registers are the ones the ISA names (16 general-purpose on x86-64, 31 on AArch64, 32 on RISC-V); behind them, physical register files hold hundreds of entries to support register renaming.
  • Everything outside the cores — L3 cache, memory controllers, on-chip network, PCIe and power management — is the uncore or SoC fabric, and it often limits multi-core performance more than the cores themselves.
  • Microcode updates are loaded at every boot by firmware or the OS to fix errata and security bugs; they can change how instructions behave but cannot add hardware, so some fixes cost performance.
  • The performance monitoring unit (PMU) counts events such as cycles, instructions retired, cache misses and branch mispredictions; Linux perf, Intel VTune, AMD uProf and Arm tools all read these counters.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Picturing one instruction finishing before the next starts: real cores keep hundreds of instructions in flight through pipelining and out-of-order execution.
  • Equating the ISA's register count with the hardware's: renaming gives a core far more physical registers than the ISA exposes.
  • Assuming 'the ALU' does everything: floating point, vectors, address calculation and memory access each use separate specialised units.

docs.title: Try it: Ask your own machine what CPU it has
docs.text:
lscpu                       # Linux: model, cores, threads, caches, flags
cat /proc/cpuinfo | head -30   # Linux: raw per-core details
# Windows PowerShell:
Get-CimInstance Win32_Processor | Select-Object Name, NumberOfCores, NumberOfLogicalProcessors, MaxClockSpeed
# macOS:
sysctl -n machdep.cpu.brand_string; sysctl hw.ncpu

docs.text: Name What it does Example ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit)General CPU design · Component · Current · Beginner Integer execution units for add, subtract, logic, shifts and compares; modern cores have several so independent operations run side by side. Checking if (score > 50) makes the ALU subtract 50 from score and set flags the next branch instruction reads. FPU (Floating-Point Unit)IEEE 754 arithmetic · Component · Current · Beginner A unit specialised for decimal-point (floating-point) maths such as 3.14 × 2.5, following the IEEE 754 number format. A physics game computing velocities with float and double variables keeps the FPU and vector units busy every frame. Registers and register fileDefined by each ISA (e.g. 16 general registers in x86-64, 31 in AArch64) · Component · Current · Beginner The handful of tiny, fastest storage slots inside the core where instructions read inputs and write results. x86-64 code keeps a loop counter in register RCX; Arm64 code might use X0 to pass a function's first argument. Flags / status registerx86 RFLAGS; Arm NZCV condition flags · Component · Current · Intermediate Bits that record facts about the last result — zero, negative, carry, overflow — used by conditional branches. After CMP eax, 10 the zero flag is set if eax equals 10, so the following JE instruction jumps. Stack pointerx86-64 RSP; Arm SP; RISC-V sp (x2) · Component · Current · Intermediate A register pointing to the top of the call stack, where return addresses and local variables live. On x86-64, a CALL pushes the 8-byte return address, moving the stack pointer down by 8 bytes. Instruction decoderGeneral CPU design · Component · Current · Intermediate Logic that turns raw instruction bytes into internal control signals or micro-operations the core can execute. x86 instructions vary from 1 to 15 bytes long, so its decoders are far more complex than a fixed 4-byte RISC decoder. MicrocodeIntel, AMD and others; updated via BIOS/UEFI or the OS · Technology · Current · Intermediate Internal firmware that breaks complex instructions into simpler steps; vendors can patch it after the chip ships. After a security flaw is found, a Windows or Linux update loads new microcode at boot to change CPU behaviour. Load/store unit and AGUGeneral CPU design · Component · Current · Advanced Hardware that calculates memory addresses (address generation unit) and moves data between registers and the caches. Reading array[i] makes the AGU compute base + i × 4 before the load unit fetches four bytes. Front end and back endStandard microarchitecture terms (Intel, AMD and Arm optimisation guides) · Concept · Current · Intermediate The front end predicts, fetches and decodes instructions; the back end renames, schedules, executes and retires them. A profiler reports a game loop as 40% front-end bound, so the team shrinks its hot code to fit the instruction cache. Execution units and portsVaries by microarchitecture; documented in vendor optimisation guides and uops.info · Component · Current · Advanced The parallel ALUs, multipliers, vector pipes and load/store units inside a core; schedulers send micro-ops to them through numbered issue ports. uops.info shows which ports an instruction can use, explaining why a loop of multiplies cannot beat the number of multiply-capable ports. Core and uncoreIntel term; AMD and Arm speak of the data fabric or SoC fabric · Concept · Current · Intermediate Cores run instructions; the uncore is the shared rest of the chip — L3, memory controllers, on-chip network, I/O and power control. A server's memory-bandwidth ceiling comes from its uncore memory controllers, so adding more threads stops helping beyond a point. Vector and floating-point registersx86 XMM/YMM/ZMM; Arm V0-V31 and SVE Z registers; RISC-V f0-f31 and v0-v31 · Component · Current · Intermediate Separate register sets holding floating-point and SIMD values, 128 to 512 bits wide, or wider with scalable vectors. An AVX-512 routine keeps sixteen floats in each 512-bit ZMM register, and x86-64 provides 32 of them. Hardware performance counters (PMU)Intel, AMD, Arm and RISC-V performance monitoring units; read by perf, VTune, AMD uProf · Component · Current · Advanced On-chip counters recording events such as cycles, instructions retired, cache misses and branch mispredictions, used for profiling. perf stat -e cycles,instructions,cache-misses ./app reads the PMU to show IPC and how often the program missed in cache.

docs.title: 2.2 Instruction Set Architectures: x86, Arm, RISC-V and Friends
docs.text:
An instruction set architecture (ISA) is the list of commands a processor family understands, plus its registers and rules — the contract between software and hardware. Programs compiled for one ISA, such as x86-64, will not run natively on another, such as Arm. Many different chips can share one ISA, which is why software runs on both an old and a new Intel laptop.

Where the ISA sits. Software above the ISA line sees only the contract; everything below it can change from chip to chip.

Think of it like…

An ISA is like a language such as Spanish: many different people (chip designs) can speak it with different accents and speeds, but a book written in Spanish cannot be read by someone who only speaks Japanese without a translator (an emulator).

Real-world example

Amara at a small app studio called Pixelfern ships a desktop tool. She builds it three times: x86-64 for most Windows PCs, Arm64 for Apple silicon Macs and Snapdragon laptops, and RISC-V as a test build for a development board. The C source is identical; only the compiler target changes. Without the Arm build, Mac users would rely on Rosetta 2 translation and lose some speed.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The ISA defines instructions (add, load, branch), registers, data types, memory addressing and privilege rules.
  2. RISC designs use simple, fixed-length instructions with separate load/store; CISC designs allow complex, variable-length instructions that can touch memory directly.
  3. A microarchitecture is one particular implementation of an ISA — e.g. AMD Zen 5 and Intel Lion Cove both implement x86-64.
  4. Compilers translate source code into the target ISA's machine code; emulators or translators (Rosetta 2, Windows Prism) bridge ISAs when needed.
  5. ISAs evolve by adding extensions (vector, security, virtualisation) grouped into versions or profiles such as Armv9 or RVA23.

Who uses it

Compiler and OS engineers, embedded developers, app developers shipping multi-platform builds and cloud engineers choosing between x86 and Arm instances all deal with ISAs.

Key takeaway

Keep 'ISA' (the contract) and 'microarchitecture' (one implementation of it) separate in your head — interviewers love that distinction.

Going deeper

  • Instruction lengths differ: x86-64 instructions are 1-15 bytes with optional prefixes, AArch64 uses a fixed 4 bytes, and RISC-V uses 4 bytes plus optional 2-byte compressed forms — fixed lengths make wide parallel decoding much simpler.
  • RISC-V names its base ISAs RV32I and RV64I and adds lettered extensions — M (multiply), A (atomics), F/D (floating point), C (compressed), V (vector) — while profiles such as RVA23 bundle what general-purpose software may assume.
  • Arm licenses in two main ways: a core licence to use Arm-designed cores, or an architecture licence to design custom cores (as Apple, Qualcomm, NVIDIA and Ampere do) that must pass Arm's compatibility tests.
  • The ABI sits on top of the ISA and fixes calling conventions, data layout and system-call numbers, so x86-64 Linux (System V ABI) and x86-64 Windows binaries are incompatible even on the same processor.
  • Translation layers made ISA switches practical: Apple moved Macs from PowerPC to x86 (2006) and from x86 to Arm (2020) using Rosetta, and Windows on Arm runs x86-64 apps through its Prism emulator.
  • Server ISA share is shifting: Arm-based cloud CPUs such as Graviton, Axion and Cobalt now make up a meaningful share of new cloud capacity, while x86 still dominates the installed base of servers.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Saying 'Arm is RISC, so it is always more efficient': efficiency depends mostly on microarchitecture, process node and design goals, not the ISA label.
  • Assuming x86-64 software runs on an Arm server: it needs recompiling or emulation, including every native library and container image layer.
  • Treating RISC-V as one chip design: it is an open specification, and features and quality vary hugely between implementations.

docs.title: Try it: See the same C function as x86-64 or Arm64 assembly
docs.text:
// add.c
int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }

// Compile to assembly for your own CPU and read add.s:
//   gcc -O2 -march=native -S add.c -o add.s
// Or paste it into https://godbolt.org and switch between
// 'x86-64 gcc' and 'ARM64 gcc' to compare the instructions.

docs.text: Name What it does Example ISA (Instruction Set Architecture)Defined per processor family · Concept · Current · Beginner The software-visible contract of a processor: its instructions, registers, data types, memory model and privilege levels. Linux distributions publish separate downloads for amd64 (x86-64), arm64 and riscv64 because each ISA needs different machine code. MicroarchitectureEach chip designer (e.g. AMD Zen 5, Arm Neoverse V3) · Concept · Current · Intermediate The internal design that implements an ISA — pipeline, caches, execution units — invisible to normal programs except as speed. AMD's Zen 5 and Intel's Lion Cove run identical x86-64 programs but differ completely inside. RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer)Pioneered at IBM, Berkeley and Stanford (1980s) · Concept · Current · Beginner A design philosophy of simple, fixed-length instructions where only loads and stores touch memory, making pipelining easier. Arm, RISC-V and POWER are RISC ISAs; adding two values in memory takes separate load, add and store instructions. CISC (Complex Instruction Set Computer)Classic examples: x86, IBM System/360, VAX · Concept · Current · Beginner A philosophy allowing rich, variable-length instructions that can operate directly on memory; modern x86 cracks them into RISC-like micro-ops. x86's ADD [rbx], eax reads memory, adds and writes back in one instruction. x86-64 (AMD64 / Intel 64)AMD (spec 2000, first chips 2003); Intel; x86 Ecosystem Advisory Group · Architecture · Current · Beginner The 64-bit extension of Intel's 1978 x86 ISA, dominant in PCs and servers; also called amd64 or x64. Most Windows PCs, game consoles like PlayStation 5, and the majority of cloud servers run x86-64 code. AArch64 / Armv8-AArm Ltd (Armv8-A announced 2011) · Architecture · Current · Beginner Arm's 64-bit ISA with 31 general registers and fixed 32-bit instructions, used in phones, Macs and cloud servers. An iPhone app, an AWS Graviton server and a Raspberry Pi 5 all execute AArch64 instructions. Armv9-AArm Ltd (announced 2021; versions v9.0 to v9.x) · Architecture · Current · Intermediate The current Arm architecture generation, adding SVE2 vectors, matrix extensions (SME) and security features such as Memory Tagging and Realms. Arm's C1 CPU cores (2025) implement Armv9.3, and NVIDIA's Vera CPU cores implement Armv9.2. RISC-VRISC-V International (open standard; began at UC Berkeley, 2010) · Architecture · Current · Beginner A free, open ISA anyone can implement without royalties, built from a small base (RV32I/RV64I) plus optional lettered extensions. A smart-sensor start-up adds a royalty-free RISC-V core to its chip and adds custom instructions for signal processing. RVA23 profileRISC-V International (ratified 2024) · Standard · Emerging · Intermediate A bundle of required RISC-V extensions — including vectors and hypervisor support — so application software targets one common baseline. Ubuntu chose RVA23 as its minimum RISC-V baseline from 25.10, so boards must support it to run new releases. APX (Advanced Performance Extensions)Intel; endorsed via x86 Ecosystem Advisory Group · Architecture · Emerging · Advanced An x86-64 extension doubling general registers from 16 to 32 and adding three-operand forms to cut memory traffic. Compilers already support APX, ready for Intel processors expected to add it in future generations. POWER / Power ISAIBM; OpenPOWER Foundation (Linux Foundation) · Architecture · Current · Intermediate IBM's RISC ISA used in high-end enterprise servers; the Power ISA was opened for royalty-free use in 2019. A bank runs its core IBM i and AIX workloads on IBM Power11 servers (launched 2025). MIPS architectureMIPS (owned by GlobalFoundries since 2025) · Architecture · Legacy · Intermediate A classic 1980s RISC ISA once common in routers, consoles and textbooks; the MIPS company now designs RISC-V cores instead. Older home routers and the original PlayStation used MIPS CPUs; many textbooks still teach its five-stage pipeline. SPARCSun Microsystems / Oracle; Fujitsu · Architecture · Legacy · Intermediate Sun's RISC ISA for Unix servers and workstations; active development has effectively ended. A university's old Solaris server room ran SPARC machines before migrating to x86 Linux. ABI and calling conventionsSystem V AMD64 ABI; Microsoft x64 convention; Arm AAPCS64; RISC-V psABI · Standard · Current · Intermediate Rules for how compiled code passes arguments, returns values, lays out data and calls the OS, so separately built code works together. On x86-64 Linux the first integer argument arrives in RDI; on Windows x64 it arrives in RCX, so the same function compiles differently. Instruction encoding (fixed vs variable length)Defined by each ISA · Concept · Current · Intermediate How instructions are packed into bytes: x86 uses 1-15 byte variable lengths, AArch64 a fixed 4 bytes, RISC-V 4 bytes plus optional 2-byte forms. objdump -d shows 'ret' as the single byte c3 on x86-64 but as the four-byte word d65f03c0 on AArch64.

docs.title: 2.3 Assembly Language and Machine-Level Programming
docs.text:
Assembly language is the human-readable form of the instructions a CPU actually runs: one short line per instruction, such as 'add these two registers' or 'jump if equal'. Reading it shows exactly what your compiled program does with registers, memory and the call stack. You rarely write whole programs in it, but understanding it is essential for debugging, performance and security work.

A typical x86-64 stack frame. An overflowing local buffer can run upwards over the return address, which is why canaries and shadow stacks exist.

Think of it like…

If a high-level language is a recipe written for a person ('make a white sauce'), assembly is the script for a robot arm: 'pick up spoon, move 3 cm left, stir 10 times'. Every tiny step is spelled out.

Real-world example

Priya's C function add(a, b) gives wrong answers only in the release build. She opens it in Compiler Explorer and GDB and sees the x86-64 code: the arguments arrive in registers EDI and ESI, one ADD instruction combines them, and the result returns in EAX. Stepping instruction by instruction, she spots that the caller never set the second argument, so ESI still held leftover data from an earlier call.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The compiler turns each function into a sequence of instructions: loads, stores, arithmetic, compares and branches.
  2. Arguments go into registers set by the calling convention (RDI, RSI and so on for Linux x86-64; a0-a7 on RISC-V), and the result comes back in RAX or a0.
  3. A call instruction saves the return address — pushed on the stack on x86, kept in a link register on Arm and RISC-V — then jumps to the function.
  4. The function's prologue sets up a stack frame for local variables and saved registers; the epilogue undoes it and returns.
  5. Ifs and loops become a compare followed by a conditional branch that either jumps or falls through.
  6. Tools such as objdump, GDB and Compiler Explorer let you read and step through this code.

Who uses it

Systems, embedded and compiler engineers, security researchers and reverse engineers, performance engineers, and students on courses such as CS:APP and CS61C read assembly regularly.

Key takeaway

Learn to read rather than write: in interviews and debugging you mostly need to recognise loads, stores, calls, compares and branches, and know which registers hold arguments and return values.

Going deeper

  • x86-64 has 16 general-purpose 64-bit registers, RAX to R15, whose lower parts are named EAX, AX and AL; writing a 32-bit register zeroes the upper 32 bits, a frequent surprise when reading compiler output.
  • RISC-V has 32 integer registers, x0 to x31, with ABI names: x0 is hard-wired to zero, ra holds the return address, sp is the stack pointer and a0-a7 carry arguments and results.
  • The System V AMD64 ABI used by Linux and macOS passes the first six integer arguments in RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8 and R9; Windows x64 uses only RCX, RDX, R8 and R9 plus 32 bytes of 'shadow space'.
  • Addressing modes describe how an operand is found: an immediate constant, a register, or memory at base + index × scale + displacement, as in mov eax, [rbx + rcx*4 + 8] for an array element.
  • x86 compare instructions set flags (zero, sign, carry, overflow) that a later conditional jump reads; RISC-V has no flags register and branches directly on a register comparison such as beq or blt.
  • Optimised code is hard to match to source: inlining, register allocation and reordering mean variables may live only in registers, so debuggers report 'optimised out' and stepping jumps around.
  • Overwriting a return address through a stack buffer overflow was the classic exploit; defences now include stack canaries, non-executable stacks, ASLR and hardware shadow stacks such as Intel CET and Arm PAC.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Mixing up AT&T and Intel syntax: AT&T, the GCC default, writes source then destination ('addl %ebx, %eax'); Intel writes the destination first ('add eax, ebx').
  • Assuming the stack grows upwards: on x86, Arm and RISC-V it grows towards lower addresses, so pushing decreases the stack pointer.
  • Judging performance from -O0 output: unoptimised code stores every variable in memory; inspect -O2 or -O3 output instead.

docs.title: Try it: See the assembly for a tiny function (x86-64 Linux with GCC)
docs.text:
printf 'int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }\n' > add.c
gcc -O2 -S -masm=intel add.c -o -      # print Intel-syntax assembly
gcc -O2 -c add.c && objdump -d -M intel add.o   # disassemble the object file

docs.text: Name What it does Example Instruction format (opcode and operands)General CPU design; RISC-V R/I/S/B/U/J formats · Concept · Current · Beginner The bit layout of an instruction: an opcode saying what to do plus fields naming registers, constants or memory addresses. The 32-bit RISC-V instruction 'add x5, x6, x7' uses the R-type format: an opcode, three 5-bit register fields and function bits. Addressing modesGeneral CPU design · Concept · Current · Intermediate Ways an instruction locates its data: an immediate constant, a register, or a memory address built from base, index, scale and offset. 'mov eax, [rdi + rsi*4]' loads element number RSI of an int array whose start address is in RDI. Load/store vs register-memory architectureRISC (Arm, RISC-V) vs CISC (x86) · Architecture · Current · Intermediate Load/store ISAs touch memory only through load and store instructions; register-memory ISAs such as x86 let arithmetic read memory directly. x86 can do 'add eax, [rbx]' in one instruction; RISC-V needs 'lw t0, 0(a1)' followed by 'add a0, a0, t0'. x86-64 general-purpose registersIntel / AMD · Concept · Current · Intermediate Sixteen 64-bit registers, RAX to R15, with 32-, 16- and 8-bit names such as EAX, AX and AL; APX adds sixteen more. Seeing 'xor eax, eax' in a disassembly is the compiler's compact way of setting RAX to zero. RISC-V integer registers (x0-x31)RISC-V International · Concept · Current · Intermediate 32 integer registers with ABI names: zero always reads 0, ra holds return addresses, sp is the stack pointer, a0-a7 carry arguments. A RISC-V function returns its result in a0, and 'ret' is shorthand for jumping to the address held in ra. AT&T vs Intel syntaxGNU assembler / Intel · Concept · Current · Beginner Two ways of writing x86 assembly: AT&T puts the source first and prefixes registers with %, Intel puts the destination first. 'movl $5, %eax' (AT&T) and 'mov eax, 5' (Intel) are the same instruction; objdump -M intel switches between styles. Condition codes and conditional branchesGeneral CPU design · Concept · Current · Intermediate Compare instructions set flags such as zero and carry; conditional branches then jump or fall through, which is how ifs and loops work. 'cmp eax, 10' followed by 'jl loop_top' repeats a loop while EAX is less than ten. Call stack and stack frameGeneral CPU design / platform ABI · Concept · Current · Beginner A memory region, growing downwards, where each active function call keeps its return address, saved registers and local variables. A debugger backtrace listing main → parse_file → read_line shows the chain of calls that led to a crash. Function prologue and epilogueCompiler convention · Concept · Current · Intermediate Instructions at a function's start that reserve stack space and save registers, and at its end that restore them and return. 'push rbp; mov rbp, rsp; sub rsp, 32' is a classic x86-64 prologue; 'leave; ret' is the matching epilogue. Caller-saved vs callee-saved registersPlatform ABIs (System V, Windows x64, RISC-V psABI) · Concept · Current · Intermediate Rules stating which registers a called function may overwrite freely and which it must restore before returning. On Linux x86-64 a function that uses RBX must save and restore it, but may overwrite RAX and RCX freely. Stack buffer overflowMITRE CWE-121 · Concept · Current · Intermediate Writing past the end of a local array, which can overwrite saved registers and the return address and hijack the program. Reading unlimited input into a 16-byte buffer lets an attacker overwrite the return address; compilers add stack canaries to detect this. Disassemblers and decompilers (objdump, Ghidra)GNU Binutils; NSA (Ghidra, open source) · Tool · Current · Intermediate Tools that turn machine code back into assembly listings, and decompilers that reconstruct approximate C-like source code. A security analyst loads a suspicious driver into Ghidra and reads its decompiled functions to work out what it does. Debuggers (GDB and LLDB)GNU Project; LLVM Project · Tool · Current · Beginner Programs that pause a running process, set breakpoints, step through instructions and inspect registers and memory. In GDB, 'layout asm' and 'stepi' advance one instruction at a time while 'info registers' shows every register's value. RISC-V assembly simulators (RARS, Venus)Open-source teaching tools · Tool · Current · Beginner Free educational simulators that run RISC-V assembly step by step, showing how registers and memory change after each instruction. Berkeley CS61C students write and debug RISC-V functions in the Venus simulator inside a web browser.

docs.title: 2.4 Pipelines and Hazards
docs.text:
Pipelining splits each instruction into stages — fetch, decode, execute, memory, write back — so a new instruction can start every clock tick while earlier ones are still finishing. It does not make any single instruction faster, but many more complete per second. Hazards are situations where the next instruction cannot safely continue, such as needing a result that is not ready yet.

The classic 5-stage RISC pipeline. In steady state five instructions occupy the five stages and one completes every cycle.

Think of it like…

A pipeline is like a laundrette with a washer, dryer and folding table: while load one is drying, load two can be washing, so three loads are in progress at once — unless load two needs the folding table that someone else is using (a hazard).

Real-world example

Tom's textbook CPU has a 5-stage pipeline. Running 100 instructions without pipelining takes 100 × 5 = 500 cycles. With pipelining it takes 5 + (100 − 1) = 104 cycles — almost 5 times faster. But 20 of the instructions use a value loaded just before them, each causing a 1-cycle stall, so the real total is 124 cycles.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Divide instruction processing into stages separated by pipeline registers (latches); classic RISC uses IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB.
  2. Each clock tick, every instruction moves one stage forward, so up to N instructions are in flight in an N-stage pipeline.
  3. Detect hazards: structural (two instructions need the same hardware), data (an input is not ready), control (a branch outcome is unknown).
  4. Resolve them by forwarding results straight between stages, stalling (inserting bubbles), or predicting branches.
  5. Deeper pipelines allow higher clock speeds but lose more cycles on every stall or misprediction.

Who uses it

Computer-architecture students, CPU designers, compiler writers who schedule instructions and performance engineers reading profiler stall counts work with pipelines.

Key takeaway

Memorise the three hazard types — structural, data, control — and their fixes: duplicate resources, forwarding/stalls, and branch prediction.

Going deeper

  • Ideal pipeline speed-up approaches the number of stages, but real CPI = 1 + stall cycles per instruction: if 20% of instructions are loads each causing a one-cycle bubble, CPI rises to 1.2.
  • Pipelining shortens the clock period because each stage does less work, but the pipeline registers between stages add overhead, so doubling the number of stages never quite doubles the frequency.
  • WAR and WAW hazards cannot happen in the simple in-order five-stage pipeline because registers are read early and written late in order; they matter in out-of-order cores, where register renaming removes them.
  • High-performance cores have roughly 10-20 stages from fetch to execute, giving misprediction penalties of about 10-20 cycles, while small embedded cores such as Arm Cortex-M parts use only 2-8 stages.
  • Long-latency work — division, floating-point maths and cache misses — uses multi-cycle or separately pipelined units, so 'one stage per cycle for every instruction' is a teaching simplification.
  • Compilers help through instruction scheduling, placing independent instructions between a load or multiply and the instruction that uses its result; this matters most on simple in-order cores.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Believing pipelining makes each instruction faster: latency stays the same or grows slightly; only throughput improves.
  • Expecting forwarding to fix every hazard: a load's value is ready only after MEM, so a dependent instruction right behind it still stalls one cycle.
  • Assuming deeper is always better: the Pentium 4's very long pipeline lost heavily on mispredictions and ran into heat limits.

docs.title: Try it: Work out pipeline speed-up with stalls (Python)
docs.text:
stages, n = 5, 100
unpipelined = stages * n                 # 500 cycles
pipelined = stages + (n - 1)              # 104 cycles
stalls = 20 * 1                           # 20 load-use stalls of 1 cycle
print(unpipelined, pipelined + stalls)    # 500 124
print(round(unpipelined / (pipelined + stalls), 2), 'x speed-up')

docs.title: Key chips, architectures, standards, tools & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example Instruction pipelineGeneral CPU design (IBM Stretch, 1961, was an early example) · Concept · Current · Beginner Overlapping the stages of several instructions so the CPU completes roughly one per cycle instead of one per several cycles. Like a car assembly line, a 5-stage pipeline holds five instructions at different stages simultaneously. Classic 5-stage RISC pipelineHennessy & Patterson; MIPS R2000 era · Architecture · Legacy · Beginner The textbook pipeline: Instruction Fetch, Instruction Decode, EXecute, MEMory access, Write Back. Exam questions draw instructions as rows and IF-ID-EX-MEM-WB as diagonal columns across clock cycles. Structural hazardPipeline hazard type · Concept · Current · Intermediate Two instructions need the same hardware resource in the same cycle, so one must wait. With a single memory port, an instruction fetch and a data load would collide; split L1 instruction and data caches fix it. Data hazard (RAW, WAR, WAW)Pipeline hazard type · Concept · Current · Intermediate An instruction depends on a value another instruction has not yet produced (read-after-write), or reorders writes unsafely. ADD r1, r2, r3 followed by SUB r4, r1, r5 must wait for r1 — a read-after-write hazard. Control hazardPipeline hazard type · Concept · Current · Intermediate The CPU does not yet know which instruction comes next because a branch's outcome or target is still being calculated. At an if-statement the pipeline must guess or wait until the comparison finishes in the execute stage. Forwarding (bypassing)General CPU design · Technology · Current · Intermediate Extra wiring that passes a result straight from one stage to a later instruction, skipping the wait for write back. The ADD's result leaves the ALU and feeds the very next SUB in the following cycle, avoiding a two-cycle stall. Stall / pipeline bubbleGeneral CPU design · Concept · Current · Intermediate A cycle where a stage does no useful work because the pipeline is waiting for a hazard to clear. A load followed immediately by an add using its value inserts one bubble even with forwarding. Load-use hazardPipeline hazard type · Concept · Current · Advanced A special data hazard: a value loaded from memory is needed by the very next instruction before it arrives. Compilers reorder code, placing an independent instruction between the load and its use to hide the delay. Pipeline depthVaries by design · Metric · Current · Intermediate The number of stages; more stages allow higher clock speeds but cost more cycles whenever the pipeline must be flushed. Intel's Pentium 4 'Prescott' (2004) used about 31 stages and hit heat limits; later designs became shallower. Instruction latency and throughputMeasured per instruction (uops.info, Agner Fog's tables, vendor guides) · Concept · Current · Intermediate Latency is cycles until an instruction's result is ready; throughput is how many such instructions can start per cycle once the pipeline is full. uops.info lists a modern x86 floating-point multiply with about 4 cycles of latency, yet two can start every cycle. Branch delay slotMIPS, SPARC (historical) · Concept · Legacy · Advanced An early fix for control hazards: the instruction after a branch always executes, filled by the compiler with useful work. MIPS assembly often shows a NOP after a jump because nothing useful fitted the delay slot. Computer Architecture: A Quantitative ApproachJohn Hennessy & David Patterson (Morgan Kaufmann) · Resource · Current · Intermediate The standard graduate textbook on CPU design; its sibling 'Computer Organization and Design' is the undergraduate version. Most university architecture modules assign pipeline and cache exercises from the Patterson & Hennessy books. Pipeline flushGeneral CPU design · Concept · Current · Intermediate Discarding all partly processed younger instructions after a misprediction, exception or serialising event, then refilling from the correct address. A mispredicted branch flushes the instructions fetched behind it, wasting every cycle they had already spent in the pipeline. Pipeline speed-up formulaHennessy & Patterson · Concept · Current · Beginner n instructions on a k-stage pipeline take k + (n − 1) cycles plus stalls, so the speed-up approaches k for long runs. 1,000 instructions on a 5-stage pipeline take 1,004 cycles instead of 5,000 — a 4.98× speed-up with no stalls.

docs.title: 2.5 Superscalar and Out-of-Order Execution
docs.text:
Modern cores don't just pipeline — they are superscalar, meaning they start several instructions every clock tick using multiple execution units. They also run instructions out of order: whichever instruction has its inputs ready goes first, while a tracking structure makes sure results still appear in the original program order. This lets the core keep busy while one slow instruction waits for memory.

In order, out of order, in order again. Only the middle of the machine runs out of order; dispatch and retirement preserve program order.

Think of it like…

It is like a busy restaurant kitchen: orders arrive in sequence, but cooks start any dish whose ingredients are ready, and the pass (the reorder buffer) only sends plates out to tables in the order they were ordered.

Real-world example

Mei's spreadsheet macro loads a value that misses the cache and takes 300 cycles. An in-order core would sit idle the whole time. Her laptop's out-of-order core, with a reorder window of several hundred instructions, keeps executing independent additions and comparisons further ahead. When the load returns, many later instructions are already done and just wait to retire in order.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The front end fetches and decodes several instructions per cycle; x86 cores split them into simpler micro-ops.
  2. Register renaming maps the few named registers onto a large pool of physical registers, removing false dependencies.
  3. Micro-ops wait in a scheduler (reservation stations) until their inputs are ready, then issue to any free execution unit.
  4. Results are recorded in the reorder buffer (ROB), which tracks original program order.
  5. Instructions retire (commit) strictly in order; if something went wrong, such as an exception or misprediction, younger work is thrown away.

Who uses it

CPU microarchitects, compiler and JIT engineers, game and HPC performance tuners, and security researchers studying speculative attacks work with these mechanisms.

Key takeaway

Remember: out-of-order execution, in-order retirement — the ROB is what makes the out-of-order chaos look sequential to software.

Going deeper

  • Reorder-buffer size sets how far ahead a core can look: high-end 2024-26 cores track several hundred micro-ops in flight, enough to keep working past multiple cache misses at once.
  • The biggest win is memory-level parallelism: by starting independent loads early, an out-of-order core can have many cache misses outstanding at the same time, tracked in miss-status holding registers (MSHRs).
  • Load-store queues let loads run ahead of older stores whose addresses are still unknown; a memory-dependence predictor guesses when that is safe, and the core replays the load if it guessed wrong.
  • Precise exceptions come from in-order retirement: when an instruction faults, everything older has committed and everything younger is discarded, so the operating system sees a clean, sequential state.
  • Out-of-order hardware costs area and power — wake-up and select logic grows quickly with window size — which is why efficiency cores and microcontrollers stay in-order or only narrowly out-of-order.
  • Apple's performance cores were among the first widely shipped 8-wide decode designs, starting with the M1 in 2020, and rival x86 and Arm designs have since widened their front ends as well.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking out-of-order execution can change program results: retirement is in order, so a single thread always sees sequential behaviour.
  • Assuming a bigger window fixes everything: a long dependency chain, where each step needs the previous result, cannot run in parallel however wide the core is.
  • Confusing superscalar (several instructions per cycle from one thread) with multicore or SMT (several threads running at once).

docs.text:
# Linux: count cycles and instructions for any command
perf stat -e cycles,instructions,branches,branch-misses -- python3 -c "sum(range(10**7))"
# 'insn per cycle' in the output is IPC; modern cores can exceed 4 on friendly code

A load from array[i] runs before an earlier store to array[j]; if j turns out to equal i, the core replays the load. Walking a linked list allows only one miss at a time, while scanning an array lets the core overlap many — often several times faster.

docs.title: 2.6 Branch Prediction and Speculative Execution
docs.text:
Programs are full of decisions (if-statements and loops), but a deep pipeline cannot wait to find out which way each one goes. So the CPU guesses — branch prediction — and keeps working down the guessed path, called speculative execution. If the guess was right, time is saved; if wrong, the work is thrown away and restarted, costing many cycles.

Predict, speculate, verify. A wrong guess costs a pipeline flush of roughly 10-20 cycles on a modern high-performance core.

Think of it like…

It is like a sat-nav that starts directing you onto the motorway before the traffic report arrives: usually correct, but if the road turns out closed you must U-turn and lose time.

Real-world example

Ravi sorts an array of random numbers before counting values above 128 and his loop gets several times faster. Unsorted, the if-test is a coin toss, so the predictor is wrong about half the time and each mistake costs roughly 15-20 cycles. Sorted, the branch goes the same way for long runs and the predictor is right over 99% of the time. Same instructions, very different speed.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. When fetching a branch, the predictor guesses taken or not-taken using history of past outcomes; a branch target buffer supplies the target address.
  2. The core fetches and executes along the predicted path speculatively, without making results permanent.
  3. When the branch actually resolves, the guess is checked.
  4. Correct guess: the speculative work retires normally. Wrong guess: the pipeline is flushed and fetching restarts on the right path.
  5. Side effects of discarded work (like data pulled into the cache) can remain — the root of Spectre-style attacks.

Who uses it

CPU architects, compiler engineers, game and trading-system developers squeezing latency, and security engineers patching speculative-execution vulnerabilities care about prediction.

Key takeaway

Spectre tricks the branch predictor into speculatively reading secrets; Meltdown abused speculative loads ignoring privilege checks — know that difference.

Going deeper

  • Branches are frequent — roughly one instruction in five to seven in typical integer code — so even a 95%-accurate predictor mispredicts every hundred or so instructions and can waste a large share of cycles.
  • Modern predictors combine components: TAGE-style tables for direction, perceptron predictors (used in AMD cores), loop predictors, indirect-target predictors and a return stack buffer for function returns.
  • Indirect branches — virtual calls, switch tables and interpreter dispatch — need a predicted target address, not just taken or not-taken; Spectre variant 2 (branch target injection) abused exactly this predictor.
  • Software can help: profile-guided optimisation lays out the likely path, C++20 [[likely]] and [[unlikely]] or __builtin_expect give hints, and branchless code removes unpredictable branches entirely.
  • Speculation goes beyond branches: cores also predict memory dependences, which is why later attacks such as Speculative Store Bypass (Spectre variant 4) targeted other predictors.
  • Mitigations cost performance: KPTI adds overhead to system calls and retpolines slow indirect calls, but newer CPUs fix many issues in hardware (for example enhanced IBRS), recovering most of the loss.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming sorted data is always faster to process: sorting helps only when a data-dependent branch was unpredictable, and sorting itself costs time.
  • Turning off speculation mitigations for speed on shared or multi-tenant machines: this reopens real cross-tenant data-leak risks.
  • Believing branchless code always wins: a well-predicted branch can beat a conditional move, which must wait for both inputs.

docs.title: Try it: Check your CPU's speculative-execution mitigations (Linux)
docs.text:
grep . /sys/devices/system/cpu/vulnerabilities/*
# e.g. spectre_v2: Mitigation: Enhanced / Automatic IBRS ...
#      meltdown:   Not affected
# Windows: the Get-SpeculationControlSettings PowerShell module reports similar info

docs.text: Name What it does Example Branch predictorGeneral CPU design · Component · Current · Intermediate Hardware that guesses the direction of conditional branches before they are computed, so the pipeline never waits. Modern predictors guess correctly well over 95% of the time on typical code like loop counters. Static branch predictionEarly CPUs; compiler hints · Concept · Legacy · Intermediate Fixed guessing rules such as 'backward branches are taken' (loops) and 'forward branches are not taken'. Without history, a loop's closing branch is guessed taken, which is right on every iteration except the last. Two-bit saturating counterClassic dynamic predictor (J. E. Smith, 1981) · Concept · Current · Intermediate A tiny counter per branch that must be wrong twice in a row before it changes its prediction. A loop exit mispredicts only once instead of twice because one surprise does not flip the counter. If 'x > 0' was true, a later 'x != 0' check is predicted true too, using shared history. TAGE predictorAndré Seznec & Pierre Michaud (2006) · Architecture · Current · Advanced A state-of-the-art predictor combining tables indexed by different history lengths; its ideas inspire many modern cores. Branch-prediction championship winners and many high-end commercial cores use TAGE-like designs. Branch target buffer (BTB)General CPU design · Component · Current · Advanced A cache that remembers where branches jump to, so the next fetch address is known immediately. A virtual function call through a pointer is redirected quickly because the BTB recalls its last target. Return stack bufferGeneral CPU design · Component · Current · Advanced A small hardware stack predicting function return addresses by mirroring call instructions. Deep recursion beyond the buffer's depth causes return mispredictions and slows the code. A hot loop with one unpredictable branch per iteration can spend more time recovering than computing. Speculative executionGeneral CPU design · Concept · Current · Intermediate Executing instructions before it is certain they are needed, then committing or discarding them later. The core runs the 'then' block of an if-statement while the condition's data is still loading. SpectreDisclosed Jan 2018 by Google Project Zero and academic researchers (CVE-2017-5753, CVE-2017-5715) · Concept · Current · Advanced A family of attacks training the predictor so speculation reads secret data, then leaking it through cache timing. A malicious script could, in principle, read another part of the browser's memory; browsers isolated sites per process as a defence. MeltdownDisclosed Jan 2018 (CVE-2017-5754) · Concept · Legacy · Advanced An attack where speculative loads ignored privilege checks, letting user programs read kernel memory on affected CPUs. Operating systems added KPTI page-table isolation; newer CPUs are fixed in hardware. Speculation mitigations (KPTI, retpoline, IBRS)Linux, Windows, Intel, AMD, Arm, Google (retpoline) · Technology · Current · Advanced Software and microcode defences that isolate kernel memory, restrict predictors or avoid exploitable indirect branches. A cloud provider applies microcode and kernel updates so tenants on shared hosts cannot leak each other's data. AMD's Zen cores include perceptron-based prediction, which captures long-range patterns that simple two-bit counters miss. A bytecode interpreter's dispatch jump runs fast only because the indirect predictor learns common opcode sequences.

docs.title: 2.7 CPU Caches: L1, L2, L3 and How They Work
docs.text:
Main memory (RAM) is roughly a hundred times slower than the CPU core, so chips keep small, very fast copies of recently used data in caches right next to the core. There are usually three levels: a tiny, ultra-fast L1, a larger L2 and a big shared L3. If the data is in a cache it is a 'hit' and arrives quickly; if not, a 'miss' means a slow trip to RAM.

Looking up an address in a set-associative cache. Example: a 32 KB, 8-way cache with 64-byte lines has 64 sets, so 6 offset bits and 6 index bits.

Think of it like…

Caches are like a student's desk, bookshelf and the campus library: the desk (L1) holds what you're using right now, the shelf (L2/L3) holds recent books, and a trip to the library (RAM) takes far longer.

Real-world example

Sofia's image filter walks a 4000 × 4000 pixel array row by row and runs in 40 ms. Her classmate's version walks it column by column and takes about 300 ms. Row order uses every byte of each 64-byte cache line it loads; column order jumps thousands of bytes each step, so almost every access misses. Same maths, very different cache behaviour.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Memory is moved in fixed blocks called cache lines, typically 64 bytes on x86 and most Arm cores.
  2. On each access the core checks L1, then L2, then L3; the first level holding the line returns it.
  3. Each address can only live in a limited set of slots (set associativity); when the set is full a replacement policy evicts a line.
  4. Writes usually go to the cache first and reach RAM later when the line is evicted (write-back).
  5. Hardware prefetchers spot patterns, such as stepping through an array, and fetch lines before they are requested.

Who uses it

Performance engineers, game and database developers, HPC programmers and anyone optimising code or sizing servers needs to understand caches.

Key takeaway

Rough latencies worth memorising: L1 about 1 ns, L2 a few ns, L3 roughly 10-20 ns, DRAM around 80-100 ns — locality is everything.

Going deeper

  • An address splits into offset (log2 of the line size), index (log2 of the number of sets) and tag; many L1 caches are virtually indexed but physically tagged, so lookup starts before address translation finishes.
  • Typical 2026 sizes: L1 data 32-64 KB per core; L2 about 1-3 MB per x86 core (larger shared L2s on Apple chips); L3 from about 16 MB in laptops to hundreds of MB in servers with stacked cache.
  • Most data caches are write-allocate and write-back: a store miss first fetches the line, then modifies it; non-temporal (streaming) stores bypass the cache for data that will not be reused soon.
  • Large L3s are split into slices, one per core or cluster, joined by a ring or mesh; an address hash spreads lines across slices, so L3 latency varies a little with distance.
  • Prefetchers detect next-line, stride and stream patterns at L1 and L2; they hide latency for regular access but waste bandwidth on random access, and software prefetch instructions exist for tricky cases.
  • Cache-aware coding — blocking (tiling) loops, structure-of-arrays layouts and keeping hot data compact — often gives bigger speed-ups than any compiler flag.
  • Inclusion policies changed over time: Intel server L3s moved from inclusive to non-inclusive with Skylake-SP, while AMD's L3s act mainly as victim caches filled by lines evicted from L2.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Choosing data structures by big-O alone: a linked list with O(1) inserts often loses to an array because each node visit can miss the cache.
  • Benchmarking with tiny inputs that fit in L1 or L2, then being surprised when production-sized data runs far slower.
  • Assuming 64-byte lines everywhere: Apple M-series chips use 128-byte lines, so padding against false sharing must match the platform.
  • Expecting more cache to always help: once the working set fits, extra cache adds nothing, and memory bandwidth becomes the limit instead.

docs.title: Try it: Cache-stride experiment in C — watch time per access jump
docs.text:
// stride.c   build: gcc -O2 stride.c -o stride   run: ./stride
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <time.h>
int main(void){
  size_t n = 64u<<20;               /* 64 MB array */
  char *a = malloc(n);
  for (size_t i=0;i<n;i++) a[i]=1;
  for (size_t s=1; s<=512; s*=2){
    clock_t t=clock(); long sum=0;
    for (size_t i=0;i<n;i+=s) sum+=a[i];
    double ns = 1e9*(double)(clock()-t)/CLOCKS_PER_SEC/(n/s);
    printf("stride %4zu: %.2f ns/access (%ld)\n", s, ns, sum);
  }
  return 0;
}
// Expect a big jump once stride passes 64 bytes: each access then needs a new cache line.
// lscpu --caches   (Linux) shows your L1/L2/L3 sizes

docs.text: Name What it does Example Memory hierarchyGeneral computer architecture · Concept · Current · Beginner Layers of storage trading speed for size: registers, L1, L2, L3 caches, DRAM, then SSD — each bigger but slower. A core reads a register in under a nanosecond but waits around 100 ns for DRAM and microseconds for an SSD. L1 cacheEvery modern CPU core · Component · Current · Beginner The smallest, fastest cache inside each core, usually split into instruction (L1i) and data (L1d), tens of kilobytes each. A typical recent core has around 32-64 KB L1 data cache answering in about 4-5 cycles. L2 cacheEvery modern CPU core or core cluster · Component · Current · Beginner A larger, slightly slower cache, often private to one core (or shared by a small cluster on Arm and Apple designs). Many current x86 cores have 1-3 MB of L2 each, catching most L1 misses within roughly 15 cycles. L3 / last-level cache (LLC)Shared cache on most desktop and server chips · Component · Current · Beginner A big cache, megabytes to hundreds of megabytes, shared by many cores before requests go out to DRAM. AMD's X3D chips stack extra L3 on the die, which games with large working sets love. Cache lineTypically 64 bytes (x86, most Arm); 128 bytes on Apple M-series · Concept · Current · Intermediate The fixed-size block in which data moves between memory and caches; touching one byte loads the whole line. Reading int arr[0] also brings arr[1] to arr[15] into L1, so the next 15 reads are almost free. Cache hit, miss and hit rateGeneral computer architecture · Metric · Current · Beginner A hit finds data in the cache; a miss must go further down. Hit rate is the percentage of hits. A database tuned from 90% to 98% L3 hit rate saw query time fall because far fewer requests reached DRAM. Three Cs of cache missesMark Hill (1987) · Concept · Current · Intermediate Misses classified as compulsory (first touch), capacity (cache too small) or conflict (too many lines mapping to one set). Doubling cache size cuts capacity misses but cannot remove compulsory misses on brand-new data. Set associativityGeneral cache design · Concept · Current · Intermediate How many slots an address may occupy: direct-mapped (one), N-way set-associative (N) or fully associative (any). An 8-way 32 KB cache with 64-byte lines has 64 sets, each holding up to 8 lines. Replacement policy (LRU, pseudo-LRU)General cache design · Concept · Current · Intermediate The rule for which line to evict when a set is full; least-recently-used or a cheaper approximation is common. Scanning a huge file once can flush useful data under pure LRU, so modern caches use smarter variants. Write-back vs write-throughGeneral cache design · Concept · Current · Intermediate Write-back updates only the cache and writes to memory on eviction; write-through updates memory every time. CPU data caches are write-back with a 'dirty' bit, saving huge amounts of memory traffic in tight loops. Inclusive, exclusive and non-inclusive cachesDesign choice (e.g. AMD L3 is largely a victim/exclusive cache) · Concept · Current · Advanced Whether a lower cache level must also hold copies of everything in upper levels (inclusive) or never duplicates them (exclusive). An exclusive L3 wastes no space on L2 duplicates, so total usable cache is larger. Hardware prefetcherGeneral CPU design · Component · Current · Intermediate Logic that detects access patterns and loads cache lines before the program asks for them. Summing a large array sequentially runs near full memory bandwidth because the prefetcher stays ahead. Locality of referenceGeneral computer science · Concept · Current · Beginner Programs tend to reuse recent data (temporal locality) and nearby data (spatial locality) — the reason caches work. Iterating a 2D array in row-major order in C exploits spatial locality; column order destroys it. AMAT (Average Memory Access Time)Hennessy & Patterson · Metric · Current · Intermediate Hit time plus miss rate times miss penalty — a formula for estimating how fast memory appears on average. 1 ns hit + 5% × 80 ns miss penalty = 5 ns AMAT; halving misses gives 3 ns. Tag, index and offsetGeneral cache design · Concept · Current · Intermediate The three fields an address splits into: the offset picks a byte within the line, the index picks the set, the tag identifies the line. With 64-byte lines and 64 sets, the low 6 address bits are the offset, the next 6 bits the index and the rest the tag.

docs.title: 2.8 Cache Coherence and Memory Ordering
docs.text:
When several cores each have their own cache, two of them might hold different copies of the same memory. Cache coherence is the set of hardware rules that keep every core seeing one consistent value, by tracking who owns each cache line and telling others when it changes. Memory ordering rules then define in which order one core's writes become visible to another.

MESI in action: two cores share line X. A write needs exclusive ownership, so every other copy is invalidated first.

Think of it like…

Coherence is like a shared online document: if one person edits a paragraph, everyone else's copy must be refreshed before they rely on it, otherwise people argue from stale versions.

Real-world example

Kofi writes a multithreaded counter where 8 threads each update their own variable, but the variables sit next to each other in one 64-byte cache line. Every update forces the line to bounce between cores, and the program runs slower with 8 threads than with 1. Padding each counter to its own 64-byte line fixes this 'false sharing' and the program scales nearly 8 times.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Every cache line carries a state, for example Modified, Exclusive, Shared or Invalid (MESI).
  2. Before a core writes, it must gain exclusive ownership; other caches' copies are invalidated.
  3. Caches learn about others' actions by snooping on a shared broadcast, or via a directory that records which cores hold each line.
  4. A core reading a line another core modified gets the fresh data from that core or from memory.
  5. Separately, the ISA's memory model plus fences and atomic instructions decide the visible order of reads and writes across cores.

Who uses it

Systems and kernel programmers, authors of lock-free data structures, game-engine and database developers and server CPU architects deal with coherence and ordering.

Key takeaway

If a parallel program gets slower as you add threads, suspect false sharing or lock contention first.

Going deeper

  • Coherence and consistency are different questions: coherence concerns a single address (all cores agree on the order of its writes); consistency concerns the order of accesses to different addresses.
  • Coherence traffic costs real time: moving a contended cache line between cores on one chip takes tens of nanoseconds and between sockets often over 100 ns — the hidden price of heavily shared counters and locks.
  • x86-TSO permits essentially one visible reordering — a later load passing an earlier store to a different address via the store buffer — so Dekker-style flag code still needs MFENCE or a locked instruction.
  • Language memory models (C11/C++11, Java, Rust) hide hardware differences: std::atomic with memory_order_acquire and memory_order_release compiles to the right barriers on x86, Arm and RISC-V automatically.
  • Armv8 added load-acquire (LDAR) and store-release (STLR) instructions, and Armv8.1 added LSE atomics such as CAS and LDADD, which scale much better than exclusive-load/store retry loops on many-core servers.
  • Directory-based protocols scale coherence to hundreds of cores and multiple sockets, and links such as CXL and NVLink-C2C extend coherent memory sharing to accelerators and memory expanders.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Using volatile for thread synchronisation in C or C++: it gives neither atomicity nor ordering; use std::atomic or proper locks.
  • Testing lock-free code only on x86: its strong ordering hides bugs that appear on weakly ordered Arm and RISC-V machines.
  • Padding every variable to 64 bytes 'just in case': it wastes cache space; pad only data that different threads write frequently.

docs.title: Try it: Avoid false sharing by padding per-thread counters (C11)
docs.text:
#include <stdalign.h>
struct counter {
    alignas(64) long value;   /* each counter gets its own 64-byte cache line */
};
struct counter per_thread[8];  /* threads 0..7 no longer fight over one line */
// C++17 alternative: alignas(std::hardware_destructive_interference_size)

docs.text: Name What it does Example Cache coherenceGeneral multiprocessor design · Concept · Current · Intermediate Hardware guarantees that all cores see a single, up-to-date value for each memory location despite private caches. Core 0 sets ready = 1; coherence ensures core 3 eventually sees 1, not a stale 0 in its own cache. MESI protocolClassic protocol (Papamarcos & Patel, 1984) · Standard · Current · Intermediate A coherence protocol with four line states: Modified, Exclusive, Shared and Invalid. When core A writes a Shared line, other copies become Invalid and A's copy becomes Modified. MOESI and MESIFAMD (MOESI); Intel (MESIF) · Standard · Current · Advanced MESI variants adding Owned (share dirty data without writing to memory) or Forward (one sharer answers requests). With MOESI, an AMD core can supply a modified line directly to another core without updating DRAM first. Snooping protocolGeneral multiprocessor design · Technology · Current · Intermediate Each cache watches a shared bus or broadcast for others' requests and reacts to keep copies consistent. Small multicore chips broadcast 'I want to write line X' and every cache checks whether it holds X. Directory-based coherenceGeneral multiprocessor design · Technology · Current · Advanced A directory records which caches hold each line, so messages go only to those cores instead of broadcasting. Many-core server chips and multi-socket systems use directories or snoop filters because broadcasting to hundreds of cores would swamp the interconnect. Snoop filterIntel, AMD, Arm server designs · Component · Current · Advanced A structure tracking which lines private caches might hold, filtering out needless coherence checks. A 128-core server avoids probing every core's cache on each L3 miss thanks to its snoop filter.
